desc: Cross-sectional bubble chart comparing all assets over time. Each asset becomes a separate bubble series plotted over timestamps (X axis). Y axis shows the input values, bubble size encodes absolute magnitude (|y|). Use for comparing value magnitudes across assets over time — larger bubbles highlight periods of extreme returns, volume, or P&L.

inputs.name: Size Values (per asset, defaults to |y| if omitted)

usageContext: TRIGGER PHRASES: Use when the user asks for 'compare asset bubbles over time', 'magnitude comparison', 'bubble chart across assets', 'which assets had the largest moves', 'volume bubble comparison'. Plot a BUBBLE CHART comparing ALL assets over time in the DASHBOARD view. Each asset becomes a separate bubble series. X-axis = timestamps (automatically derived from the DataFrame index). Y-axis = first input values. Z (bubble size) = second input if provided (e.g., volume), otherwise |y|. Larger values produce larger bubbles. CS_BUBBLE vs BUBBLE: bubble (non-CS) takes EXPLICIT x/y/z columns for a single asset with full control over all three dimensions. cs_bubble DERIVES Z from |y| automatically and uses timestamps as X. Use bubble when you have three distinct metrics. Use cs_bubble when you want to compare value magnitudes across assets over time. CS_BUBBLE vs CS_SCATTER: cs_scatter shows position only (no size encoding). cs_bubble adds size as a third dimension. Use cs_scatter for simple position comparison. Use cs_bubble when value MAGNITUDE matters and should be visually emphasized via bubble size. CS_BUBBLE vs CS_LINES: cs_lines connects points (time series). cs_bubble shows disconnected points with size encoding. Use cs_lines when the trend over time is the focus. Use cs_bubble when the magnitude at each point matters more than the connection between points. CONFIGURATION: 'min_size' and 'max_size' control the bubble size range (default: 8px min, 20% max). 'max_assets' limits the number of asset series (default: 20). 'asset_filter' can restrict which assets appear. EXAMPLES: (1) Return magnitude over time: y=daily_returns. Larger bubbles = larger absolute returns (up or down). Visually highlights volatile periods per asset. (2) Volume comparison: y=trading_volume. Each asset = series of bubbles showing volume over time. Large bubbles = high-activity periods. (3) P&L tracking: y=daily_pnl, y_axis_format=MonetaryFormat. See which assets had the largest absolute P&L impacts.
limitations: Multi-asset only (isCrossSectional=true). Takes ONE input (y). Z is ALWAYS |y| — bubble size is automatically derived from the absolute value of y. You cannot provide a custom Z column (unlike non-CS bubble which takes explicit x/y/z). X-axis is always timestamps — you cannot use a custom X metric. Null values are replaced with 0.0 (not filtered) — this means null data points appear as zero-value bubbles at minimum size. max_assets defaults to 20 — excess assets are silently truncated. No aggregation mode — each data point is plotted individually (unlike cs_scatter which supports XY aggregation).

usageContext: TRIGGER PHRASES: Use when the user asks for 'labeled asset scatter', 'risk-return map with names', 'which asset is where', 'factor map with labels', 'identify assets on scatter', 'named scatter comparison'. Plot a LABELED SCATTER CHART where EACH ASSET becomes a NAMED POINT. Unlike cs_scatter which shows anonymous points, cs_labeled_scatter automatically labels each point with the asset name — ideal for identifying which asset is which in risk-return maps, factor comparisons, and cross-sectional snapshots. desc: Scatter chart comparing all assets. With 1 input: each asset becomes a series over time (X=timestamps, Y=values). With 2 inputs (x, y): each asset becomes a single aggregated point at (agg(x), agg(y)). Supports Mean, Median, Sum, Last, and other aggregation functions. Asset count limited by max_assets (default 20).

inputs.name: X Values (or single value in simple mode)

usageContext: Plot a SCATTER CHART comparing ALL assets in a single visualization in the DASHBOARD view. Supports TWO MODES depending on the number of inputs: MODE 1 — XY AGGREGATION (2 inputs: x + y): Each asset's x and y time series are aggregated using the 'agg' function (default: Mean), producing ONE point per asset at (agg(x), agg(y)). This is ideal for cross-sectional snapshots like 'mean return vs mean volatility per asset'. The result is a single scatter series named 'Assets'. MODE 2 — SIMPLE TIME SERIES (1 input: x only): Each asset becomes a separate scatter series. X-axis = timestamps (as numeric), Y-axis = values. Each asset traces its path through time as unconnected scatter points. TRIGGER PHRASES: Use when the user asks for 'compare assets scatter', 'cross-sectional scatter', 'scatter all assets', 'asset comparison plot', 'scatter comparison', 'which assets cluster together', 'factor map across assets'. CS_SCATTER vs XY_SCATTER: xy_scatter is for a SINGLE asset with multiple Y metrics. cs_scatter is for MULTIPLE assets in one chart. Use xy_scatter for 'plot risk vs return for AAPL'. Use cs_scatter for 'plot risk vs return for ALL assets'. CS_SCATTER vs CS_BUBBLE: cs_scatter encodes TWO dimensions (position only). cs_bubble adds a THIRD dimension via bubble size. Use cs_scatter when two metrics suffice. Use cs_bubble when a third metric (e.g., market cap, trading volume) should be visible as size. CS_SCATTER vs CS_BOXPLOT: cs_scatter shows individual or aggregated points per asset. cs_boxplot shows distributional summaries (quartiles, outliers). Use cs_scatter for relationship analysis. Use cs_boxplot for distribution comparison. CONFIGURATION: 'agg' controls the aggregation function in XY mode (Mean, Median, Sum, Last, Min, Max, etc.). 'max_assets' limits the number of assets displayed (default: 20). 'asset_filter' can filter which assets appear. EXAMPLES: (1) Risk-return map: x=volatility, y=return, agg=Mean. Each asset = one point. Clusters reveal asset groupings. x_axis_format=PercentFormat, y_axis_format=PercentFormat. (2) Factor scatter: x=beta, y=alpha. See which assets have high alpha for their beta level. (3) Simple mode: x=daily_returns (1 input only). Each asset shows its return time series as scatter points. Useful for spotting outlier days per asset.
limitations: Multi-asset only (isCrossSectional=true). In XY mode, each asset is reduced to a SINGLE point via aggregation — all temporal detail is lost. In simple mode, X-axis is raw timestamp numeric values (nanoseconds), which may not be human-readable without axis formatting. No per-asset colors or markers in XY mode — all assets share the same styling (single 'Assets' series). In simple mode, each asset is a separate series with default colors. max_assets defaults to 20 — excess assets are truncated. No point labels showing asset names in XY mode.

desc: Boxplot comparing distributions across ALL assets on one chart. Simple mode: one box per asset. Multi-metric mode: multiple boxes per asset (one per metric via metric_names option).
usageContext: Compare DISTRIBUTIONS ACROSS ALL ASSETS as side-by-side boxplots in the DASHBOARD view. Each asset gets one box (or multiple boxes in multi-metric mode), showing Q1, median, Q3, whiskers, and outliers. This is the standard cross-asset distributional comparison chart — the multi-asset counterpart to histogram. TRIGGER PHRASES: Use when the user asks for 'compare distributions across assets', 'cross-sectional boxplot', 'boxplot per asset', 'which assets have higher spread', 'outlier comparison across stocks', 'asset return distributions side by side', 'compare volatility distributions', 'universe distribution overview', 'dispersion across assets', 'which stocks have more outliers', 'median comparison'. TWO MODES: (A) Simple mode: one scalar input per asset → one box per asset. The cross-sectional execution provides one column per asset automatically, where each column contains the full time series of that asset's values. Each column's values are summarized as a box. This is the default and most common mode. (B) Multi-metric mode: struct input with N fields + metric_names option → N boxes per asset. Useful for comparing distributions of return AND volatility simultaneously across all assets (each asset gets a 'return' box and a 'volatility' box). KEY CHOICE - cs_boxplot vs cs_bars: cs_boxplot shows the FULL DISTRIBUTION of each asset's time series (spread, quartiles, outliers). cs_bars shows ONE AGGREGATED VALUE per asset (mean, sum, last). Use cs_boxplot when distributional shape matters (is AAPL more volatile than MSFT?). Use cs_bars when a single summary number suffices (which stock returned the most?). KEY CHOICE - cs_boxplot vs cs_summary_table: cs_boxplot gives a VISUAL distributional comparison — you see median position, box width (IQR), and outlier dots at a glance. cs_summary_table gives EXACT NUMBERS in a grid. Best practice: pair cs_boxplot with cs_summary_table showing the same metrics — the boxplot for visual intuition, the table for precise values. KEY CHOICE - cs_boxplot vs histogram: histogram shows the FULL SHAPE of ONE series (skew, modality, kurtosis). cs_boxplot summarizes MANY series compactly side by side. Use histogram when shape detail matters for a single asset. Use cs_boxplot when comparing across 5+ assets where individual histograms would be overwhelming. KEY CHOICE - cs_boxplot vs cs_heatmap: Both compare metrics across assets. cs_heatmap uses color intensity on a grid — best for two-dimensional comparisons (assets × time periods or assets × metrics). cs_boxplot shows distributional detail (quartiles, outliers) — best when spread and outliers are the insight. EXAMPLES: (1) Return distribution comparison: values=daily_returns. One box per asset showing the full distribution of daily returns. Wider boxes = more volatile. Higher median = better central tendency. Outlier dots reveal extreme move days. max_assets=20 to keep the chart readable. (2) Volatility dispersion: values=rolling_volatility (e.g., 20-day). Shows how stable each asset's volatility is over time — narrow box = steady volatility, wide box = volatility-of-volatility (important for options traders). (3) Multi-metric comparison: metric_names=['Return','Volatility'], values=(daily_returns, rolling_vol). Each asset gets two boxes side by side. Reveals whether high-return assets are also high-volatility (risk-return tradeoff visual). (4) Drawdown severity comparison: values=drawdown_depth. Shows which assets have deeper drawdowns (more negative medians) and more extreme tail events (outlier dots). Pair with cs_summary_table showing max drawdown, avg drawdown, recovery time. (5) Factor exposure dispersion: values=momentum_score. Shows how concentrated or dispersed momentum is across the universe. Narrow boxes mean similar momentum; wide boxes mean heterogeneous momentum exposure.
limitations: Dashboard widget, not the TV chart. Does not show the full distribution shape per asset — for detailed shape analysis (bimodality, skewness) of a single asset use histogram. Each asset is reduced to a five-number summary + outliers. For single aggregated values per asset (mean, sum) use cs_bars or cs_summary_table. For single-asset grouped analysis use boxplot (per-asset variant). Chart becomes crowded with too many assets — use max_assets and filters to limit to 20-30 meaningful boxes. No kernel density or histogram overlay per asset — use separate histograms in the same dashboard category for selected assets if detailed shape is needed.

desc: Bar chart comparing all assets on the X-axis in the dashboard. Simple mode: one bar per asset. Stacked mode: struct (value, label) input creates grouped/stacked bars per asset. Use for ranking, comparison, decomposition.
usageContext: Compare a metric across all assets as a bar chart in the DASHBOARD view. Each asset gets one bar on the X-axis, with bar length encoding magnitude for instant visual ranking. The cross-sectional execution provides one column per asset automatically. TWO MODES: (A) Simple mode: one scalar input per asset → one bar per asset. The values input is time-aggregated via 'agg' (Last, Mean, Sum, etc.) to produce a single bar height. (B) Stacked mode: struct input with (value, label) fields → stacked bars per asset. Each unique label becomes a separate bar series. Auto-stacks to NormalStack when multiple labels are detected (NoStack is overridden). Use stack_type=Percent for 100% stacked composition view. KEY CHOICE - cs_bars vs cs_summary_table: cs_bars is for VISUAL magnitude comparison where bar length makes relative size instantly readable (which stock had highest return? which sector has most weight?). cs_summary_table is for EXACT numbers in a grid where the user needs to read precise values. Best practice: pair cs_bars with cs_summary_table in the same dashboard category — bars for the visual, table for the detail. KEY CHOICE - cs_bars vs cs_lines: cs_bars shows ONE aggregated value per asset (a snapshot). cs_lines shows the FULL CURVE per asset over time. Use cs_bars when the question is 'which asset has the highest X right now?' Use cs_lines when the question is 'how did each asset's X evolve over time?' KEY CHOICE - cs_bars vs cs_cards: cs_bars shows per-asset values visually (N bars for N assets). cs_cards collapses ALL assets into a single aggregate number. Use cs_bars to see individual asset differences, cs_cards for universe-level headlines. FEATURES: color_by_value=true colors bars green (positive) and red (negative). Per-bar colors via 'colors' option. Vertical/horizontal orientation. max_assets limits displayed bars. Asset filtering narrows the displayed universe. EXAMPLES: (1) Return ranking: values=ytd_return, agg=Last, color_by_value=true. Bars sorted by magnitude show which assets outperformed (green) and underperformed (red). Pair with cs_summary_table for exact numbers. (2) Factor exposure decomposition: values=(momentum, value, quality) as struct, agg=Last, stack_type=Normal. Stacked bars show each asset's composite factor profile. Helps PMs identify concentrated factor bets in the portfolio. (3) Sector allocation vs benchmark: values=(portfolio_weight, benchmark_weight) as struct, agg=Last. Grouped bars show over/underweight per sector at a glance. (4) Top/bottom performers: values=monthly_return, agg=Sum, color_by_value=true, max_assets=20. Quick screening chart for portfolio review meetings.
limitations: Dashboard widget, not the TV chart. Does not support lazy loading or large datasets. Each asset is reduced to one bar (or one stacked group) — cannot show how values evolved over time (use cs_lines for curves). Cannot show exact numbers on bars clearly when there are many assets (use cs_summary_table alongside). Stacked mode requires struct input with (value, label) fields. For single-asset categorical analysis use xy_bars. For distribution shape analysis use cs_boxplot.

usageContext: TRIGGER PHRASES: Use when the user asks for 'compare equity curves', 'multi-asset line chart', 'overlay returns', 'cumulative return comparison', 'line chart across assets', 'which asset performed best over time'. Plot lines comparing a metric across multiple assets in the DASHBOARD view (not the TV chart). Each asset gets its own line on a shared X-axis. The cross-sectional execution provides one column per asset automatically, where each column contains struct(x, y) data. X values can be numeric (doubles) OR timestamps - timestamp X values are automatically detected and converted to milliseconds with the axis set to datetime mode, just like xy_lines. ASSET FILTERING: Use 'filters' to rank and select assets (e.g., top 10 by return, bottom 5 by volatility). Chain multiple filters with AND/OR operators. 'max_assets' limits the total number of lines after filtering (default 20). AGGREGATION MODE: Set 'agg' to collapse all asset lines into a SINGLE aggregated line. At each X position, Y values from all assets are collected and aggregated (e.g., Mean, Median, Sum). By default aggregation uses ALL assets; set 'agg_filtered=true' to aggregate only the filtered subset. This is useful for showing the universe average or median curve. KEY DIFFERENCE from cs_cards / cs_summary_table: Those reports COLLAPSE each asset's time series to a single aggregated value (cs_cards via two-stage agg, cs_summary_table via per-asset agg). cs_lines PRESERVES full row-level granularity - it plots every (x, y) point for each asset (or the aggregated curve). Use cs_lines when the user needs to see the full CURVE, not just the endpoint. EXAMPLES: (1) Cumulative return comparison: x_values=timestamp, y_values=cumulative_return. Each asset gets a line showing its equity curve over time. The timestamp X-axis is automatically detected and formatted. Use filters=[{rank=top, count=10, column=0}] to show only the top 10 performers. (2) Universe average curve: x_values=timestamp, y_values=cumulative_return, agg=Mean. Produces a single line showing the average cumulative return across all assets in the universe. (3) Rolling Sharpe comparison: x_values=rolling_window_size (10,20,30,...90), y_values=rolling_sharpe. Each asset gets a line showing how Sharpe stability changes with lookback window. (4) Filtered median sensitivity: x_values=parameter_value, y_values=backtest_metric, filters=[{rank=top, count=20, column=0}], agg=Median, agg_filtered=true. Shows the median performance curve of the top 20 assets only.
limitations: Renders in the dashboard grid, not the TV chart. Does not support lazy loading. Aggregation mode produces a single line - if you need both individual lines AND an aggregate overlay, use two separate cs_lines instances. For single-value-per-asset summaries use cs_cards or cs_summary_table.

desc: Single-value gauge for cross-sectional (market-wide) metrics. Aggregates input across assets to produce one gauge for the entire universe. Ideal for Fear & Greed indices, market breadth, and composite indicators.
usageContext: TRIGGER PHRASES: Use when the user asks for 'market gauge', 'fear and greed', 'sentiment indicator', 'market breadth gauge', 'portfolio risk gauge', 'aggregate risk dial'. Display a SINGLE AGGREGATE VALUE for the entire asset universe as a gauge dial in the DASHBOARD view. Takes a single numeric column (typically the output of a cs_agg transform) and aggregates it over time using the 'agg' option (default: Last). Two display modes: (A) NUMERICAL mode (default): Shows value on a min/max scale. Set min/max to the expected range. Use 'use_traffic_light_colors=true' for red-yellow-green gradient, or 'color' for a solid color. Example: Sharpe ratio gauge with min=-1, max=3. (B) CATEGORICAL mode: Provide 'categories' list (e.g., ['Extreme Fear','Fear','Neutral','Greed','Extreme Greed']). The input value is AUTO-SCALED from [min,max] to [0,N] categories. Gradient colors (red->yellow->green) are applied automatically. This creates a CNN Fear & Greed / TradingView sentiment gauge. KEY CHOICE - cs_gauge vs cs_cards: Use cs_gauge when the value represents a LEVEL within a known range (utilization %, sentiment score, risk rating). The gauge's visual dial communicates 'where are we in the range' instantly. Use cs_cards when the value is a standalone number without a meaningful range (total market cap, count of assets, average return). KEY CHOICE - cs_gauge vs cs_summary_table: Use cs_gauge for a SINGLE headline metric that needs visual emphasis. Use cs_summary_table when presenting multiple metrics in a grid (each asset × each metric). EXAMPLES: (1) Fear & Greed index: cs_agg computes composite score (0-100). categories=['Extreme Fear','Fear','Neutral','Greed','Extreme Greed'], min=0, max=100. Produces a CNN-style sentiment gauge. (2) Market breadth: cs_agg computes % of stocks above 200-day MA. min=0, max=100, value_type=PercentFormat, use_traffic_light_colors=true. (3) Portfolio risk score: cs_agg computes composite VaR. min=0, max=10, solid=false (dial style), decimal_places=1.
limitations: Displays only ONE value — for multiple metrics use cs_cards or cs_summary_table. Cannot show trends over time (use cs_lines for that). The categorical auto-scaling divides [min,max] into equal-width zones — for unequal zones, use numerical mode with custom color stops via traffic light colors. Cross-sectional input is typically a single column from cs_agg; multi-column DataFrames use only the first column.

usageContext: Plot a BUBBLE CHART with THREE-DIMENSIONAL encoding: X position, Y position, and Z (bubble size) from a single asset in the DASHBOARD view. Takes three required numeric columns: x, y, z. The Z column controls bubble diameter — larger Z values produce larger bubbles, enabling simultaneous visualization of position and magnitude. TRIGGER PHRASES: Use when the user asks for 'bubble chart', 'bubble plot', '3D scatter', 'three-dimensional', 'size-encoded scatter', 'risk-return-volatility', 'multi-factor plot', 'xyz plot', 'scatter with size', 'weighted scatter', 'show me three variables'. BUBBLE vs SCATTER: Scatter encodes TWO dimensions (x, y position). Bubble adds a THIRD dimension via bubble size (z). Use scatter when two metrics suffice. Use bubble when the user wants to visualize THREE metrics simultaneously — e.g., return (y) vs risk (x) with position size (z) as bubble size. BUBBLE vs HEATMAP: Both can visualize three dimensions. Heatmap uses a color grid (x category, y category, value as color intensity). Bubble uses spatial position + size. Use heatmap when both axes are categorical or binned. Use bubble when axes are continuous and the third dimension should be encoded as physical size rather than color. CONFIGURATION: 'series_name' labels the bubble series (default: 'Series 1'). 'color' sets the fill color for all bubbles (Select from Color enum: Blue, Red, Green, Orange, Purple, Teal, etc.; empty = default). 'min_size' sets minimum bubble diameter in pixels (default: 8px). 'max_size' sets maximum bubble diameter as percentage of chart area (default: 20%). Adjust these when bubbles are too small or too large relative to chart size. EXAMPLES: (1) Risk-Return-Size: x=volatility, y=return, z=market_cap. Bubble position shows risk/return tradeoff, size shows market capitalization. x_axis_format=PercentFormat. (2) Factor exposure: x=beta, y=alpha, z=abs(residual). Size shows model fit quality. Pair with cards showing R-squared and regression coefficients. (3) Liquidity analysis: x=avg_spread, y=avg_volume, z=market_cap. Large bubbles = large caps, position shows spread vs volume relationship. (4) Portfolio allocation: x=weight, y=return_contribution, z=risk_contribution. See how portfolio weights map to risk and return contributions.
limitations: Single asset only (isCrossSectional=false). Requires ALL THREE inputs (x, y, z) — if any is missing the chart is not produced. All bubbles share the same color (single series). Z values are used as-is for bubble sizing — negative Z values may produce unexpected behavior (use absolute values upstream if needed). No automatic legend showing the Z scale — the user must infer size meaning from context or add cards showing Z range. Only one series per chart — for multiple bubble series, use multiple bubble reports in the same category or use cs_bubble for cross-asset comparison.

SCATTER vs LINES: Lines connect data points in ORDER (time series). Scatter shows INDIVIDUAL UNCONNECTED points. Use lines when temporal order matters (prices, returns over time). Use scatter when you want to see the RELATIONSHIP between two variables regardless of time (e.g., risk vs return, factor loading vs alpha). SCATTER vs BUBBLE: Scatter encodes TWO dimensions (x, y position). Bubble encodes THREE dimensions (x position, y position, z size). Use scatter for bivariate analysis. Use bubble when a third metric (e.g., volume, market cap, volatility) should be encoded as bubble size. SCATTER vs HEATMAP: Both show bivariate relationships. Scatter shows individual points; heatmap shows density/value over a grid. Use scatter when each observation matters individually. Use heatmap for many observations across two dimensions. SERIES CONFIGURATION: The 'series' option takes a ScatterSeriesSchema with an array of ScatterSeriesSpec entries. Each spec has: name (string), color (optional Color enum: Blue, Red, Green, Orange, Purple, Teal, Cyan, Amber, etc.), marker (optional MarkerSymbol: CircleMarker, SquareMarker, DiamondMarker, TriangleMarker, TriangleDownMarker). The number of specs MUST match the number of Y inputs (NumericTuple columns). If series is not provided, default names ('Series 1', 'Series 2', ...) are used with default styling. EXAMPLES: (1) Risk vs Return: x=annualized_volatility, y_values=annualized_return. Classic efficient frontier visualization. x_axis_format=PercentFormat, y_axis_format=PercentFormat. (2) Factor exposure: x=beta, y_values=(alpha, tracking_error). Use series=[{name: 'Alpha', color: 'Blue', marker: 'CircleMarker'}, {name: 'Tracking Error', color: 'Red', marker: 'SquareMarker'}] to distinguish the two metrics. (3) Correlation scatter: x=sp500_returns, y_values=stock_returns. Shows how closely a stock tracks the market. (4) Multi-factor: x=value_score, y_values=(momentum_score, quality_score). Two Y series with different markers to visualize factor relationships simultaneously.
limitations: Single asset only (isCrossSectional=false). Each Y input becomes one scatter series — the number of ScatterSeriesSchema entries must exactly match the number of Y columns (NumericTuple fields), otherwise an error is thrown. NULL, NaN, and Inf values are silently filtered — points with any non-finite coordinate are dropped entirely. Set show_trend_line=True to add an OLS best-fit line computed from the first Y series. The line is a global regression (slope = cov(x,y)/var(x)), not a rolling window fit. No point labels by default.

desc: Color-coded grid from explicit x, y, value columns. Each cell's color intensity encodes magnitude, revealing 2D patterns at a glance. The standard visualization for seasonality analysis (month × year returns), temporal pattern discovery, and any analysis where two categorical dimensions intersect with a continuous value.
usageContext: Color-coded 2D grid in the DASHBOARD view where each cell's color intensity encodes a numeric value at the intersection of two categorical axes. This is the STANDARD visualization for discovering 2D patterns — especially calendar-based seasonality (month × year returns heatmaps seen in pyfolio, QuantStats, and portfolio tearsheets). HOW IT WORKS: Provide three columns — x (categories for columns), y (categories for rows), and value (the number that determines cell color). The color gradient maps from min_color (lowest values) through to max_color (highest values). Data labels show the exact value in each cell by default. CATEGORY AXIS TYPES: Numeric x/y values can be automatically converted to readable names using x_category_type / y_category_type: Month (1-12 → Jan-Dec), DayOfWeek (1-7 → Mon-Sun), or Exact (raw values). Categories are auto-sorted in logical order (Jan, Feb, ... Dec — not alphabetical). KEY CHOICE — heatmap vs xy_bars: Use heatmap when you have TWO categorical dimensions and want to see where patterns cluster in a grid. Use xy_bars when you have ONE categorical dimension and want to compare magnitudes as bar lengths. A monthly returns heatmap shows month × year; a monthly returns bar chart shows just months. KEY CHOICE — heatmap vs summary_table: Both display 2D grids. Use heatmap when color intensity is the primary insight (quickly spot hot/cold regions). Use summary_table when the user needs to read exact numbers in a structured grid. Best practice: pair both in the same dashboard category for complementary views. KEY CHOICE — heatmap vs cs_heatmap: heatmap is PER-ASSET with explicit x, y, value columns you define. cs_heatmap is CROSS-SECTIONAL where assets become the axes (correlation matrix or values grid). Use heatmap for calendar/temporal patterns within one asset. Use cs_heatmap for pairwise relationships across assets. EXAMPLES: (1) Monthly seasonality: x=month_number (x_category_type=Month), y=year, value=monthly_return, min_color=Red, max_color=Green, value_format=PercentFormat. The classic month × year returns grid used to validate calendar effects (e.g., 'October has 63% win rate'). This is the standard pyfolio/QuantStats heatmap. (2) Day-of-week × hour intraday patterns: x=hour, y=day_of_week (y_category_type=DayOfWeek), value=avg_volume. Reveals when trading activity clusters — useful for execution timing optimization. (3) Factor × regime analysis: x=market_regime (bull/bear/neutral), y=factor_name, value=factor_return. Shows which factors work in which regimes. (4) Rolling window sensitivity: x=lookback_period, y=threshold_level, value=strategy_sharpe. Parameter sweep grid showing which parameter combinations produce the best risk-adjusted returns.
limitations: Dashboard widget, not the TV chart. Requires pre-computed x, y, value columns — does aggregates duplicate (x, y) cells using the 'agg' option (default: Last). Use agg=Mean for frequency heatmaps, agg=Sum for count heatmaps, agg=Count for density maps. Both axes are categorical (no continuous axis). Large grids (50×50+) become hard to read — consider filtering or aggregating first. For cross-asset correlation or comparison grids use cs_heatmap. For distribution analysis use histogram. For single-dimension categorical comparison use xy_bars.

usageContext: TRIGGER PHRASES: Use when the user asks for 'portfolio allocation pie', 'asset weight breakdown', 'PnL contribution chart', 'cross-asset composition', 'which assets have the most weight'. Show proportional composition across assets as a pie or donut chart in the DASHBOARD view. Takes a multi-asset DataFrame (one column per asset, each a time series), aggregates each asset's series to a scalar using the 'agg' option (default: Last), takes absolute values, and normalizes as percentage of total. Each asset becomes a slice with area proportional to its share of the total. Set inner_size > 0 (typically 50-70) for donut style. KEY CHOICE - cs_pie vs cs_bars: Use cs_pie when the key insight is 'part of whole' (what fraction does each asset represent?) and the number of assets is small (2-8). This renders alongside cards, tables, histograms, and other dashboard widgets, making it ideal for building cohesive analysis sections where multiple chart types complement each other. Unlike timeseries_lines (which renders as a separate pane in the TV chart view), xy_lines lives in the dashboard grid. KEY CHOICE - xy_lines vs timeseries_lines: Use xy_lines when (a) the X-axis is NOT timestamps (parameter values, percentiles, maturity dates), (b) you want the chart in the dashboard next to related tables/cards for a cohesive report section, or (c) the data is small enough that lazy loading is unnecessary. Use timeseries_lines when the data is time-indexed and should sit in the chart view, especially for large intraday datasets that require lazy loading. Use 'reference_lines' for horizontal thresholds. area=true for filled area charts. stack_type for stacked area (Normal or Percent). split_by_label=true with a label input creates one line per unique label value. (2) Autocorrelation analysis: x_values=lag_periods (1..60), y_values=(autocorrelation, partial_autocorrelation). series=[{name:'ACF', color:Blue}, {name:'PACF', color:Orange, dash_style:Dash}]. reference_lines at +/-1.96/sqrt(N) confidence bounds. Place in dashboard alongside histogram of residuals and summary stats cards for a complete time series diagnostics section. (3) Term structure / yield curve: x_values=maturity_months, y_values=yield. smooth=true for spline interpolation. Shows the yield curve shape that fixed income analysts use to identify inversions, steepening, or flattening.

desc: Render aggregated values as a fixed grid table. Cells are positioned by row/col coordinates with optional row and column headers.
usageContext: TRIGGER PHRASES: Use when the user asks for 'monthly returns table', 'statistics grid', 'metrics matrix', 'row-column table', 'performance grid', 'tabular summary', 'structured table'. Display aggregated metrics in a fixed-position grid table with row/column headers. Cells are placed at explicit (row, col) coordinates, making this the right choice when data has a MATRIX structure. Supports two modes: (A) Standard mode: each cell maps 1:1 to a separate input series. You provide N inputs and N cells, each with explicit grid_row, grid_col, grid_agg. Use when each cell represents an independently computed metric. (B) RowSpec GROUP BY mode: exactly 2 inputs (values + grouping_key). The grouping key is a numeric column (e.g., month number 1-12). Cells are auto-generated from rows × col_headers. IMPORTANT: filtering is by COLUMN DIMENSION ONLY - each column filters WHERE grouping_key == (col_index + 1). Different rows apply different AGGREGATION FUNCTIONS to the same column-filtered data. Rows do NOT filter by a second dimension. SUMMARY_TABLE vs CARDS: Use summary_table when metrics have a natural GRID structure with row and column headers. If the metrics are a flat unrelated list of 3-8 KPIs with no row/column relationship, use cards instead. SUMMARY_TABLE vs DETAILED_TABLE: Summary table aggregates each cell to a single value. Detailed table shows every row of raw data. Use summary_table for computed statistics. EXAMPLES: (1) Monthly statistics grid (RowSpec mode): inputs are (returns, month_number). col_headers=['Jan','Feb',...,'Dec']. rows=[{name:'Sum', agg:Sum}, {name:'Mean', agg:Mean}, {name:'Std Dev', agg:Std}]. Each column filters returns WHERE month_number == col+1, then each row applies its aggregation. Result: 3 rows × 12 columns showing sum/mean/std of returns per month. Color map: green for positive, red for negative. (2) Risk/return matrix (Standard mode): row_headers=['1Y','3Y','5Y'], col_headers=['Return','Vol','Sharpe']. 9 inputs, each a pre-computed metric series (return_1y, vol_1y, sharpe_1y, return_3y, ...). Each cell uses agg=Last. This is the standard multi-horizon performance comparison that institutional investors expect in quarterly reports. (3) Brinson attribution grid (Standard mode): col_headers=['Port Weight', 'Bench Weight', 'Allocation', 'Selection']. Each row represents a sector. row_headers=['Technology','Healthcare','Financials',...]. Cells use PercentFormat with 2dp. Tells the PM whether outperformance came from sector allocation or stock selection.
limitations: Fixed grid layout requires explicit row/col positioning for each cell. Grid size must be known at definition time. Cannot handle variable-length data or per-row filtering. Use cards for flat KPI lists, or cs_summary_table for cross-asset comparison.

name: Datetime Difference

options.name: Time Unit
options.desc: Time unit for the difference. Sub-day (exact): seconds, milliseconds, microseconds, minutes, hours. Calendar (approximate): days, weeks (truncated 7-day blocks), months, quarters, years. Result is a truncated signed integer: SLOT1 - SLOT0.

desc: Calculate elapsed time between two timestamp columns. Result = SLOT1 - SLOT0 in the selected unit, as a signed integer. Negative values indicate SLOT0 is after SLOT1.
usageContext:
ROLE: Elapsed time between two timestamps. Result = SLOT1 - SLOT0, signed.
Positive means SLOT1 is after SLOT0.

KEY CHOICE -- datetime_diff vs datetime_extract:
- datetime_diff → DISTANCE between two points (e.g., 45 days since earnings)
- datetime_extract → COMPONENT of a single point (e.g., month=3)

UNITS (10 total):
Sub-day (exact arithmetic): seconds, milliseconds, microseconds, minutes, hours
Calendar (approximate): days, weeks (÷7 truncated), months, quarters, years

ACADEMIC APPLICATIONS:
- Options DTE (Black-Scholes): days to expiration drives theta decay
- PEAD (Ball & Brown 1968): 60-90 day post-earnings drift window
- Holding period: short-term capital gains ≤ 365 days (US tax code)
- T+1 settlement: trade date to settlement date = 1 business day
- Data staleness: filter stale fundamental data (>90 days old)

EXAMPLES:
1. Days since earnings release:
   days_since = datetime_diff(unit='days')(earnings.report_date, index())
2. Options DTE:
   dte = datetime_diff(unit='days')(index(), expiry_date)
3. Data staleness filter:
   age = datetime_diff(unit='days')(filing.period_end, index())
   fresh = age.value <= 90
limitations:
Result is a signed integer (truncated, not rounded). Negative values mean
SLOT0 is after SLOT1. Calendar units (months, quarters, years) use
approximate arithmetic — not exact calendar month boundaries. Weeks are
truncated 7-day blocks (13 days = 1 week). No business-day awareness:
weekends and holidays count as elapsed time. For bar-index-to-timestamp
diff, use datetime_diff(timestamp, index()).

name: Timestamp Scalar

options.name: Timestamp Value
options.desc: Timestamp string. Supported formats: 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS' (space separator) or 'YYYY-MM-DD' (date only, midnight assumed). The 'T' separator (ISO 8601 'YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS') is rejected — use a space instead.

options.name: Timezone
options.desc: IANA timezone for the timestamp (e.g., 'America/New_York', 'Asia/Tokyo'). The timestamp is interpreted as local time in this timezone, then converted to UTC internally. DST-aware: '2024-07-15 09:30:00' with 'America/New_York' uses EDT (UTC-4), not EST (UTC-5). Abbreviations like 'EST' are not accepted.

desc: Create a constant timestamp value for comparisons, filtering, and regime definition. Returns a single-row scalar DataFrame. Supports timezone-aware timestamp creation for market open/close times and event dates.
usageContext:
ROLE: Fixed timestamp constants for regime filtering and event studies.
Returns a single-row scalar DataFrame — not a time series.

KEY CHOICE -- timestamp_scalar vs datetime_extract:
- timestamp_scalar → fixed reference POINT (e.g., "2020-02-19" COVID peak)
- datetime_extract → COMPONENT of each bar's timestamp (e.g., hour=9)
Use timestamp_scalar for "before/after event X" logic.

REGIME EVENTS (common reference dates):
- COVID crash: 2020-02-19 (S&P 500 peak) / 2020-03-23 (trough)
- GFC: 2008-09-15 (Lehman bankruptcy)
- Flash Crash: 2010-05-06
- SVB collapse: 2023-03-10
- Fed pivots: 2022-03-16 (first hike) / 2024-09-18 (first cut)

TIMEZONE: Local time interpretation → UTC storage. DST-aware for market
open/close. '09:30:00' with 'America/New_York' correctly uses EST (winter)
or EDT (summer).

EXAMPLES:
1. Pre/post COVID filter:
   covid = timestamp_scalar(value='2020-02-19'); is_post = index() >= covid.value
2. NY market open reference:
   open = timestamp_scalar(value='2024-01-15 09:30:00', timezone='America/New_York')
3. Fed pivot date:
   pivot = timestamp_scalar(value='2022-03-16')
limitations:
Returns single-row DataFrame (scalar), not a time series — cannot be plotted
directly. The 'T' separator (ISO 8601) is rejected; use space separator.
Timezone must be IANA format ('America/New_York'), not abbreviations ('EST').
No support for recurring timestamps (e.g., "every Monday at 09:30"). Years
must be 1970-2100.

name: Week of Month

options.name: Week of Month
options.desc: Which week of the month to detect

desc: Detects specific weeks within a month for intramonth pattern analysis. Research by Fosback (1976) and Ariel (1987) shows stock returns are positive only during the first half of calendar months. The first week benefits from payroll-related capital inflows and turn-of-month overlap (Ogden 1990). The third week contains options expiration (OPEX) effects -- triple witching weeks (March, June, September, December) show 2x normal volume and elevated volatility. The last week shows anticipatory turn-of-month buying.
usageContext:
Use to identify intramonth patterns and options expiration effects for position timing.
- First week: increase long exposure for payroll-driven inflows and turn-of-month momentum continuation.
- OPEX week (Third week): reduce position size or hedge -- volatility spikes from options expiration and delta hedging flows.
- Triple witching (3rd Friday of March/June/September/December): expect 2x volume and elevated volatility.
- Last week: begin building positions for the next turn-of-month window.
- Combine with turn_of_month for the overlap period (last week + first week = strongest intramonth window).
- Use with atr or basic_volatility to dynamically adjust position sizes based on expected OPEX-week volatility.
limitations:
The week-of-month effect is closely related to (and partially redundant with) the turn-of-month effect --
the first and last week signals largely capture the same phenomenon. Options expiration effects are
concentrated on Thursday-Friday of OPEX week, not the full week. Triple witching occurs only 4 times per
year, providing very small sample sizes. Weekly aggregation may mask the precise day-level pattern -- daily
data with turn_of_month provides finer granularity. Market maker hedging flows during OPEX are complex and
direction-dependent (gamma exposure can be positive or negative), making simple long/short timing unreliable.

name: Quarter

options.name: Quarter
options.desc: The specific quarter to detect

desc: Detects specific quarters for quarterly calendar patterns including window dressing by fund managers, pension fund rebalancing, and earnings seasonality. Q4 is historically the strongest quarter, with the S&P 500 averaging +4.4% gains when positive year-to-date through Q3. Research shows approximately $32 billion in quarterly pension rebalancing equity flows occur at quarter-end. However, the quarter-end effect outside of Q4/December is largely unsupported by backtests -- excluding December, quarter-end returns average -0.11% per trade.
usageContext:
Use to capture quarterly seasonal patterns and institutional flow effects.
- Q4 rally: go long at Q4 start (October) for the historically strongest quarter, especially when YTD returns are positive.
- Window dressing anticipation: buy recent winners ahead of quarter-end as fund managers add to top performers.
- Pension rebalancing: anticipate equity selling when stocks have outperformed bonds significantly during the quarter.
- Earnings positioning: use Q1 filter (January-March) to position for earnings season momentum.
- Avoid the Q3 trap: September is historically the weakest month -- reduce exposure or hedge during late Q3.
- Combine with turn_of_month for quarter-end turn-of-month overlap (strongest seasonal window).
limitations:
The quarter-end effect is almost entirely driven by Q4/December seasonal strength -- excluding December,
backtests show negative returns. Window dressing has become less impactful as SEC moves to monthly reporting
requirements. Pension rebalancing flows are becoming less predictable as funds adopt continuous rather than
calendar-based rebalancing. Requires daily data for quarter-boundary timing. Q4 strength may be regime-
dependent -- during bear markets, the Q4 rally often fails. Transaction costs and the small per-trade edge
make this unsuitable as a standalone strategy. With only 4 quarters, finding one strong quarter is expected
by chance alone.

name: Month of Year

options.name: Month
options.desc: The specific month to detect

desc: Detects specific months for seasonal calendar patterns documented in decades of academic research. The January effect (Rozeff & Kinney 1976, Keim 1983) shows small-cap stocks outperforming significantly in January, with nearly half the annual size premium concentrated in a single month. 'Sell in May and Go Away' (Bouman & Jacobsen 2002) validated November-April outperformance across 36 of 37 international markets. The Santa Claus rally (Yale Hirsch 1972) covers the last 5 trading days of December plus first 2 of January, occurring 79% of years since 1950 with average S&P 500 returns of +1.3%.
usageContext:
Use to implement month-of-year seasonal strategies based on well-documented academic anomalies.
- January effect: overweight small-cap stocks (IWM, Russell 2000) in January for tax-loss selling rebound.
- 'Sell in May': go long November through April, move to bonds/cash May through October (Halloween indicator).
- Santa Claus rally: go long last week of December through first 2 days of January for the seasonal lift.
- Summer doldrums: reduce exposure June-September when historical returns are weakest.
- Combine with returns and sma for trend confirmation -- do not trade against the primary trend for seasonality alone.
- Use as a cross-sectional filter: long small-caps in January, large-caps in other months.
limitations:
The January effect has weakened substantially since the 1980s as tax-loss harvesting became a year-round
practice with tax-advantaged accounts (IRAs, 401ks). 'Sell in May' leaves significant returns on the table
during summer bull markets. Monthly frequency data is the minimum but daily data provides better entry/exit
precision. Small-cap January outperformance may be driven by illiquidity and bid-ask bounce rather than
genuine alpha. Multiple month comparisons inflate the risk of data mining -- 12 months tested means high
false positive rates without correction. Not suitable as a standalone strategy without additional filters.

name: Day of Week

options.name: Weekday
options.desc: The specific weekday to detect

desc: Detects specific weekdays for day-of-week calendar effects. The Monday/weekend effect, first documented by Cross (1973) and rigorously studied by French (1980) and Gibbons & Hess (1981), showed significantly negative Monday returns and positive Friday returns in the S&P 500 (1953-1977). A 2024 meta-analysis of 85 studies confirms Mondays/Tuesdays provide lower average daily returns while Wednesdays/Fridays indicate higher returns. However, the effect has largely vanished in US large-cap markets since the 1990s and is now mainly observed in emerging markets and small caps.
usageContext:
Use to test and exploit day-of-week return patterns in your target market.
- Avoid entering long positions on Mondays in markets where the effect persists (emerging markets, small caps).
- Use as an exit timing filter: close positions before the weekend if holding costs are a concern.
- Combine with session_window for intraday day-of-week patterns (e.g., Monday morning selloff, Friday afternoon rally).
- Apply as a position sizing modifier: reduce exposure on historically weak days, increase on strong days.
- Pair with volatility measures (atr, basic_volatility) since Monday volatility tends to be higher.
- Use in cross-sectional strategies: small-cap Monday underperformance may create buying opportunities.
limitations:
The Monday effect has largely disappeared in US large-cap equities since the early 1990s.
Requires daily frequency data; intraday or weekly bars will not capture the pattern. The effect may persist
in emerging markets and small-cap stocks but with high transaction costs that erode the edge. Settlement
timing changes (T+2 to T+1) and 24-hour electronic trading have altered the informational landscape.
Data mining concern: with 5 weekdays to test, finding one significant day by chance is likely (multiple
testing bias). Not recommended as a standalone strategy in developed markets post-2000.

name: Upsample

options.name: Target Timeframe
options.desc: Target higher-frequency timeframe (e.g., 1Min, 5Min)

options.name: Fill Method
options.desc: Method for filling new timestamps

name: N Largest

options.name: N
options.desc: Number of largest values to select

desc: Returns a boolean mask that is true for the N largest values in the entire series. Scans globally, not rolling.
usageContext: Identify the N most extreme high values in a series. Returns a boolean mask (true for selected rows, false otherwise) — NOT the values themselves. PIPELINE PATTERN: (1) Compute nlargest(n=10)(volume) to get a boolean mask of the 10 highest volume days, (2) use boolean_select_number(mask, value, fallback) to isolate or replace those days. EXAMPLES: (1) Best days analysis: nlargest(n=10)(daily_ret) → boolean_select_number → cumulative(agg=Sum) shows equity curve with only the 10 best days kept. (2) Volume spikes: nlargest(n=20)(volume) marks the 20 highest volume days as potential breakout or institutional activity events. (3) Return attribution: Compare cumulative returns with vs without top N days to measure performance concentration. Trigger phrases: 'best N days', 'top N values', 'N largest', 'highest volume days', 'biggest gains', 'peak performance days'.
limitations: Scans the entire series GLOBALLY — result depends on the full date range, not a rolling window. This means nlargest applied to expanding data may change which rows are selected as new data arrives. Ties at the Nth boundary are broken by position (earlier values chosen). Output is Boolean, not the actual values — use boolean_select_number to extract values.

name: Winsorize (Time-Series)

options.name: Lower Percentile
options.desc: Values below this percentile are capped to the percentile value
options.tuningGuidance: 0.01 = cap only most extreme 1% (very light). 0.05 = standard (default), clips ~5% of each tail. 0.10 = aggressive, clips 10% of each tail. For fundamental data with fat tails (P/E ratios, earnings surprises), use 0.05-0.10. For already-clean return data, use 0.01-0.02.

options.name: Upper Percentile
options.desc: Values above this percentile are capped to the percentile value
options.tuningGuidance: 0.99 = very light clipping. 0.95 = standard (default). 0.90 = aggressive. Should be symmetric with lower_limit for balanced treatment (e.g., 0.05/0.95 or 0.01/0.99).

desc: Caps extreme values at specified percentile cutoffs within each asset's own time-series history. Preserves data points by replacing outliers with the boundary value rather than removing them. Applied per-column (per-asset) along the time axis.
usageContext: Cap extreme values in a single asset's time series at specified percentile cutoffs. Percentiles are computed from the asset's OWN history (per-column, along the time axis). KEY DIFFERENCE from cs_winsorize: winsorize operates along TIME within a single asset. cs_winsorize operates CROSS-SECTIONALLY across assets at each point in time. Use winsorize for cleaning one asset's data history; use cs_winsorize for normalizing across a universe of assets at each bar. PIPELINE PATTERN: (1) Compute raw fundamental metric (e.g., P/E ratio from earnings data), (2) winsorize(lower=0.05, upper=0.95) to cap extreme values, (3) feed into ML model or further indicators. Without winsorization, a single outlier bar can dominate z-score or rolling statistics. EXAMPLES: (1) Clean P/E ratios: winsorize(0.05, 0.95)(pe_ratio) caps extreme P/E values caused by near-zero earnings quarters, preventing them from distorting ratio-based signals. (2) Robust returns: winsorize(0.01, 0.99)(daily_returns) clips the 1% most extreme return days (flash crashes, circuit breakers) before computing rolling statistics. (3) ML preprocessing: Apply winsorize before z-score normalization to prevent outliers from inflating standard deviation and compressing the useful signal range. Trigger phrases: 'cap outliers', 'clip extreme values', 'winsorize', 'handle outliers', 'clean data', 'robust preprocessing', 'percentile clipping'.
limitations: Percentiles are computed from the FULL series history, not a rolling window — this means boundaries can shift as new data arrives (look-ahead risk in expanding window context). Values exactly at the percentile boundary are NOT clipped. Only handles univariate outliers — doesn't detect multivariate outliers (use DBSCAN for that). For cross-sectional outlier handling (across assets at each time), use cs_winsorize instead.

options.name: Fraction
options.desc: Kelly fraction (0.5 = half-Kelly, more conservative)
options.tuningGuidance: 0.5 (half-Kelly, default) achieves ~75% of full Kelly growth rate with ~50% of the volatility. 0.25 (quarter-Kelly) for uncertain or unstable edge. 1.0 (full Kelly) only appropriate with 500+ trades and demonstrably stable edge — extremely aggressive.

options.name: Minimum Trades
options.desc: Minimum trades required before using Kelly (uses fallback_pct until reached)
options.tuningGuidance: 30 (default) minimum for statistical reliability. 50-100 for variable win rates or strategies with fat-tailed returns. Until reached, uses fallback_pct as static allocation.

options.name: Fallback Percent
options.desc: Equity percentage to use when insufficient trade history (10 = 10%)
options.tuningGuidance: 10.0 (default). Should roughly match expected Kelly allocation to avoid a size discontinuity when switching from fallback to Kelly at min_trades threshold.

desc: Kelly Criterion optimal sizing. f* = W - (1-W)/R where W = win rate, R = avg_win/avg_loss. Uses historical trades to estimate edge. Half-Kelly commonly used for stability.
usageContext:
Kelly Criterion position sizing, based on Kelly (1956). Computes the theoretically optimal
fraction of equity to risk on each trade to maximize long-term geometric growth.

FORMULA: f* = W - (1-W)/R
where W = historical win rate, R = average win / average loss (payoff ratio).
The actual allocation = f* * fraction (the fraction option scales Kelly down).

HALF-KELLY RECOMMENDATION: Full Kelly is extremely aggressive and assumes stationary edge
(constant win rate and payoff ratio). In practice, half-Kelly (fraction=0.5) is standard
because it achieves ~75% of the growth rate with ~50% of the volatility.

BOOTSTRAP BEHAVIOR: Until min_trades completed trades are available, the strategy uses
fallback_pct as a static percentage of equity. Once min_trades is reached, Kelly sizing
activates using the rolling trade history.

EXAMPLES:
(1) Standard half-Kelly: kelly(fraction=0.5, min_trades=30)
(2) Conservative quarter-Kelly: kelly(fraction=0.25, min_trades=50, fallback_pct=5.0)
(3) Aggressive full Kelly: kelly(fraction=1.0, min_trades=20, fallback_pct=15.0)
limitations:
Requires trade history to compute win rate and payoff ratio - uses fallback_pct as a static
equity percentage until min_trades completed trades are recorded. Full Kelly (fraction=1.0)
is extremely aggressive and can lead to large drawdowns. Assumes stationary edge (constant
win rate and payoff ratio over time), which rarely holds in practice. No inputs - reads from
execution context automatically.

name: Position Size

options.name: Size Type
options.desc: How to interpret size: 'unit' = raw units (shares for stocks, contracts for futures, base currency units for FX — e.g. 100000 = 1 standard lot EURUSD), 'notional' = $ value, 'percent' = % of equity (5 = 5%)
options.tuningGuidance: percent (default) most flexible — scales with equity automatically. unit for fixed-size positions (specific share/contract counts). notional for dollar exposure targets. FX: prefer notional or percent over unit to avoid manual lot math.

desc: Dynamic position sizing. Takes a size input and outputs to fixed 'size' key. Unit meaning varies by asset class: stocks=shares, futures=contracts, FX=base currency units (100000=1 std lot), crypto=base coins. For long/short strategies, use conditional_select to merge weights before this component. Only ONE position_size is allowed per strategy. Use rebalance_on to gate when sizing recalculates (e.g., rebalance_on=is_new_month).
usageContext:
General-purpose position sizer with three modes controlled by the `type` option:

SIZE MODES:
- `type="percent"` (default): Size as percentage of equity. 5 = 5% of equity.
- `type="notional"`: Size as a dollar value. 10000 = $10,000 notional position.
- `type="unit"`: Size as raw asset units. What "1 unit" means depends on asset class:
  * Stocks: 1 unit = 1 share. position_size(type="unit")(100) = 100 shares.
  * Futures: 1 unit = 1 contract. position_size(type="unit")(5) = 5 contracts.
  * FX: 1 unit = 1 base currency unit. 1 standard lot = 100,000 units.
    position_size(type="unit")(100000) = 1 lot EURUSD.
    For FX, prefer type="notional" or type="percent" to avoid manual lot math.
  * Crypto: 1 unit = 1 base coin. position_size(type="unit")(0.5) = 0.5 BTC.

LONG/SHORT STRATEGIES: Use conditional_select to merge long and short weights into a single
column before passing to position_size. This avoids needing two sizers.
  size_pct = conditional_select(long_signal, long_weight*100, short_signal, short_weight*100)
  position_size(type="percent")(size_pct)

REBALANCE GATING: Use rebalance_on to control when sizing recalculates. Without it, size
recalculates every bar. With rebalance_on=is_period_boundary(period="month"), only on month start.

EXAMPLES:
(1) Fixed percent: position_size(type="percent")(20) -- always 20% of equity
(2) Dynamic weight: position_size(type="percent")(weight * 100) -- transform-driven weight
(3) Fixed notional: position_size(type="notional")(50000) -- always $50k position
(4) FX lot sizing: position_size(type="unit")(100000) -- 1 standard lot (100k base currency)
(5) Futures contracts: position_size(type="unit")(5) -- 5 contracts
limitations:
Only ONE position_size allowed per strategy. Size must be > 0 (NaN or zero skips sizing).
Does not include built-in stop loss or take profit - pair with standalone stop_loss/take_profit
components for exit management. For risk-based sizing with bundled SL/TP, use risk_unit instead.

name: Risk Unit

options.name: Risk Mode
options.desc: How to interpret risk_pct: 'percent' = percentage of equity (1 = 1%), 'fixed' = fixed dollar amount (200 = $200 risk per trade)
options.tuningGuidance: percent (default) scales with equity — standard for most strategies. fixed = constant dollar risk regardless of equity. Use fixed for drawdown recovery or income strategies where position size shouldn't shrink with losses.

options.name: Risk/Reward Ratio
options.desc: Risk/reward ratio for take profit. 0 = no take profit (default). Set > 0 to enable automatic TP at rr_ratio * stop_distance from entry (e.g., 2.0 = TP at 2x the stop distance)
options.tuningGuidance: 0 (default) = no TP, exit only via signal or SL. 1.5-2.0 for trend-following (captures moves at 1.5-2x risk). 3.0+ for reversal strategies with low win rate. Match to historical payoff ratio — if avg_win/avg_loss is 2.5, start with rr_ratio=2.0-2.5.

options.name: Minimum Size
options.desc: Minimum position size (0 = no minimum)
options.tuningGuidance: 0 (default) = no minimum. Set to 1 for stocks/futures (whole shares/contracts). Leave 0 for crypto (fractional sizing allowed).

options.name: Maximum Size
options.desc: Maximum position size (0 = no maximum)
options.tuningGuidance: 0 (default) = no max. Set to prevent concentration: max_size = equity * max_allocation_pct / price. For futures, cap at account margin limits.

options.name: Lot Size
options.desc: Round position size to multiples of lot_size. Examples: 1 = whole shares/contracts, 100 = board lots, 0.001 = crypto. 0 = no rounding (fractional allowed)
options.tuningGuidance: 0 (default) = fractional. 1 = whole shares/contracts. 100 = board lots (US equities). FX: 1000 = micro lot, 10000 = mini lot, 100000 = standard lot.

options.name: Size Scalar
options.desc: Multiplier applied to final size. Use 0.5 for half-positions, 2.0 for double.
options.tuningGuidance: 1.0 (default) = no scaling. 0.5 for paper trading or risk reduction. 2.0 for scaling up a validated strategy. Applies after all other size calculations.

options.name: Contract Multiplier Override
options.desc: Override asset.GetMultiplier(). 0 = use asset's multiplier from AssetSpecification (stocks=1, E-mini=50, CL=1000, etc.). Set >0 to override for custom lot sizes.
options.tuningGuidance: 0 (default) = auto-detect from asset specification (E-mini=50, CL=1000, GC=100, stocks=1). Override only for non-standard contracts or synthetic data where the asset spec is missing or incorrect.

options.name: Stop Distance Unit
options.desc: Unit for stop_distance: 'price' = absolute price units (default), 'pips' = FX pips (0.0001 or 0.01 for JPY pairs), 'percent' = percentage of entry price (1 = 1%)
options.tuningGuidance: price (default) for stocks/futures — use with ATR-based stops. pips for FX (auto-detects JPY 0.01 vs standard 0.0001). percent for multi-asset portfolios where you want uniform percentage-based stops across different price levels.

desc: Atomic risk-based sizing that computes position size and stop loss, with optional take profit. By default, position size is computed ONCE at entry and held until the position is closed (stop loss and take profit still update dynamically). To enable periodic resizing, connect a rebalance_on input (e.g., rebalance_on=is_new_week). Supports two risk modes: 'percent' (default) where risk_pct is a percentage of equity (1 = 1%), and 'fixed' where risk_pct is an absolute dollar amount ($200 = risk $200 per trade). Formula (percent): size = (equity * risk_pct/100) / (stop_distance * contract_multiplier) * size_scalar. Formula (fixed): size = risk_pct / (stop_distance * contract_multiplier) * size_scalar. stop_distance can be in price units, pips, or percent (see stop_unit option). contract_multiplier defaults to asset.GetMultiplier() (E-mini=50, CL=1000, stocks=1). SL is always set at stop_distance from entry. TP is opt-in: set rr_ratio > 0 to add TP at rr_ratio * stop_distance, or pass tp_distance input for explicit TP.
usageContext:
Atomic risk-based position sizer that bundles size calculation and stop loss,
with optional take profit. Two risk modes control how `risk_pct` is interpreted:

RISK MODES:
- `risk_mode="percent"` (default): risk_pct is a percentage of current equity.
  risk_amount = equity * risk_pct / 100. Example: risk_pct=1 on $100k equity = $1,000 risk.
- `risk_mode="fixed"`: risk_pct is a fixed dollar amount used directly as risk_amount.
  risk_amount = risk_pct. Example: risk_pct=200 = always risk $200 per trade regardless of equity.

IMPORTANT: "risk 100 pips" refers to STOP DISTANCE (use stop_unit="pips"), NOT risk amount.
The stop_unit option (price/pips/percent) controls how stop_distance is interpreted. This is
a separate axis from risk_mode, which controls how risk_pct (the dollar risk) is interpreted.

SIZE-ONCE-AT-ENTRY (default): Position size is computed once when the position opens and
held constant until close. Stop loss and take profit still update dynamically each bar.
This prevents volatility-driven inputs (like ATR) from causing daily position rebalancing.
To enable periodic resizing, connect rebalance_on (e.g., rebalance_on=is_new_week).

TAKE PROFIT (opt-in): By default, rr_ratio=0 means NO take profit is placed. To add an
automatic take profit, set rr_ratio > 0 (e.g., rr_ratio=2.0 places TP at 2x stop distance).
Alternatively, pass an explicit tp_distance input for a custom TP distance.

CONTRACT MULTIPLIER: Defaults to asset.GetMultiplier() which is auto-detected from the asset
specification (stocks=1, E-mini S&P=50, crude oil=1000, gold futures=100). Override with
contract_multiplier option only when the auto-detected value is wrong.

CORE FORMULA: size = risk_amount / (stop_distance_in_price * contract_multiplier) * size_scalar

EXAMPLES:
(1) Stop-loss only (no TP): risk_unit()(risk_pct=1, stop_distance=atr(14)*2)
    $100k equity, 1% risk = $1000, ATR*2 = $5 stop -> 200 shares, SL at entry-5, no TP.
(2) With 2:1 TP: risk_unit(rr_ratio=2.0)(risk_pct=1, stop_distance=atr(14)*2)
    Same sizing as (1), but adds TP at entry+10 (2x the stop distance).
(3) FX with pip stop + TP: risk_unit(stop_unit="pips", rr_ratio=1.5)(risk_pct=0.5, stop_distance=50)
    50 pips * 0.0001 = $0.005 price distance, 0.5% of equity as risk, TP at 75 pips.
(4) Futures with percent stop: risk_unit(stop_unit="percent")(risk_pct=2, stop_distance=1.5)
    1.5% of entry price as stop distance, E-mini multiplier auto-detected at 50. No TP.
(5) Fixed dollar risk with TP: risk_unit(risk_mode="fixed", rr_ratio=2.0)(risk_pct=200, stop_distance=atr(14))
    Always risk $200 per trade regardless of equity size, TP at 2x stop.
(6) Dynamic rebalance: risk_unit(rr_ratio=3.0)(risk_pct=1, stop_distance=atr(20)*3, rebalance_on=is_new_week)
limitations:
Requires both risk_pct and stop_distance inputs (NaN on either bar skips sizing).
In percent mode: risk_pct must be in (0, 100]. In fixed mode: risk_pct must be > 0 (no upper cap).
stop_distance must be > 0 after unit conversion. Bundled SL/TP overrides any standalone stop_loss
or take_profit components on the same strategy. Only one sizing sink (risk_unit OR position_size)
allowed per strategy.

name: Take Profit

options.name: Distance Unit
options.desc: How to interpret the distance value
options.tuningGuidance: Same as stop_loss unit. price (default) for stocks/futures. pips for FX. percent for multi-asset portfolios.

options.name: R-Multiple Levels
options.desc: R-multiple levels for tiered exits (e.g., [1, 2, 3]). Must sum to 1.0 with exit_pcts.
options.tuningGuidance: Empty (default) = single level, use distance input. Common setups: [1,2,3] equal spacing, [1,1.5,3] front-loaded, [1,3] runner style. Array length must match exit_pcts length.

options.name: Exit Percentages
options.desc: Exit percentage at each level (e.g., [0.33, 0.33, 0.34]). Must sum to 1.0.
options.tuningGuidance: Must sum to ~1.0. [0.33,0.33,0.34] equal thirds. [0.50,0.30,0.20] front-loaded — takes half off at first target. [0.75,0.25] runner style — secures most at 1R, lets remainder run.

desc: Take profit exit level(s). Supports single level or tiered exits. For tiered: use r_levels and exit_pcts with risk_distance. Long positions: exit at entry + distance. Short positions: exit at entry - distance.
usageContext:
Take profit component supporting both single-level and tiered (R-multiple) exits.

SINGLE-LEVEL MODE: Provide `distance` input for a simple fixed take profit.
  take_profit()(distance=atr(14)*4) -- exit at 4x ATR profit from entry.

TIERED EXIT MODE: Use `risk_distance` input with `r_levels` and `exit_pcts` options to scale
out of a position at multiple R-multiple targets. R-multiples are measured relative to the
risk_distance (which is typically the stop loss distance).

R-MULTIPLE SCALING: r_levels=[1, 2, 3] with exit_pcts=[0.33, 0.33, 0.34] means:
  - Exit 33% of position at 1R profit (1x risk_distance from entry)
  - Exit 33% at 2R profit
  - Exit remaining 34% at 3R profit

DIRECTION AWARENESS:
- Long: tp_price = entry_price + distance (or entry + R * risk_distance per level)
- Short: tp_price = entry_price - distance (or entry - R * risk_distance per level)

EXAMPLES:
(1) Single level: take_profit()(distance=atr(14)*4)
(2) Tiered equal thirds: take_profit(r_levels=[1,2,3], exit_pcts=[0.33,0.33,0.34])(risk_distance=atr(14)*2)
(3) Front-loaded: take_profit(r_levels=[1,1.5,3], exit_pcts=[0.50,0.30,0.20])(risk_distance=stop_dist)
(4) Runner style: take_profit(r_levels=[1,3], exit_pcts=[0.75,0.25])(risk_distance=atr(14))
limitations:
Distance must be > 0 (NaN or zero means no take profit for that bar). For tiered mode:
r_levels and exit_pcts arrays must have the same length, and exit_pcts must sum to approximately
1.0 (within floating point tolerance). Overridden by risk_unit's bundled take profit if both
are present. Only one take_profit component allowed per strategy.

name: Stop Loss

options.name: Distance Unit
options.desc: How to interpret the distance value
options.tuningGuidance: price (default) for stocks/futures — use with ATR-based stops. pips for FX (auto-detects JPY 0.01 vs standard 0.0001). percent for multi-asset portfolios with uniform stop rules.

desc: Stop loss exit level. Sets exit at a fixed distance from entry. Long positions: exit at entry - distance. Short positions: exit at entry + distance.
usageContext:
Standalone stop loss component that sets a fixed exit level at a specified distance from
the entry price. Use this when you want explicit control over stop placement separate from
position sizing. For risk-based sizing with bundled SL, use risk_unit instead.

DISTANCE UNITS (via `unit` option):
- `unit="price"` (default): Distance in absolute price units. stop_loss()(distance=5) on a
  $100 stock sets stop at $95 (long) or $105 (short).
- `unit="pips"`: Distance in FX pips. stop_loss(unit="pips")(distance=50) = 50 pips.
  Auto-detects pip value: 0.0001 for most pairs, 0.01 for JPY pairs.
- `unit="percent"`: Distance as percentage of entry. stop_loss(unit="percent")(distance=2)
  sets stop 2% below entry (long) or 2% above (short).

DIRECTION AWARENESS: Automatically adjusts based on position direction:
- Long: stop_price = entry_price - distance_in_price_units
- Short: stop_price = entry_price + distance_in_price_units

STANDALONE vs BUNDLED: When used alongside risk_unit, the risk_unit's built-in SL takes
precedence. Use standalone stop_loss only with position_size or other non-risk sizers.

EXAMPLES:
(1) ATR-based: stop_loss()(distance=atr(14)*2) -- 2x ATR trailing from entry
(2) Fixed pips: stop_loss(unit="pips")(distance=50) -- 50 pip stop for FX
(3) Percentage: stop_loss(unit="percent")(distance=3) -- 3% stop
(4) Dynamic: stop_loss()(distance=swing_low_distance) -- distance from a computed level
limitations:
Distance must be > 0 (NaN or zero means no stop is placed for that bar). Overridden by
risk_unit's bundled stop loss if both are present on the same strategy. Only one stop_loss
component allowed per strategy. The distance is fixed at entry time and does not adjust
during the trade - for dynamic stops, use trailing_stop instead.

name: Multi-Linear Fit (Multi-Factor Regression)

options.name: Number of Independent Variables
options.desc: Number of independent variables (regressors) in the model
options.tuningGuidance: Set to match your factor model: 1 for CAPM, 3 for Fama-French 3-factor, 5 for Fama-French 5-factor. More factors increase model complexity and risk of overfitting.

options.name: Window Size
options.desc: Rolling window size for OLS regression
options.tuningGuidance: Use 60-120 for stable factor exposure estimates (matches academic practice). Shorter windows (20-40) for tactical factor timing. Minimum observation count should exceed number of factors by at least 10x for reliable estimates.

desc: Multi-variate OLS regression: y = β₀ + β₁x₁ + β₂x₂ + ... + βₙxₙ + ε. Computes factor exposures (betas), intercept (alpha), residuals (idiosyncratic returns), and R-squared. Essential for Fama-French factor regressions and multi-factor models.
usageContext: Use for multi-factor models like Fama-French. Pass stock returns as y, and factor returns (market excess return, SMB, HML, etc.) as x_vars tuple. Extract: factor betas for risk attribution, intercept as alpha (abnormal return), residuals for idiosyncratic volatility calculation. Key for: market timing with idiosyncratic variance, factor-neutral strategies, alpha generation research. KEY DIFFERENCE from linear_fit: multi_linear_fit handles 2-10 independent variables simultaneously. For single-factor regression (one X, one Y), use linear_fit instead — it's simpler and gives the same results for the bivariate case. Trigger phrases: 'multi-factor regression', 'Fama-French', 'factor exposure', 'alpha generation', 'idiosyncratic returns', 'risk attribution', 'factor betas', 'multi-variate regression', 'factor model'.
limitations: Requires sufficient window size (10x+ factors) for stable estimates. Assumes linear factor relationships and homoscedastic errors. Sensitive to factor multicollinearity. Results depend heavily on factor construction methodology.

name: Z-Score

options.name: Window
options.desc: Rolling window size for calculating mean and standard deviation
options.tuningGuidance: Shorter windows (10-15) for responsive mean-reversion entries, captures recent regime quickly but noisier. Standard 20 balances stability with adaptation. Longer windows (40-60) for stable normalization in ML features or cross-asset comparisons. Match window to your mean-reversion timeframe.

desc: Rolling z-score of the input series: (x_t - mean)/stddev over the configured window.
usageContext: Use for mean-reversion strategies and outlier detection. Normalizes any indicator to standard deviations from rolling mean. Z > +2 indicates overbought (2 std devs above mean), Z < -2 oversold. Ideal for comparing signal strength across different assets or making indicators stationary for ML models. Common thresholds: +/-1.5 (aggressive), +/-2.0 (standard), +/-2.5 (conservative).
limitations: Assumes distribution is roughly normal - breaks down with skewed or heavy-tailed data. Extreme values can persist longer than expected in trending regimes. Window size critical - too short creates noise, too long misses regime changes. Not suitable for non-stationary series without detrending first.

name: Beta (Rolling)

options.name: Window Size
options.desc: Rolling window size for beta calculation
options.tuningGuidance: Minimum 20-30 bars for stable beta estimates. Use 60-120 for standard equity beta (matches industry practice). Shorter windows (20-40) for tactical trading and rapid regime detection. Longer windows (200-252) for strategic allocation and long-term beta characteristics.

desc: Calculates rolling beta coefficient measuring an asset's sensitivity to market movements. Beta = Cov(asset, market) / Var(market). Beta > 1 indicates higher volatility than market, < 1 lower, = 1 matches market.
usageContext: Essential for risk management, portfolio construction, and hedging. Track time-varying market sensitivity for dynamic allocation. Identify defensive (low beta) vs aggressive (high beta) assets. Use for CAPM-based expected returns, hedge ratio calculation, and sector rotation based on beta regimes. Trigger phrases: 'market sensitivity', 'beta exposure', 'systematic risk', 'market beta', 'CAPM beta', 'hedge ratio', 'beta-neutral', 'market exposure'.
limitations: Assumes linear relationship between asset and market. Beta is backward-looking and may not predict future sensitivity. Requires sufficiently long window for stable estimates. Market definition affects results (SPY vs sector index).

name: Rolling Correlation

options.name: Window Size
options.desc: Rolling window size for correlation calculation (ignored when window_type=expanding)
options.tuningGuidance: Minimum 10-20 bars for stable estimates. Use 20-50 for tactical correlation (daily regime changes), 60-120 for strategic allocation (monthly trends). Larger windows (200+) for long-term relationship analysis. Balance stability vs responsiveness to regime shifts.

options.name: Window Type
options.desc: Rolling (fixed-size sliding) or Expanding (cumulative from start)
options.tuningGuidance: Rolling: fixed lookback window, captures recent regime. Expanding: uses all data from start, gives stable full-period correlation.

options.name: Correlation Method
options.desc: Type of correlation coefficient to compute
options.tuningGuidance: Pearson: measures linear relationship strength, sensitive to outliers. Spearman: rank-based, robust to outliers and non-linear monotonic relationships. Kendall: concordance measure, most robust but computationally expensive.

desc: Calculates correlation coefficient between two series over a rolling window. Supports Pearson (linear), Spearman (rank), and Kendall (concordance) methods. Values range from -1 (perfect negative) to +1 (perfect positive correlation).
usageContext: Use for lead-lag analysis, pairs trading, and cross-asset relationship monitoring. Track evolving correlation between assets for pair selection, hedge effectiveness, or diversification analysis. Common use: rolling correlation between stock and sector index to detect beta changes, or between two assets in pairs trading to identify correlation breakdowns. KEY DIFFERENCE from rolling_cov: Correlation is normalized to [-1,+1], making it comparable across different asset pairs regardless of scale. Use rolling_cov when absolute comovement magnitude matters (portfolio risk), rolling_corr when relationship strength matters (pair selection). Trigger phrases: 'correlation between', 'how correlated', 'relationship strength', 'correlation breakdown', 'diversification', 'co-movement', 'pair selection'.
limitations: Only detects linear relationships - may miss non-linear dependencies. Window size critical: too small creates noise, too large misses regime changes. Sensitive to outliers. Correlation doesn't imply causation. Non-stationary series can show spurious correlations.

name: Volatility Estimator

options.name: Estimator Type
options.desc: Volatility estimation method to use
options.tuningGuidance: garman_klass: Best general-purpose, ~8x more efficient than close-to-close, uses full OHLC. parkinson: High-low range only, ~5x efficient, good when open/close unavailable. yang_zhang: Best for markets with overnight gaps (stocks), combines overnight and intraday components. hodges_tompkins: Bias-corrected for small samples, close-to-close only.

options.name: Period
options.desc: Lookback window for volatility calculation
options.tuningGuidance: Shorter periods (7-10) track volatility changes quickly but are noisier. Standard 14-21 for tactical trading. Longer periods (30-60) for strategic allocation. For options pricing, match to the target expiration horizon.

options.name: Trading Periods Per Year
options.desc: Annual trading period count for annualizing volatility
options.tuningGuidance: Use 252 for US stocks, 365 for crypto (24/7 markets), ~260 for international equities. For hourly data, use 252*6.5 (~1638). For 5-min data, 252*6.5*12 (~19656).

desc: Range-based volatility estimators that are more efficient than close-to-close standard deviation. Garman-Klass (1980) and Yang-Zhang (2000) use full OHLC data. Parkinson (1980) uses high-low range. Hodges-Tompkins (2002) provides bias-corrected estimates for small samples using close-to-close returns.
usageContext: Compute annualized realized volatility using range-based estimators that are statistically more efficient than simple close-to-close standard deviation. OUTPUT SCALE: Decimal fraction, NOT multiplied by 100. A value of 0.20 means 20% annualized volatility. Use vol > 0.30 for 30% threshold (not > 30). KEY CHOICE - Estimator Selection: (1) garman_klass: Best general-purpose estimator. Uses OHLC for ~8x efficiency gain over close-to-close (Garman & Klass 1980). Assumes no drift and continuous trading. Best for: liquid instruments with no overnight gaps (futures, forex). (2) parkinson: High-low range estimator, ~5.2x efficient (Parkinson 1980). Only needs high and low prices. Best for: data with missing open/close, or when you want a simple, robust measure. (3) yang_zhang: Combines overnight (close-to-open) and intraday (open-to-close) components. Handles opening jumps (Yang & Zhang 2000). Best for: stocks and ETFs with regular overnight gaps. (4) hodges_tompkins: Bias-corrected close-to-close estimator (Hodges & Tompkins 2002). Only needs closing prices. Best for: small sample windows or assets with limited OHLC. PIPELINE PATTERN: (1) Compute volatility_estimator with appropriate type, (2) use for position sizing: position_size = target_risk / volatility, (3) or for volatility targeting: scale returns by target_vol / realized_vol. EXAMPLES: (1) Position sizing: garman_klass(period=14) outputs 0.20 (20% annualized vol). Target risk 1% per trade. Position size = 0.01 / (0.20 / sqrt(252)) = ~0.79 of capital. (2) Vol regime detection: Track 14-day vs 60-day volatility. Short > long suggests rising vol regime, reduce position sizes. (3) Options: Compare realized vol to implied vol for vol arbitrage signals.
limitations: All range-based estimators assume continuous trading - less accurate with gaps or limited hours (use yang_zhang for gapped markets). Parkinson assumes no drift and no overnight trading.
