Garman-Klass assumes zero drift. Annualization assumes volatility scales with sqrt(time) which breaks during regime changes. Not suitable for tick data - use realized variance estimators instead.

name: Fractional Differentiation (FFD)

options.name: Differentiation Order
options.desc: Fractional differentiation order. Values between 0 and 1 balance stationarity and memory preservation.
options.tuningGuidance: Start with d=0.5 and test stationarity with rolling_adf. If not stationary, increase d. The goal is the MINIMUM d that achieves stationarity (p < 0.05 on ADF test). Typical range: 0.3-0.7 for most financial series. d=1.0 equals standard differencing (full memory loss). d < 0.3 rarely achieves stationarity. d > 1.0 is over-differencing.

options.name: Weight Threshold
options.desc: Minimum weight threshold. Weights below this are truncated, determining the effective window size.
options.tuningGuidance: Default 1e-5 works well. Lower thresholds (1e-8) use more history (longer effective window) for higher fidelity but more NaN warm-up. Higher thresholds (1e-3) truncate more aggressively for faster computation and less warm-up.

desc: Fixed-Width Window Fractional Differentiation (FFD). Transforms a time series to achieve stationarity while preserving maximum memory/predictive information. Unlike integer differencing (d=1) which removes all memory, fractional differencing with d < 1 maintains a controlled amount of historical information. Based on Lopez de Prado's 'Advances in Financial Machine Learning' (2018), Chapter 5.
usageContext: Transform price series into stationary features for ML models while preserving maximum predictive memory (Lopez de Prado, AIFML 2018, Chapter 5). THE PROBLEM: Raw prices are non-stationary (unit root) and break ML model assumptions. Standard differencing (d=1) achieves stationarity but destroys all memory - the differenced series has no relationship to price levels. THE SOLUTION: Fractional differencing with d < 1 finds the sweet spot: minimum differentiation needed for stationarity while retaining maximum memory for prediction. PIPELINE PATTERN (Lopez de Prado methodology): (1) Compute log prices: log(close). (2) Test stationarity range: For d in {0.1, 0.2, ..., 1.0}, compute frac_diff(log_price, d). (3) For each d, run rolling_adf on the output. Find minimum d where p_value < 0.05. (4) Use that minimum d for all future feature engineering. (5) Feed frac_diff features into ML models (gradient boosting, neural networks). KEY INSIGHT: The minimum d varies by asset and time period. Highly persistent assets (trending) need higher d. Mean-reverting assets may be stationary at d=0 (no differencing). EXAMPLES: (1) Feature engineering: frac_diff(log(SPY), d=0.4) achieves stationarity while retaining 60% of price memory. Use as primary feature in a gradient boosting classifier. (2) Cross-asset features: Apply optimal d per asset. Some assets need d=0.3, others d=0.7. The varying d reflects different persistence characteristics. (3) Regime-adaptive: Recalibrate d quarterly as persistence changes with market conditions.
limitations: Early values are NaN due to warm-up (window = number of weights above threshold). The warm-up period grows with lower threshold and higher d. Optimal d varies by asset and time period - should be recalibrated periodically (quarterly or when regime changes detected). d > 1 is over-differencing and may remove useful signal. The FFD approximation introduces small approximation error compared to exact fractional differencing. Input should be log prices, not raw prices.

name: Engle-Granger Cointegration

options.name: Window Size
options.desc: Rolling window size for cointegration test. Minimum 100 recommended.
options.tuningGuidance: Use 100-250 for stable hedge ratios on daily data. Shorter windows (60-100) for more adaptive but noisier hedge ratios. Match to expected regime duration. Too short = noisy hedge ratio, too long = stale hedge ratio.

options.name: ADF Lags
options.desc: Number of lags for ADF test on residuals (default 1).

options.name: Significance Level
options.desc: Significance level for is_cointegrated output (default 0.05).

desc: Two-step Engle-Granger cointegration test (1987 Nobel Prize methodology). Step 1: Regress Y on X via OLS to get hedge ratio (beta) and intercept (alpha). Step 2: Test residuals (Y - alpha - beta*X) for stationarity using ADF. If residuals are stationary, the series are cointegrated - their linear combination is mean-reverting even if individual series are non-stationary.
usageContext: The foundational pairs trading tool: test if two price series are cointegrated and compute the optimal hedge ratio for spread construction (Engle & Granger 1987). FULL PIPELINE: (1) Select candidate pairs (sector peers, fundamental similarity), (2) run engle_granger to test cointegration and get hedge_ratio, (3) if is_cointegrated=1, construct spread = Y - hedge_ratio * X, (4) compute zscore of the spread, (5) enter long spread when zscore < -2, short when zscore > +2, (6) use half_life_ar1 on the spread to size positions and set holding period limits. KEY OUTPUTS: hedge_ratio is the number of units of X to short per unit of Y long. spread is the portfolio P&L when properly hedged. is_cointegrated is the quick answer to 'should I trade this pair?'. EXAMPLES: (1) Classic pairs trade: engle_granger(KO, PEP, window=120). If cointegrated, buy $1 of KO, sell $hedge_ratio of PEP. Trade the spread with z-score signals. (2) Rolling pair health: Run with rolling window. Track is_cointegrated over time. When cointegration breaks (is_cointegrated flips to 0), exit all positions. (3) Hedge ratio stability: Compare hedge_ratios across windows (60, 120, 250). Stable ratios across windows indicate robust cointegration.
limitations: Only tests pairwise cointegration (2 series). For 3+ series, use Johansen test. Hedge ratio may vary significantly over time - always use rolling estimation. Results depend on which series is Y vs X (not symmetric). Critical values for Engle-Granger residual ADF test differ from standard ADF tables. In-sample cointegration doesn't guarantee out-of-sample persistence.

name: Long & Short Zone

options.name: Hold Long
options.desc: Duration to hold long position after entry. 0 = no hold, 20 = 20 bars, 20D = 20 days.
options.tuningGuidance: 0 (default) = signal-driven exit. 5-20 bars for momentum/PEAD. 5D-20D for calendar holds. Longer holds reduce turnover but increase drawdown risk.

options.name: Hold Short
options.desc: Duration to hold short position after entry. 0 = no hold, 20 = 20 bars, 20D = 20 days.
options.tuningGuidance: Typically match hold_long unless asymmetric conviction (e.g., faster short exits in trending markets).

options.name: Strict Hold
options.desc: When true, opposing signals are ignored during hold period. Position only exits when hold expires or TP/SL triggers. When false (default), opposing signals override current hold.
options.tuningGuidance: false (default) = opposing signals flip position immediately. true = locked during hold. Use true with risk_unit SL/TP for clean exit management.

desc: Consolidated zone executor for long/short signals with hold options. Outputs signal column: 0=close, 1=long, -1=short. By default, opposing signals override hold. Use strict_hold=True to ignore opposing signals during hold.
usageContext:
Zone-based signal manager that consolidates long and short entry signals into a single
position state column (1=long, -1=short, 0=flat). This is the primary signal executor
for strategies that need to manage directional positions with optional hold periods.

STRICT HOLD BEHAVIOR: When strict_hold=true, opposing signals are completely ignored during
an active hold period. The position only exits when the hold duration expires or a stop
loss/take profit triggers. When strict_hold=false (default), an opposing signal immediately
flips the position direction and resets the hold counter.

HOLD DURATION FORMATS:
- Bar count: hold_long=20 means hold for 20 bars after entry.
- Calendar duration: hold_long=20D means hold for 20 calendar days. Also supports H (hours),
  W (weeks), M (months). The duration is measured from the entry bar's timestamp.

DOWNSTREAM SIZING: The output signal column feeds into sizers. Use conditional_select to
assign different sizes for long vs short positions:
  size = conditional_select(zone.signal > 0, long_size, zone.signal < 0, short_size, 0)
  position_size(type="percent")(size)

LONG-ONLY / SHORT-ONLY: Omit one input for directional strategies. For long-only, provide
only long_entry. For short-only, provide only short_entry.

EXAMPLES:
(1) Basic dual-direction: long_and_short_zone()(buy_signal, sell_signal)
(2) PEAD with 20-bar hold: long_and_short_zone(hold_long=20, hold_short=20)(earnings_beat, earnings_miss)
(3) Strict momentum: long_and_short_zone(hold_long=5D, hold_short=5D, strict_hold=true)(golden_cross, death_cross)
(4) Long-only event: long_and_short_zone(hold_long=10)(breakout_signal)
(5) Calendar hold: long_and_short_zone(hold_long=2W, hold_short=1W)(long_entry, short_entry)
limitations:
Requires at least one input (long_entry or short_entry). NaN/null values in inputs are
treated as false (no entry signal). Output is a signal column, not a trade command - it must
be paired with a sizing sink (risk_unit or position_size) to generate actual trades. Hold
duration is measured from entry bar, not from signal generation. Same-direction signals
during an active hold reset the hold counter (extend the hold).

name: Half-Life AR(1)

options.name: Window Size
options.desc: Rolling window size for half-life calculation. Minimum 20 recommended for statistical validity.
options.tuningGuidance: Use 50-100 for stable half-life estimates on daily data. Shorter windows (20-30) capture recent regime changes but are noisier. Longer windows (200+) for strategic pair evaluation. Window should be at least 10x the expected half-life.

desc: Estimate mean-reversion half-life using AR(1) model. Fits y(t) = alpha + beta*y(t-1) + epsilon, then computes half_life = -ln(2)/ln(beta). Used in pairs trading to estimate how quickly a spread reverts to mean. Lower half-life indicates faster mean reversion.
usageContext: Estimate how quickly a spread or residual reverts to its mean using AR(1) regression. The half-life (in bars) tells you: after a deviation from equilibrium, half the deviation will be corrected in approximately half_life bars. KEY INTERPRETATION: half_life = 5 days means a $1 deviation reverts to $0.50 in ~5 days. is_mean_reverting = 1 when AR(1) coefficient (beta) is between 0 and 1. beta < 0 indicates oscillation, beta >= 1 indicates explosive/non-stationary behavior. PIPELINE PATTERN: (1) Compute engle_granger to get spread and hedge ratio, (2) feed spread into half_life_ar1 to estimate reversion speed, (3) use half-life for position sizing: allocate more to pairs with shorter half-lives, (4) set trade duration limits at 2-3x half-life as maximum holding period. EXAMPLES: (1) Pair selection: Compare half-lives across 50 potential pairs. Select pairs with half-life between 5-30 days (fast enough to trade, slow enough to execute). (2) Stop-loss timing: If half-life = 10 days and spread hasn't reverted after 30 days (3x half-life), the relationship may have broken down - exit the trade. (3) Dynamic sizing: Weight positions inversely proportional to half-life. Half-life of 5 gets 2x the allocation of half-life of 10.
limitations: Assumes AR(1) process - real spreads may have higher-order dynamics. May produce negative or very large values for non-mean-reverting series (check is_mean_reverting output). Half-life can change significantly over time - always use rolling estimation, not static. Sensitive to outliers in the spread. Does not account for transaction costs, which matter more for short half-lives.

name: Pivot Point Support & Resistance
desc: Classic floor trader pivot points with three levels of support (S1-S3) and resistance (R1-R3). Calculated from previous bar's high, low, and close. Pivot = (H+L+C)/3, then support and resistance levels are derived from the pivot, high, and low.
usageContext: Calculate classic floor trader pivot points for identifying potential support and resistance levels. Widely used by professional day traders and institutional desks since the 1930s. KEY LEVELS: Pivot = (High + Low + Close) / 3 is the central equilibrium. S1/R1 are first targets, S2/R2 are extension targets, S3/R3 are extreme levels rarely reached. TRADING RULES: (1) Price opens above pivot = bullish bias for the session, target R1. (2) Price opens below pivot = bearish bias, target S1. (3) Breakout above R1 targets R2, failure at R1 targets pivot. (4) S2/R2 reached = likely overextended, watch for reversal. PIPELINE PATTERN: (1) Compute pivot levels from prior day/week OHLC, (2) classify current price position relative to pivot (above/below), (3) set entry at pullback to pivot or S1/R1, (4) set targets at next S/R level, (5) stop loss beyond opposite level. EXAMPLES: (1) Range day: Price oscillates between S1 and R1 - buy near S1, sell near R1 with stops beyond S2/R2. (2) Trend day: Price breaks R1 and holds above - add to longs, target R2/R3. (3) Gap analysis: Open significantly above/below pivot suggests strong directional bias.
limitations: Purely price-level based - no volume or momentum confirmation. Assumes previous bar's range is relevant for current bar's levels. Most effective on liquid, actively-traded instruments with regular sessions. Less useful on weekly/monthly timeframes where the range may not provide meaningful levels. No parameter customization - uses classic formula only (no Woodie, Camarilla, or Fibonacci variants).

name: Rolling Hurst Exponent

options.name: Window Size
options.desc: Rolling window size for Hurst exponent calculation
options.tuningGuidance: Use 50-100 for tactical regime detection (responds faster to regime shifts). Use 200-500 for strategic classification (more stable). Lag grid is automatically scaled to window size. Minimum 20 for any meaningful estimate.

desc: Rolling-window Hurst exponent using rescaled range (R/S) analysis. Computes H over a fixed rolling window to detect time-varying regime changes. H < 0.5 = mean-reverting, H = 0.5 = random walk, H > 0.5 = trending. Lag grid automatically adapts to window size.
usageContext: Detect time-varying market regimes by computing the Hurst exponent over a rolling window. Unlike the expanding version, this captures when an asset transitions between mean-reverting and trending behavior. KEY DIFFERENCE from hurst_exponent: Rolling window enables regime change detection. The expanding version gives stable long-term estimates but misses transitions. Use rolling for active strategy switching based on current regime. PIPELINE PATTERN: (1) Compute rolling Hurst on daily prices with window=100, (2) when H drops below 0.45, activate mean-reversion signals (zscore, Bollinger), (3) when H rises above 0.55, activate trend-following signals (MA crossovers, momentum). This creates an adaptive strategy that matches the current market regime. EXAMPLES: (1) Strategy switching: Rolling H(100) on SPY alternates between 0.35-0.65 over market cycles. Use H < 0.45 to trigger pairs trading, H > 0.55 for momentum. (2) Risk management: Rising H towards 0.5 from below suggests mean-reversion weakening - reduce position size in mean-reversion strategies. (3) Cross-asset regime comparison: Compute rolling H across multiple assets. Assets with diverging H values may offer diversification benefits.
limitations: Window size creates a trade-off: shorter windows respond faster to regime changes but are noisier; longer windows are more stable but lag. The lag grid scales with window size, so very small windows (< 30) have limited lag diversity. H values near 0.5 are ambiguous - could be random walk or transition point. Market microstructure noise affects short windows. Not robust to structural breaks.

name: Vortex Indicator

options.name: Period
options.desc: Lookback period for Vortex Indicator calculation
options.tuningGuidance: Standard 14. Shorter periods (7-10) for faster but noisier signals. Longer periods (21-30) for smoother trend identification. Use 14 for daily charts as a good balance.

desc: Two-line trend indicator (VI+ and VI-) based on the concept of positive and negative trend movements. Introduced by Etienne Botes and Douglas Siepman (2010), inspired by Viktor Schauberger's vortex flow analysis. VI+ measures upward trend strength, VI- measures downward trend strength.
usageContext: Identify trend direction and strength using the Vortex Indicator (Botes & Siepman 2010). VI+ captures upward price momentum, VI- captures downward momentum. Their crossovers signal trend changes. KEY SIGNALS: (1) VI+ crosses above VI- = bullish trend change (enter long). (2) VI- crosses above VI+ = bearish trend change (enter short/exit long). (3) Wide spread between VI+ and VI- = strong trend. (4) Lines converging = trend weakening. PIPELINE PATTERN: (1) Compute Vortex(14) on daily OHLC, (2) go long when VI+ > VI-, (3) go short or flat when VI- > VI+. Simple binary crossover system. KEY DIFFERENCE from ADX: While ADX measures trend strength without direction, Vortex provides both direction (which line is higher) AND strength (spread between lines). Simpler than Ichimoku, more directional than ADX. EXAMPLES: (1) Crossover entry: VI+ crosses above VI- after prolonged VI- dominance = new uptrend starting. Enter long at the crossover bar close. (2) Trend confirmation: Use Vortex crossover to confirm Donchian Channel breakout - only trade breakouts when Vortex agrees on direction. (3) Divergence: Price making new highs but VI+ declining = weakening upward momentum.
limitations: Crossover signals can whipsaw in ranging markets. Single-period parameter limits adaptability. Based on True Range concept, so sensitive to gaps. No built-in signal threshold - relies purely on crossovers. May lag trend starts due to the rolling sum calculation.

name: Rollover Policy
desc: Provides front contract info for futures rollover detection. Connect the active input to a futures_continuation.s output. At runtime, the execution engine reads the current front contract and compares with held positions to detect rollovers.
usageContext:
Pass-through executor that enables automatic futures contract rollover detection.
When the front-month contract changes (as reported by futures_continuation), the execution
engine automatically liquidates the old contract position and re-enters on the new contract.

WIRING: Connect futures_continuation.s (the active contract ticker output) to
rollover_policy.active. The execution engine monitors this value each bar and triggers
a rollover when it changes.

  futures_continuation(depth=1)  →  .s  →  rollover_policy.active

INTERACTION WITH ZONE EXECUTOR: rollover_policy works alongside long_and_short_zone.
The zone executor manages entry/exit signals and hold periods, while rollover_policy
handles the mechanical contract switch. Both are required for a complete futures strategy.

TYPICAL FUTURES STRATEGY WIRING:
  # Data layer
  cont = futures_continuation(depth=1)(ZC)
  # Signal layer
  signal = long_and_short_zone(hold_long=20)(buy_signal)
  # Execution layer
  rollover_policy()(cont.s)          # rollover detection
  risk_unit()(risk_pct=1, stop_distance=atr(14)*2)  # sizing + SL

BEHAVIOR: On rollover bars, the engine closes the expiring contract at the current bar's
close and opens an equivalent position on the new front contract. This is transparent to
the strategy logic — signals and sizing continue uninterrupted.
limitations:
Requires futures_continuation transform to provide contract ticker data via the .s output.
Only meaningful for futures assets — has no effect on stocks, FX, or crypto strategies.
Does not control rollover timing (that is determined by futures_continuation's roll logic).
Only one rollover_policy allowed per strategy. The rollover is executed at the bar's close
price, not at a specific time of day.

name: Three White Soldiers
desc: Bullish reversal pattern with three consecutive white candles with higher closes. Strong signal of continued upward momentum.
usageContext: Powerful three-candle bullish reversal. Three consecutive green candles with progressively higher closes. Each candle opens within previous body and closes near high. Shows sustained buying pressure. Best after downtrend at support. Signals strong conviction. More reliable than single-candle patterns. Each candle should have small/no lower wicks.
limitations: Requires clear downtrend context. Three-candle pattern slower to develop. Size of candles matters - small candles less reliable. Can appear mid-uptrend (continuation not reversal). Each candle should close in upper third of range. Opening gaps between candles weaken pattern. Watch for exhaustion after three soldiers (potential top). Very strong when proper but rare.

name: Three Black Crows
desc: Bearish reversal pattern with three consecutive black candles with lower closes. Strong signal of continued downward momentum.
usageContext: Powerful three-candle bearish reversal. Three consecutive red candles with progressively lower closes. Each candle opens within previous body and closes near low. Shows sustained selling pressure. Best after uptrend at resistance. Signals strong conviction. More reliable than single-candle patterns. Each candle should have small/no upper wicks.
limitations: Requires clear uptrend context. Three-candle pattern slower to develop - miss early entry. Size of candles matters - small candles less reliable. Can appear mid-downtrend (continuation not reversal). Each candle should close in lower third of range. Opening gaps between candles weaken pattern. Very strong pattern when properly formed, but rare.

name: Star
desc: Price gap between the current candle's body and the previous candle's body. Often a component of more complex patterns.
usageContext: Detects the 'star' component: a small-body candle that gaps away from the previous candle's body. Building block for morning/evening star patterns. Standalone star signals potential trend exhaustion through gap + small body. PIPELINE PATTERN: use as early warning of potential star pattern formation. EXAMPLE: star appearing after uptrend = watch for evening star completion.
limitations: Primarily a component pattern, not a complete signal. Gap requirement makes it less relevant in gapless markets (forex, crypto). Small body definition is subjective. Must be followed by confirmation candle (day 3) to form complete morning/evening star pattern.

name: Spinning Top
desc: Candle with a small body and longer upper and lower shadows. Indicates indecision between buyers and sellers.
usageContext: Small body with upper and lower shadows exceeding body length. Similar to doji but with a visible body. Indicates indecision but less extreme than doji. After trend = potential reversal warning. In range = continued indecision. PIPELINE PATTERN: detect spinning_top after extended trend as early reversal warning. EXAMPLE: multiple spinning tops at resistance = buying momentum weakening.
limitations: Weaker signal than doji since there is a small directional body. Very common pattern - many spinning tops don't lead to reversals. Body and shadow size thresholds subjective. Best as warning signal, not entry trigger. Needs confirmation from subsequent candles.

name: Morning Star
desc: Bullish reversal pattern with a down candle, followed by a small body candle gapped down, then an up candle gapped up.
usageContext: Three-candle bullish reversal pattern. Day 1: bearish continuation. Day 2: small body (star) gaps down showing exhaustion. Day 3: bullish candle closes well into day 1 body. Middle candle can be any color. Gaps strengthen signal but not required. Best at support after downtrend. Use for swing long entries. Morning Doji Star (middle is doji) is stronger variant.
limitations: Requires clear downtrend and support context. Gaps less common in 24/7 crypto markets. Three-candle patterns slower to develop than single candles. Middle candle size subjective. Day 3 candle should close >50% into day 1. False signals without volume confirmation. Best combined with oversold indicators or support confluence. Consider waiting for confirmation candle.

name: Inverted Hammer
desc: Bullish reversal pattern with a small body at the bottom and a long upper shadow, appearing after a downtrend.
usageContext: Bullish reversal appearing in downtrends. Long upper shadow shows buyers attempted to push price up but were repelled. However, the attempt itself signals emerging buyer interest. Small body at bottom (any color). Requires confirmation: next candle must close above inverted hammer's body. PIPELINE PATTERN: detect inverted_hammer at support, wait for confirmation candle.
limitations: Weaker than standard hammer - buyer attempt failed during the session. Requires strong confirmation from subsequent candle. Identical to shooting star visually - only context differentiates. Less reliable than hammer or engulfing patterns. Best at strong support with volume.

name: Hammer
desc: Bullish reversal pattern with a small body at the top and a long lower shadow. Indicates rejection of lower prices in a downtrend.
usageContext: Strong bullish reversal signal appearing after downtrends at support levels. Long lower shadow (2-3x body size) shows sellers pushed price down but buyers rejected lower levels. Small body at top (any color, but green stronger) shows closing near high. Requires confirmation (next candle closes higher). Most reliable at key support, with high volume.
limitations: Must appear in downtrend to be valid - hammer in uptrend is different pattern (hanging man). Needs confirmation from next candle. Lower shadow length threshold subjective. Color matters less than structure, but green preferable. False signals common without support level confluence. Consider trend strength and volume.

name: Gravestone Doji
desc: Doji with no lower shadow but a long upper shadow. Indicates rejection of higher prices and potential bearish reversal.
usageContext: Bearish doji variant with inverted T-shape (no lower wick, long upper wick). Buyers pushed price up but sellers drove it back to open. Open/close at low = strong rejection of highs. More bearish than standard doji. Best after uptrend at resistance. Very similar to shooting star but with perfect doji body. Requires next candle confirmation.
limitations: Rare pattern - strict doji body requirement. Similar to shooting star, can be misidentified. Must appear after uptrend at resistance. Needs strong confirmation candle. Upper shadow length threshold subjective. False signals in ranging markets. Best with volume spike on upper shadow. Consider shooting star as less restrictive alternative.

name: Evening Star
desc: Bearish reversal pattern with an up candle, followed by a small body candle gapped up, then a down candle gapped down.
usageContext: Three-candle bearish reversal pattern. Day 1: bullish continuation. Day 2: small body (star) gaps up showing exhaustion. Day 3: bearish candle closes well into day 1 body. Middle candle can be any color. Gaps strengthen signal but not required. Best at resistance after uptrend. Use for short entries or long exits. Evening Doji Star (middle is doji) is stronger variant.
limitations: Requires clear uptrend and resistance context. Gaps less common in 24/7 crypto markets. Three-candle patterns slower to develop. Middle candle size subjective. Day 3 candle should close >50% into day 1. False signals without volume confirmation. Best combined with overbought indicators or resistance confluence. Consider waiting for confirmation candle.

name: Gauge Chart - ONE PER ASSET

options.name: Chart Title
options.desc: Title for the gauge chart

options.name: Category
options.desc: Category for grouping in dashboard

options.name: Aggregation
options.desc: Aggregation function to apply to the input series before display

options.name: Minimum Value
options.desc: Minimum value for the gauge. For categorical gauges, defines the lower bound of the input range for auto-scaling to categories.

options.name: Maximum Value
options.desc: Maximum value for the gauge. For categorical gauges, defines the upper bound of the input range for auto-scaling to categories.

options.name: Value Type
options.desc: Format type for the value (Decimal, Percent, Monetary, Integer)

options.name: Decimal Places
options.desc: Number of decimal places to display (default: 2)

options.name: Solid Gauge
options.desc: Use solid gauge (true) or dial gauge (false)

options.name: Gauge Color
options.desc: Color for the gauge (ignored if using traffic light colors)

options.name: Traffic Light Colors
options.desc: Use red-yellow-green color scheme

options.name: Categories
options.desc: Category labels for categorical gauge (e.g., ['Extreme Fear', 'Fear', 'Neutral', 'Greed', 'Extreme Greed']). When set, the input value is auto-scaled from [min, max] to [0, N] where N is the category count. For example, with RSI (0-100) and 5 categories, set min=0, max=100 and the gauge maps RSI to the appropriate category.

options.name: Display Order
options.desc: Display order within dashboard category (lower values appear first, 0 = default position)

desc: Single-value gauge display for KPIs and metrics. One gauge per asset.
usageContext: TRIGGER PHRASES: Use when the user asks for 'gauge', 'dial', 'speedometer', 'risk score', 'RSI gauge', 'level indicator', 'utilization meter', 'sentiment gauge'. Display a SINGLE VALUE per asset as a gauge dial in the DASHBOARD view. Takes a numeric column and aggregates it over time using the 'agg' option (default: Last). Two display modes: (A) NUMERICAL mode (default): Shows value on a min/max scale. Set min/max to the expected range. Use 'use_traffic_light_colors=true' for red-yellow-green gradient, or 'color' for a solid color. 'solid=true' (default) for filled arc, 'solid=false' for classic dial with needle. (B) CATEGORICAL mode: Provide 'categories' list (e.g., ['Low','Medium','High']). The input value is AUTO-SCALED from [min,max] to [0,N] categories. Gradient colors (red->yellow->green) are applied automatically. KEY CHOICE - gauge vs cards: Use gauge when the value represents a LEVEL within a known range (utilization, risk score, allocation %). The visual dial instantly communicates 'how full' or 'how far along the scale'. Use cards when the value is a standalone number without a meaningful range (total return, trade count, PnL). KEY CHOICE - gauge vs summary_table: Use gauge for ONE headline metric with visual emphasis. Use summary_table for multiple metrics in a grid layout. EXAMPLES: (1) RSI gauge: value=rsi_column, min=0, max=100, categories=['Oversold','Neutral','Overbought'], title='RSI'. Creates a 3-zone gauge. (2) Sharpe ratio: value=sharpe_column, min=-1, max=3, use_traffic_light_colors=true, decimal_places=2. (3) Portfolio allocation: value=equity_weight, min=0, max=100, value_type=PercentFormat, color=Info.
limitations: Displays only ONE value per asset — for multiple metrics use cards or summary_table. Cannot show trends over time (use lines for that). The categorical auto-scaling divides [min,max] into equal-width zones. Per-asset only — for market-wide gauges use cs_gauge.

name: Exponentially Weighted Moving Correlation

options.name: Span
options.desc: Span for exponential weighting (decay = 2/(1+span)). Higher values give more weight to history.
options.tuningGuidance: Use span=10-20 for fast adaptation to correlation shifts (tactical trading). Use span=30-60 for balanced responsiveness and stability. Use span=100+ for strategic allocation with smooth estimates. Roughly equivalent to rolling window of span/2 bars but smoother.

desc: Calculates correlation between two series using exponential weighting, giving more weight to recent observations. Adapts faster to regime changes than simple rolling correlation while maintaining stability.
usageContext: Use when you need correlation estimates that adapt to changing market regimes faster than rolling windows. Ideal for dynamic hedging where recent correlation matters more than historical. Exponential weighting provides smooth adaptation without abrupt window edge effects. KEY DIFFERENCE from rolling_corr: Faster adaptation to regime changes. Roughly equivalent to a rolling window of span/2 bars but smoother and without edge effects. Use rolling_corr when you need a clear, interpretable lookback period; use ewm_corr when you need smooth, fast-adapting correlation for dynamic strategies. Trigger phrases: 'adaptive correlation', 'dynamic correlation', 'recent correlation', 'fast-adapting', 'exponential weighted correlation'.
limitations: Span parameter requires tuning - too low creates noise, too high lags regime changes. No clear lookback period like rolling windows, making interpretation less intuitive. Early values (first 10-20 bars) are unstable. Still only captures linear relationships.

name: Evening Doji Star
desc: Bearish reversal pattern with an up candle, followed by a doji gapped up, then a down candle gapped down. Stronger signal than Evening Star.
usageContext: Enhanced evening star where the middle candle is specifically a doji. Three candles: (1) bullish, (2) doji gapped up (total indecision at the top), (3) bearish closing into day 1. The doji middle candle makes this more reliable than standard evening star. PIPELINE PATTERN: detect evening_doji_star at resistance for high-probability short entries.
limitations: Rarer than standard evening star due to doji requirement. Gap requirement may not apply in all markets. Three-candle pattern develops slowly. Day 3 should close well into day 1 body for validity. Needs volume confirmation.

name: Engulfing Bull
desc: Bullish pattern where a large up candle completely engulfs the previous down candle. Strong signal of trend reversal to upside.
usageContext: Powerful two-candle bullish reversal pattern. Second candle's body completely engulfs first candle's body (shadows don't matter). Shows momentum shift: sellers controlled day 1, but buyers overwhelmed them day 2. Best after downtrend at support. Larger engulfing candle = stronger signal. High volume on engulfing candle increases reliability. Use for swing trading entries.
limitations: Requires clear downtrend context to be valid. Pattern frequency varies by timeframe. Body size matters - small bodies less reliable. Gaps between candles strengthen pattern. False signals increase in choppy markets. Consider engulfing candle size relative to recent range. Best combined with support levels, volume confirmation, or other bullish indicators.

name: Dragonfly Doji
desc: Doji with no upper shadow but a long lower shadow. Indicates rejection of lower prices and potential bullish reversal.
usageContext: Bullish doji variant with T-shape (no upper wick, long lower wick). Sellers pushed price down but buyers drove it back to open. Open/close at high = strong rejection of lows. More bullish than standard doji. Best after downtrend at support. Very similar to hammer but with smaller body (doji). Requires next candle confirmation.
limitations: Rare pattern - strict doji body requirement. Similar to hammer, can be misidentified. Must appear after downtrend at support. Needs strong confirmation candle. Lower shadow length threshold subjective. False signals in ranging markets. Best with volume spike on lower shadow. Consider hammer as less restrictive alternative.

name: Doji
desc: Candle with virtually no body where open and close are at the same level. Indicates market indecision and potential reversal.
usageContext: Neutral candlestick signaling indecision between buyers and sellers. Context matters: doji after uptrend suggests potential top, after downtrend suggests potential bottom. Often precedes reversals but needs confirmation from next candle. Use with support/resistance levels or other indicators. Multiple dojis signal consolidation.
limitations: Not directional on its own - requires context and confirmation. Can appear frequently in ranging markets without significance. Different doji types (dragonfly, gravestone, long-legged) have different implications. Body size threshold subjective. Best used as warning signal, not entry trigger. Combine with volume and trend analysis.

name: Big White Candle
desc: Large bullish candle with a long body. Indicates strong buying pressure and potential upward momentum.
usageContext: Large bullish candle with body significantly exceeding average range. Signals strong buying conviction. In uptrend = continuation. At resistance = potential breakout. Body should be >1.5x average body size. PIPELINE PATTERN: detect big_white_candle, use as momentum confirmation or breakout signal. EXAMPLE: big_white_candle breaking above resistance = strong bullish breakout.
limitations: Single-candle pattern - less reliable than multi-candle patterns. Can appear as climactic buying (reversal possible). Body size threshold is parameter-dependent. Needs context (trend, support/resistance) for interpretation.

name: Big Black Candle
desc: Large bearish candle with a long body. Indicates strong selling pressure and potential downward momentum.
usageContext: Large bearish candle with body significantly exceeding average range. Signals strong selling conviction. In downtrend = continuation. At support = potential breakdown. Body should be >1.5x average body size. PIPELINE PATTERN: detect big_black_candle, use as momentum confirmation or breakdown signal. EXAMPLE: big_black_candle breaking below support = strong bearish breakdown.
limitations: Single-candle pattern - less reliable than multi-candle patterns. Can appear as climactic selling (reversal possible). Body size threshold is parameter-dependent. Needs context (trend, support/resistance) for interpretation.

name: Rolling ADF Test

options.name: Window Size
options.desc: Rolling window size for ADF test. Minimum 50 recommended for reliable results.
options.tuningGuidance: Use 100-200 for reliable p-values on daily data. Minimum 50 for any meaningful result. Shorter windows track stationarity changes faster but give less reliable statistics. Match to your trading horizon.

options.name: ADF Lags
options.desc: Number of lags for ADF regression (default 1).
options.tuningGuidance: Default 1 is sufficient for most applications. Use higher lags (2-4) for series with strong autocorrelation. Too many lags reduce test power.

options.name: Significance Level
options.desc: Significance level for is_stationary output (default 0.05, options: 0.01, 0.05, 0.10).

options.name: Deterministic Terms
options.desc: Deterministic terms: 'nc' (no constant), 'c' (constant only, default), 'ct' (constant + trend).
options.tuningGuidance: Use 'c' for spreads and residuals (most common). Use 'ct' if the series has a deterministic trend component. Use 'nc' for already-demeaned series.

desc: Rolling Augmented Dickey-Fuller test for stationarity. Tests null hypothesis that series has a unit root (non-stationary). Returns test statistic, p-value, and critical values at 1%, 5%, 10% significance. Uses MacKinnon (1994, 2010) tables for p-value computation.
usageContext: Test whether a time series (spread, residual, or price) is stationary over a rolling window. The ADF test's null hypothesis is that the series has a unit root (non-stationary). Rejecting (p_value < significance) indicates stationarity/mean-reversion. KEY INTERPRETATION: p_value < 0.01 = strong evidence of stationarity. p_value < 0.05 = moderate evidence. p_value > 0.10 = cannot reject unit root. adf_stat more negative than critical values = reject null (stationary). PIPELINE PATTERN: (1) Compute engle_granger spread for a pair, (2) feed spread into rolling_adf to monitor stationarity over time, (3) only trade when is_stationary = 1 (spread is mean-reverting), (4) exit or pause when spread loses stationarity. REGIME MONITORING: Track p_value over time. Stable p < 0.05 = healthy pair. Rising p_value approaching 0.10+ = cointegration weakening, consider reducing exposure. EXAMPLES: (1) Pair health check: rolling_adf(spread, window=100). When p_value < 0.05 for 3+ consecutive periods, pair is actively cointegrated - trade normally. (2) Entry filter: Only enter new positions when rolling ADF confirms stationarity. Combine with zscore for entry timing. (3) Pre-trade validation: Before deploying a new pair, verify that the spread maintains p < 0.05 across multiple rolling windows (robustness check).
limitations: Requires sufficient data points - minimum 50 observations per window for reliable results. Small samples inflate p-values (fail to reject null even when stationary). Low power against near-unit-root alternatives. The test is one-sided: it can reject non-stationarity but cannot confirm stationarity (absence of evidence is not evidence of absence). Choice of deterministic terms ('nc'/'c'/'ct') affects critical values and must match the data-generating process.

name: Williams %R
desc: Williams %R. Momentum oscillator that indicates overbought/oversold conditions relative to high-low range.
usageContext: Inverted stochastic oscillator ranging from 0 to -100. -20 to 0 = overbought, -80 to -100 = oversold. Shows where close is relative to high-low range. More volatile than RSI. Use for timing entries in trends (buy oversold in uptrend, sell overbought in downtrend). Divergence signals valuable. Default period 14.
limitations: Inverted scale (-100 to 0) can be confusing. Very similar to Fast Stochastic %K. Can remain in extreme zones during strong trends. High false signal rate without filters. Best combined with trend indicator. Less popular than RSI/Stochastic. Consider using regular Stochastic instead for clearer interpretation.

name: Weighted Close Price
desc: Weighted Close Price. Average of OHLC prices with extra weight given to close: (H+L+C+C)/4.
usageContext: Close-weighted bar price: (H+L+C+C)/4. Gives double weight to closing price since close is generally considered the most important price of the bar. Smoother than raw close while emphasizing settlement price. PIPELINE PATTERN: use wcprice() as input when close price importance should be maintained. EXAMPLE: ma(wcprice()) for a close-biased smoothed price series.
limitations: Arbitrary weighting scheme (2x close). Marginal improvement over raw close for most applications. Ignores open price. Consider using close directly for simplicity unless smoothing is specifically desired.

name: Volume Oscillator
desc: Volume Oscillator. Shows difference between two volume moving averages as percentage, indicating volume trends.
usageContext: Percentage difference between short and long volume MAs. Positive = short-term volume above long-term average (increasing activity). Negative = declining volume relative to average. Use to confirm breakouts (rising vosc confirms volume participation). PIPELINE PATTERN: compute vosc(), require positive vosc for breakout entries. EXAMPLE: price breaks resistance + vosc >0 = volume-confirmed breakout.
limitations: Only measures volume trend, not price direction. Volume alone doesn't determine if moves are sustainable. Short/long period parameters need tuning per instrument. Can stay elevated during choppy high-volume periods. Best as confirmation tool.

name: Variance Over Period
desc: Variance Over Period. Calculates the variance over the specified period.
usageContext: Rolling variance (stddev squared) over a lookback window. Used in portfolio optimization, risk budgeting, and volatility targeting. Variance is additive for independent assets, making it useful for portfolio-level risk calculations. PIPELINE PATTERN: compute var for each asset, use for minimum variance portfolio weights. EXAMPLE: var(period=20) for rolling variance-based position sizing.
limitations: Units are squared, making interpretation less intuitive than stddev. Assumes stationarity. Very sensitive to outliers (squared deviations). Consider using stddev for more interpretable volatility measure.

name: Trix
desc: Trix. Triple exponentially smoothed moving average oscillator, showing percentage rate of change.
usageContext: One-period rate of change of a triple-smoothed EMA. Heavy smoothing filters out insignificant price moves, focusing on dominant trend changes. Positive = upward trend, negative = downward. Zero crossings signal trend changes. Divergences with price are reliable. PIPELINE PATTERN: compute trix(period=15), use zero-line crossovers for filtered trend signals. EXAMPLE: trix crossing above zero = dominant trend turning bullish after triple smoothing.
limitations: Very lagging due to triple smoothing - slow to react. Misses short-term moves by design. Not suitable for short-term trading. Primarily a long-term trend indicator. Period selection significantly affects responsiveness.

name: True Range
desc: True Range. Measures market volatility by comparing current price range to previous close.
usageContext: Maximum of: (high - low), abs(high - prev_close), abs(low - prev_close). Accounts for gaps by including previous close. Foundation for ATR. Individual bars' true range useful for identifying volatility spikes. PIPELINE PATTERN: compute tr(), smooth with ma() for custom ATR variants, or use raw for spike detection. EXAMPLE: tr significantly above atr = unusual volatility bar (potential news event or breakout).
limitations: Single-bar measure - very noisy without smoothing. Absolute value depends on price level (use NATR for normalization). Spikes from gaps can distort. Usually used as building block for ATR rather than directly.

name: Sum Over Period
desc: Sum Over Period. Calculates the sum over the specified period for each element position.
usageContext: Rolling sum over a lookback window. Fundamental building block for many indicators. Use for cumulative volume analysis, counting signal occurrences, or computing rolling totals. PIPELINE PATTERN: sum binary signals over period to count occurrences. EXAMPLE: sum(period=10) on boolean up-day flags counts bullish days in the last 10 bars.
limitations: Raw sum is scale-dependent - larger values dominate. Not normalized. For averaging use ma() instead. Sensitive to window size selection. Cumulative sums can drift over long periods.

name: Stochastic RSI
desc: Stochastic RSI. Applies stochastic formula to RSI values, creating a more sensitive oscillator.
usageContext: More sensitive version of RSI using stochastic calculation on RSI values. OUTPUT SCALE: 0 to 1 (decimal fraction, NOT 0-100). Use > 0.80 for overbought, < 0.20 for oversold. More responsive to price changes than RSI - better for short-term trading. Generates more signals than RSI. Best with %K and %D lines for crossovers. Popular for crypto and volatile assets.
limitations: Extremely sensitive - very high false signal rate. Can stay overbought/oversold for extended periods in trends. Requires heavy filtering or confirmation. Not suitable as standalone indicator. Best in strongly ranging markets. Too noisy for position trading. Consider using only in confirmed ranges with other filters.

name: Stochastic Oscillator
desc: Stochastic Oscillator. Compares closing price to price range over a period, indicating momentum and overbought/oversold conditions.
usageContext: Two lines: %K (fast) and %D (slow, smoothed). Overbought >80, oversold <20. Signals: K crosses D (bullish/bearish), divergence with price, extreme readings. More sensitive than RSI - reacts faster to price changes. Use for timing entries in range-bound markets or pullback entries in trends. Common settings: 14,3,3 (standard) or 5,3,3 (faster).
limitations: Very sensitive - many false signals in trending markets. Can remain overbought/oversold during strong trends. Requires smoothing (%D) to reduce noise. Best in ranging/oscillating markets. Not reliable as standalone - combine with trend filter. Parameter sensitivity high - different settings dramatically change signals.

name: Standard Error Over Period
desc: Standard Error Over Period. Calculates the standard error over the specified period.
usageContext: Rolling standard error of the mean - measures precision of the sample mean estimate. Smaller than stddev by factor of sqrt(n). Use with linear regression to build confidence intervals around trend estimates. PIPELINE PATTERN: compute linreg + stderr to create regression channel bands. EXAMPLE: linreg +/- 2*stderr gives ~95% confidence band for regression forecast.
limitations: Assumes independent observations, which time series data violates due to autocorrelation. Less intuitive than stddev for volatility analysis. Mainly useful as a component for regression-based strategies.

name: Standard Deviation Over Period
desc: Standard Deviation Over Period. Calculates the standard deviation over the specified period.
usageContext: Rolling standard deviation measures price dispersion around the mean. Core component of Bollinger Bands and many volatility models. Use for position sizing (higher stddev = smaller position), regime detection (rising stddev = trending), or z-score normalization. PIPELINE PATTERN: compute stddev(period=20), then z-score = (price - sma) / stddev for normalized overbought/oversold. EXAMPLE: stddev squeeze (falling stddev) precedes breakouts.
limitations: Assumes returns are normally distributed, which is rarely true in financial markets. Sensitive to outliers. Backward-looking - cannot predict future volatility. Consider GARCH models for heteroskedastic data.

name: Acceleration Bands

options.name: Period
options.desc: SMA period for the middle band and band width calculation
options.tuningGuidance: Standard 20 for daily charts. Shorter periods (10-15) for intraday or more responsive bands. Longer periods (30-50) for strategic volatility analysis.

options.name: Width Multiplier
options.desc: Multiplier for band width based on high-low range percentage
options.tuningGuidance: Default 4.0. Higher values widen bands (fewer breakout signals, more conservative). Lower values (2.0-3.0) for tighter, more responsive bands.

desc: Volatility envelope based on the high-low range as a percentage of the typical price. Upper and lower bands expand and contract with market volatility, providing adaptive breakout and overbought/oversold levels. Middle band is a simple moving average.
usageContext: Adaptive volatility bands based on the high-low range as a percentage of typical price. Unlike Bollinger Bands (which use standard deviation), Acceleration Bands use the raw price range, making them more responsive to actual intra-bar volatility. KEY SIGNALS: (1) Price closing above upper band = strong bullish momentum, potential breakout or acceleration phase. (2) Price closing below lower band = strong bearish momentum. (3) Bands narrowing = decreasing volatility, breakout imminent. (4) Bands widening = increasing volatility, trend in progress. KEY DIFFERENCE from Bollinger Bands: Acceleration Bands use high-low range rather than standard deviation. This makes them more sensitive to intra-bar volatility and less affected by closing price distribution assumptions. KEY DIFFERENCE from Keltner Channels: Keltner uses ATR for band width, which is smoother. Acceleration Bands use raw range percentage, which is more responsive. PIPELINE PATTERN: (1) Compute Acceleration Bands, (2) enter long when price closes above upper band for N consecutive bars (acceleration), (3) hold while price stays above middle band, (4) exit when price closes below middle band. EXAMPLES: (1) Breakout entry: Price closes above upper band after period of narrow bands = volatility expansion breakout. Enter in direction of break. (2) Mean reversion: In ranging market, buy at lower band, sell at upper band. (3) Trend filter: Only take trend-following signals when price is between middle and upper band (bullish acceleration zone).
limitations: Band width depends on the high-low range, which can be artificially inflated by single outlier bars (news events, gaps). Less smooth than ATR-based channels. No standard academic backing compared to Bollinger Bands. The multiplier parameter needs calibration per asset and timeframe.

name: Accumulation/Distribution Line
desc: Accumulation/Distribution Line. Volume-based indicator designed to measure cumulative flow of money into and out of a security.
usageContext: Cumulative volume-weighted indicator using the close location value (CLV) to weight each bar's volume. CLV = (close - low - (high - close)) / (high - low). Rising A/D with rising price confirms uptrend. Divergence between A/D and price signals potential reversal. PIPELINE PATTERN: compute ad(), apply ma() for smoothing, look for divergences with price. EXAMPLE: price makes new high but A/D doesn't = bearish divergence, distribution is occurring.
limitations: Cumulative nature makes absolute values meaningless - focus on direction and divergences. Gaps between close and previous close are not accounted for. Can be distorted by large volume spikes. Requires quality volume data.

name: Cross-Sectional Momentum

options.name: Group By
options.desc: Group assets before applying cross-sectional operation. When set, the transform operates within each group independently.
options.tuningGuidance: Use 'sector' for industry-neutral stock strategies. Use 'category' for futures. Use 'auto_detect' to let the system choose.

desc: Computes cumulative cross-sectional mean returns across all assets at each timestamp. Calculates the average percentage change across the universe, then compounds it into a cumulative index representing aggregate market momentum.
usageContext: Compute aggregate momentum across a universe of assets, following cross-sectional momentum methodology (Jegadeesh & Titman 1993). At each timestamp, the mean return across all assets is calculated and cumulatively compounded. The result is broadcast back to each asset column, providing a universe-level momentum index. KEY DIFFERENCE from per-asset momentum: This does NOT rank individual assets. It measures the AVERAGE momentum of the entire universe. To rank individual assets by momentum and select winners/losers, use cs_rank or cs_select on per-asset returns instead. cs_momentum answers 'how is the universe performing overall?' while cs_rank + cs_select answers 'which assets are outperforming?' PIPELINE PATTERN: Typical cross-sectional momentum strategies combine multiple transforms: (1) compute per-asset returns, (2) cs_zscore to normalize, (3) cs_select(direction=top, k=10) to pick winners, or cs_rank to assign portfolio weights proportional to rank. Use cs_momentum as a market regime filter: when universe-wide momentum is positive, tilt long; when negative, reduce exposure. EXAMPLES: (1) Universe momentum regime filter: Feed daily returns from 50 stocks into cs_momentum. When the resulting index is rising (positive slope), the broad market has positive momentum - favor long positions. When falling, reduce risk. (2) Sector rotation signal: Group by sector via group_by option, compute cs_momentum per sector. Compare sector momentum indices to identify which sectors lead. (3) Risk-on/risk-off: Compare cs_momentum of equity universe vs bond universe. Divergence signals regime shifts useful for tactical asset allocation.
limitations: Requires multiple assets in the universe (10+ recommended for stable estimates). Single-asset strategies will fail. The cumulative product can drift significantly over long horizons - consider windowed analysis for multi-year backtests. This is a universe-level aggregate, NOT a per-asset ranking signal. For asset selection based on momentum, use cs_rank or cs_select instead.

name: Trailing Stop

options.name: Step Size
options.desc: Discrete step size for trailing (0 = continuous)
options.tuningGuidance: 0 (default) = continuous trailing, updates every bar. Best for trending markets. 0.25-1.0 for stocks — reduces whipsaw in choppy markets by requiring meaningful moves before adjusting. Larger steps for more volatile assets.

desc: Trailing stop that follows price. Activates after reaching activation_distance profit, then trails at distance from highest (long) or lowest (short) price.
usageContext:
Dynamic trailing stop that ratchets in the direction of profit, protecting gains while
allowing the trade to run. Based on the Chandelier Exit concept (Chuck LeBeau).

BASIC MECHANISM: Once activated, the stop trails behind the highest high (for longs) or
lowest low (for shorts) at a fixed distance. The stop only moves in the profitable direction
and never retreats.

ACTIVATION DISTANCE: The `activation` input controls when trailing begins. If provided, the
trailing stop does not activate until price has moved at least `activation` distance in
profit from entry. Before activation, the stop remains at entry - distance (long) or
entry + distance (short). Default activation=0 means immediate trailing.

STEPPED vs CONTINUOUS:
- step=0 (default): Continuous trailing - stop updates every bar to track the extremum.
- step=N: Stepped trailing - stop only moves in increments of N. This reduces whipsaw in
  choppy markets by requiring a meaningful move before adjusting the stop.

DIRECTION AWARENESS:
- Long: trail_stop = highest_high_since_entry - distance. Stop only moves UP.
- Short: trail_stop = lowest_low_since_entry + distance. Stop only moves DOWN.

EXAMPLES:
(1) ATR trailing: trailing_stop()(distance=atr(14)*2) -- 2x ATR continuous trail
(2) With activation: trailing_stop()(distance=atr(14), activation=atr(14)*3) -- activate at 3R
(3) Stepped: trailing_stop(step=0.50)(distance=2.0) -- trail in $0.50 increments
(4) Chandelier exit: trailing_stop()(distance=atr(22)*3) -- classic Chandelier parameterization
limitations:
Distance must be > 0 (NaN or zero means no trailing stop for that bar). Activation distance
defaults to 0 (immediate activation). The stop only follows the profitable direction and
never retreats. Step=0 means continuous trailing (updates every bar). Only one trailing_stop
component allowed per strategy. Works standalone or combined with stop_loss (SL acts as
disaster floor beneath the trailing stop) or risk_unit (trail adds dynamic protection
beyond the bundled stop).

name: Ulcer Index

options.name: Period
options.desc: Lookback window for measuring drawdown severity
options.tuningGuidance: Standard 14 for short-term pain measurement. Use 21-30 for typical drawdown analysis. Longer periods (60+) for strategic risk assessment. Martin (1987) originally used 14 for mutual fund evaluation.

options.name: Use Sum
options.desc: If true, returns the sum of squared drawdowns instead of the RMS (root mean square). The standard Ulcer Index uses RMS (false). Sum variant useful for cumulative pain measurement.

desc: Downside volatility measure that focuses on drawdowns from rolling peaks rather than overall volatility. Developed by Peter Martin (1987). Also known as the 'pain index'. Measures the root mean square of percentage drawdowns from the highest value in the window.
usageContext: Measure downside risk through the severity and duration of drawdowns from rolling peaks. Unlike standard deviation, Ulcer Index penalizes only downside moves, reflecting what investors actually worry about. KEY METRIC - Martin Ratio: return / ulcer_index. Superior to Sharpe ratio for risk-averse investors because it only penalizes downside volatility. A strategy with high returns and low Ulcer Index has good risk-adjusted performance. KEY DIFFERENCE from max drawdown: Ulcer Index captures the PERSISTENCE and DEPTH of drawdowns, not just the maximum. A strategy with many small drawdowns may have higher Ulcer Index than one with a single deep but brief drawdown. PIPELINE PATTERN: (1) Compute Ulcer Index on strategy equity curve, (2) compute Martin Ratio = annualized_return / ulcer_index, (3) compare across strategies - higher Martin Ratio = better risk-adjusted returns. EXAMPLES: (1) Strategy comparison: Strategy A has 15% return, UI=5%. Strategy B has 20% return, UI=12%. Martin ratios: A=3.0, B=1.67. Strategy A is better risk-adjusted. (2) Risk monitoring: Rising Ulcer Index signals deepening drawdown - reduce exposure. (3) Fund selection: Screen mutual funds by Martin Ratio over 3-year period.
limitations: Only captures downside risk - ignores upside volatility which may matter for short sellers or options strategies. The RMS calculation means brief but deep drawdowns have different impact than long but shallow ones. Less suitable for mean-reversion strategies where drawdowns are expected trading opportunities. Sensitive to the starting point of the lookback window.

name: Balance Sheet

options.name: Reporting Period
options.desc: Reporting period: quarterly (10-Q) or annual (10-K). TTM is not available for balance sheets (point-in-time snapshot, not a flow).

desc: Load balance sheet fundamental data. Provides assets, liabilities, equity, and other balance sheet metrics over time.
usageContext:
Balance sheet snapshots from SEC filings.
- Value investing: Evaluate book value, debt/equity, working capital.
- Leverage analysis: Track debt levels and liquidity ratios over time.
- Quality screening: Monitor cash positions and asset composition trends.
Combine with income_statement and cash_flow for full fundamental picture.
Use finance_ratio transform to compute derived ratios from raw data.
limitations:
Sparse: Quarterly (~4 rows/year) or annual (~1 row/year) per asset. NullPolicy=AllowAll.
Use ffill to forward-fill last known values when joining with daily price data.
SEC-filed US equities only. Reporting lag: typically 30-60 days after period end.
Keyed to filing_date (when filed with SEC), not period_end.

name: Swing Highs and Lows

options.name: Swing Length
options.desc: Number of bars on each side required to confirm swing point
options.tuningGuidance: 3-5 for scalping/intraday (more sensitive). 5-10 for swing trading (balanced). 10-20 for position trading (major swings only). Higher values reduce noise but increase lag.

desc: Identifies swing high and low points in price data by finding local peaks and valleys within a specified lookback period.
usageContext: Foundation for Smart Money Concepts (SMC) analysis. Identifies key pivot points that form market structure. Feed into other SMC transforms (BOS/CHOCH, liquidity, order blocks). Also useful for support/resistance levels and trend analysis.
limitations: Lagging indicator - swing confirmed only after N bars. Shorter swing_length = more noise, longer = less responsive. In strong trends, may miss minor swings. Works best on clean price action.

name: Engulfing Bear
desc: Bearish pattern where a large down candle completely engulfs the previous up candle. Strong signal of trend reversal to downside.
usageContext: Powerful two-candle bearish reversal pattern. Second candle's body completely engulfs first candle's body (shadows don't matter). Shows momentum shift: buyers controlled day 1, but sellers overwhelmed them day 2. Best after uptrend at resistance. Larger engulfing candle = stronger signal. High volume on engulfing candle increases reliability. Use for short entries or long exits.
limitations: Requires clear uptrend context to be valid. Pattern frequency varies by timeframe. Body size matters - small bodies less reliable. Gaps between candles strengthen pattern. False signals increase in choppy markets. Consider engulfing candle size relative to recent range. Best combined with resistance levels, volume confirmation, or other bearish indicators.

name: Cross-Sectional Factor Analysis

options.name: Correlation Method
options.desc: Type of correlation for IC calculation
options.tuningGuidance: Spearman (default): robust to outliers, captures monotonic relationships. Pearson: linear relationships, sensitive to outliers. Kendall: most robust, but computationally expensive.

options.name: Minimum Observations
options.desc: Minimum valid observations required per timestamp
options.tuningGuidance: Use 10+ for stable IC estimates. Increase for smaller universes with potential missing data.

options.name: IR Window
options.desc: Rolling window for Information Ratio calculation
options.tuningGuidance: 252 (1 year) is standard for annualized IR. Use 63 (quarterly) for faster adaptation.

desc: Computes Information Coefficient (IC) and related statistics for factor research. Correlates a factor signal with forward returns ACROSS assets at each timestamp, returning time series of IC, t-statistic, p-value, and Information Ratio.
usageContext: Evaluate factor predictive power using the Information Coefficient (IC), the standard metric for factor quality in quantitative finance. IC measures the cross-sectional rank correlation between a factor signal and subsequent returns at each timestamp. Implements the methodology described in Grinold & Kahn's 'Active Portfolio Management' and used by Alphalens (Quantopian), Qlib (Microsoft), and all institutional quant research platforms. OUTPUT INTERPRETATION:   IC: Cross-sectional correlation at each timestamp. |IC| > 0.05 is meaningful,     > 0.10 is strong. Positive IC = factor predicts returns correctly.   t_stat: Statistical significance of the IC. |t| > 2.0 indicates significance.   p_value: Two-sided p-value. p < 0.05 = statistically significant.   IR (Information Ratio): Rolling mean(IC) / std(IC). IR > 0.5 is good, > 1.0 is     excellent. Measures IC consistency over time (Grinold's 'Fundamental Law of     Active Management': alpha ~= IC * sqrt(breadth)). METHOD CHOICE:   Spearman (default): Rank correlation. Most robust to outliers and non-linear     relationships. Standard choice for IC analysis in factor research.   Pearson: Linear correlation. Sensitive to outliers but captures magnitude.     Use when the relationship between signal and returns is known to be linear.   Kendall: Concordance-based. Most robust but computationally expensive.     Use for small universes or when ties are common. EXAMPLES: (1) Momentum factor evaluation: signal_x=12-month return, signal_y=next-month return. Track IC over time to detect momentum crashes (IC sign reversal). (2) Multi-factor comparison: Run cs_factor_analysis on each factor separately, compare mean IC and IR to identify the strongest predictors. (3) Factor decay analysis: Run with signal_y=1-day, 5-day, 20-day, 60-day forward returns to see how quickly the signal's predictive power decays.
limitations: Requires multi-asset universe (min_obs parameter controls minimum, default 10). Fewer observations produce NaN output. IC assumes monotonic relationship between factor and returns (rank-based for Spearman/Kendall). IR requires sufficient history (ir_window bars, default 252 = 1 year) to be meaningful - early values are NaN until the window fills. Both signals must be numeric with matching timestamps across assets.

name: Psychological Support Levels (PSL)

options.name: Period
options.desc: Lookback window for computing the percentage of bars closing above the open
options.tuningGuidance: Use 10-20 for responsive sentiment readings. Standard 12 captures ~2 weeks of daily data. Longer periods (30-60) for stable market sentiment assessment.

desc: Measures the percentage of bars in the lookback window where the close exceeded the open. Acts as a market sentiment oscillator: values above 50% indicate bullish sentiment (more up-closes than down-closes), below 50% bearish. Based on psychological market behavior patterns.
usageContext: Gauge market sentiment through the ratio of bullish to bearish bars. PSL > 50% means more bars closed higher than they opened (bullish), < 50% means bearish sentiment. KEY INTERPRETATION: PSL near 50% = balanced/neutral market. PSL > 75% = extreme bullishness (potential overbought contrarian signal). PSL < 25% = extreme bearishness (potential oversold contrarian signal). PIPELINE PATTERN: (1) Compute PSL(12) on daily bars, (2) when PSL > 75% AND price at resistance, prepare for potential reversal, (3) when PSL < 25% AND price at support, look for bounce entries. KEY DIFFERENCE from RSI/Stochastic: PSL is a pure binary counting indicator - it doesn't consider magnitude of moves, only direction (close > open). This makes it robust to outliers but insensitive to move size. EXAMPLES: (1) Contrarian signal: PSL(20) reaches 80% after a strong rally - 16 out of 20 bars closed up. Historically extreme, suggests exhaustion and potential pullback. (2) Trend confirmation: PSL stays above 60% persistently = healthy uptrend with broad bar-level participation. (3) Divergence: Price makes new highs but PSL declining = fewer bars closing up, suggesting weakening breadth beneath surface-level strength.
limitations: Binary measure (close > open) ignores magnitude - a bar closing 0.01% up counts the same as 5% up. Not effective on tick data or very short timeframes where close-to-open differences are dominated by noise. Requires open price data - not available for all instruments. Extreme readings can persist in strong trends.

name: Financial Ratio

options.name: Ratio Type
options.desc: Select the financial ratio to calculate

options.name: Reporting Period
options.desc: Financial statement reporting period for underlying data

desc: Calculates financial ratios from fundamental data using vectorized operations. Valuation ratios (P/B, B/M, P/S) correctly use market cap (price × shares) per academic standards (Fama-French 1992).
usageContext:
Calculate financial ratios from fundamental data. All ratios output RAW DECIMAL values.

OUTPUT SCALE BY RATIO TYPE:
- Margin ratios (gross_margin, operating_margin, net_margin): Decimal fraction [0,1].
  A value of 0.25 means 25% margin. Use > 0.10 for 10% threshold (not > 10).
- Return ratios (roe, roa, gpoa): Decimal fraction. 0.15 = 15% return on equity/assets.
- Liquidity ratios (current_ratio, quick_ratio, cash_ratio): Raw ratio, typically [0, 5+].
  current_ratio > 1.5 means current assets are 1.5x current liabilities.
- Leverage ratios (debt_to_equity, debt_ratio): Raw ratio. debt_to_equity of 2.0 means
  liabilities are 2x equity. debt_ratio of 0.60 means 60% of assets funded by debt.
- Valuation multiples (price_to_earnings, price_to_sales, price_to_book, ev_to_ebitda,
  ev_to_sales): Raw ratio/multiple. P/E of 20 means price is 20x earnings.
- Inverse valuation (earnings_yield, book_to_market): Decimal fraction. earnings_yield
  of 0.05 = 5% yield. book_to_market of 0.50 = book value is half of market cap.
- Market value (market_cap, enterprise_value): Raw dollar amounts.
- Free cash flow: Raw dollar amount (operating CF + capex).

Valuation ratios use proper market cap (price x shares) per Fama-French (1992).
limitations: Values are only calculated when all required fundamental data is available. Valuation ratios require both price and shares data. Margin and return ratios output decimal fractions (0.25 = 25%), not whole-number percentages.

name: CUSUM Change Point Detector

options.name: Threshold
options.desc: Amplitude threshold for detecting a change (used if use_std_threshold=false)
options.tuningGuidance: Higher = fewer but more significant detections. Start with 4-6x expected noise level.

options.name: Drift
options.desc: Drift term to prevent false alarms in stable periods
options.tuningGuidance: Use 0 for sensitive detection, 0.5-1.0x noise level for robustness.

options.name: Use Std-Based Threshold
options.desc: If true, threshold = std_multiplier * std(differences)

options.name: Std Multiplier
options.desc: Number of standard deviations for threshold (when use_std_threshold=true)
options.tuningGuidance: 3-4 for sensitive, 5-6 for conservative. Like a z-score threshold.

desc: CUSUM (Cumulative Sum) change-point detection algorithm (Page 1954). Detects abrupt mean shifts and structural breaks in time series by tracking cumulative deviations. Signals when accumulated drift exceeds threshold. Detects both upward and downward regime changes.
usageContext: Detect structural breaks in prices, spreads, or returns for regime-switching strategies. Best applied to DIFFERENCED or stationary data (returns, spread residuals) — raw prices will trigger false alarms due to trending. Workflow: compute returns → apply cusum → use change_signal as regime gate. cusum_pos/cusum_neg rise before alarm — use as leading indicators. Combine with hmm for confirmation: cusum detects the break, hmm classifies the new regime.
limitations: Assumes stationary process between change points. May produce false alarms in trending markets. Works best on differenced data or spreads.

name: Equal Weight

options.name: Maximum Weight
options.desc: Maximum weight per asset (caps individual weights)

desc: Cross-sectional allocator that assigns equal weights (1/N) to active assets. Inactive assets (where mask is false) get weight 0. Weights are always unsigned (0 to 1) - direction comes from trade signals.
usageContext: Connect to a boolean mask indicating active assets (e.g., cs_rank(momentum) <= 10). Outputs equal weights for active assets, 0 for inactive. Connect weight output to dynamic_size(type='percent') for sizing. Example: equal_weight()(active_mask)
limitations: Cross-sectional only. All active assets get same weight. Use max_weight option to cap individual positions.

name: Is Valid
desc: Element-wise validity check. Returns true where input value is not null/missing, false otherwise. Unlike x != null which propagates null, this always returns a boolean result.
usageContext: Detect valid (non-null) data points for conditional execution. Use for indicator warm-up detection (is_valid checks if MA has enough data), data quality monitoring, and conditional logic that should only execute when data exists. Common pattern: is_valid(indicator) AND signal.
limitations: None - always produces a valid boolean output. Never returns null.

name: Index
desc: Returns bar index timestamps as a column, bridging bar data and datetime analysis. Every datetime workflow starts with index() to expose the bar's timestamp for extraction, differencing, or boundary detection.
usageContext:
ROLE: Every datetime workflow begins with index(). It exposes the bar's
timestamp as a column so downstream transforms can operate on it. Without
index(), bar timestamps are invisible to the transform graph.

KEY CHOICE -- index() vs direct column reference:
- index() → bar timestamps from the OHLCV timeline (what you see on the chart)
- Direct column (e.g., econ.observation_date) → timestamps embedded in datasource rows
Use index() for "when did this bar occur?" questions. Use direct columns for
"when was this data point recorded/released?" questions.

COMPOSITION: index() feeds into three downstream transforms:
- datetime_extract(component='hour')(index()) → extract hour/day/month
- datetime_diff(unit='days')(event_date, index()) → elapsed time since event
- is_period_boundary(period='month')(index()) → rebalance signals

EXAMPLES:
1. Hour extraction for intraday session logic:
   bar_hour = datetime_extract(component='hour')(index())
2. Days since reference event:
   days_since = datetime_diff(unit='days')(event_ts, index())
3. Monthly rebalance signal:
   rebal = is_period_boundary(period='month')(index())
limitations:
Returns bar index timestamps only — not arbitrary columns. Output frequency
matches the bar timeframe (daily bars → one timestamp per day). For fixed
reference timestamps use timestamp_scalar(). Cannot access sub-bar timing.

name: Is Null
desc: Element-wise null check. Returns true where input value is null/missing, false otherwise. Unlike x == null which propagates null, this always returns a boolean result.
usageContext: Detect missing data points for data quality monitoring. Use for identifying gaps in indicator output, detecting periods where data feeds dropped, or creating masks to exclude null periods from calculations. Unlike x == null which propagates null, this always returns a definite boolean result.
limitations: None - always produces a valid boolean output. Never returns null.

name: Session Window

options.name: Aggregation Per Extra Input
options.desc: List of AggregationType values for extra inputs. Not needed for OHLC (fixed: First, Max, Min, Last).

desc: Computes OHLCV statistics for defined session windows using predefined sessions (NewYork, London, Tokyo), custom time ranges, or session deltas. Captures intraday market microstructure patterns including the U-shaped volume curve (Admati & Pfleiderer 1988), overnight drift (NY Fed research shows 60%+ of equity returns accrue overnight), and event-driven volatility (NFP releases create 50-100 bps moves). SessionDelta enables precise windows like 'first 30 minutes of NY session' for studying opening reversals, closing auction dynamics, or macro data release reactions.
usageContext:
Use for session-based analysis, intraday pattern detection, and event-driven trading strategies.
- Morning reversal: track session_window for first 30 minutes of NY open to detect opening gap fade patterns.
- NFP reaction: define SessionDelta(type=NewYork, anchor=Start, offset=-60Min) to study pre-NFP positioning.
- Overnight vs. intraday: compare close-to-open returns (overnight drift) vs. open-to-close for strategy timing.
- London-NY overlap (12:00-17:00 GMT): highest FX liquidity window for mean-reversion strategies.
- Closing auction: session_window for last 30 minutes captures the 'power hour' positive drift.
- Kill zone trading: use predefined kill zone sessions for ICT-style setups.
limitations:
Requires intraday (minute-level or hourly) data -- daily bars cannot capture session-level patterns.
Session boundary detection depends on accurate timezone handling -- DST transitions can shift windows.
The overnight drift anomaly may not be exploitable due to overnight margin requirements and the inability
to trade at the exact close/open prices. NFP and other macro event reactions are highly unpredictable in
direction despite being predictable in magnitude. High-frequency patterns (opening reversal, closing auction)
are subject to severe execution slippage and transaction costs. Market microstructure has shifted with the
rise of extended hours trading (pre-market 4 AM, after-hours to 8 PM), diluting traditional session
boundaries.

name: Directional Movement Index
desc: Directional Movement Index. Measures trending strength by comparing +DI and -DI indicators.
usageContext: Unsmoothed version of ADX - measures absolute difference between +DI and -DI as a percentage. More responsive than ADX but noisier. DX >25 = trending, <20 = ranging. PIPELINE PATTERN: use dx for faster trend strength detection, or smooth it to get ADX. EXAMPLE: dx spiking above 30 = strong directional move starting.
limitations: More volatile than ADX since it's unsmoothed. Can spike on single large bars. Primarily used as building block for ADX. Most traders prefer the smoother ADX. No directional information.

name: Pie Chart - ONE PER ASSET

options.name: Chart Title
options.desc: Title for the pie chart

options.name: Category
options.desc: Category for grouping in dashboard

options.name: Inner Size (Donut)
options.desc: Inner cutout percentage (0 = pie, 50+ = donut)

options.name: Slice Colors
options.desc: Colors for each pie slice (e.g., Red, Blue, Green)

options.name: Display Order
options.desc: Display order within dashboard category (lower values appear first, 0 = default position)

desc: Pie/donut chart showing proportional composition from label and value columns. Groups by label, sums values per group, normalizes as percentage of total. Set inner_size > 0 (typically 50-70) for donut style. Use for portfolio allocation, sector breakdown, win/loss composition with 2-8 categories.
