usageContext: TRIGGER PHRASES: Use when the user asks for 'pie chart', 'donut chart', 'composition', 'allocation breakdown', 'proportion', 'percentage split', 'part of whole', 'sector weights', 'portfolio composition'. Show proportional composition as a pie or donut chart in the DASHBOARD view. Takes a label column (string) and a value column (numeric). Groups by label, sums values per group, then normalizes as percentage of total — so duplicate labels are correctly aggregated before slicing. Each unique label becomes a slice with area proportional to its share of the total. Set inner_size > 0 (typically 50-70) for donut style. KEY CHOICE - pie vs xy_bars: Use pie when the key insight is 'part of whole' (what fraction does each category represent?) and the number of categories is small (2-8). Use xy_bars when comparing absolute magnitudes across categories, when there are many categories (>8), or when the user needs to compare bar heights precisely. Pie charts are poor for comparing similar-sized slices — the human eye compares lengths (bars) much better than angles (slices). KEY CHOICE - pie vs cs_bars (Percent stack): For cross-asset composition, cs_bars with stack_type=Percent is better because it handles multiple assets automatically and shows proportion as stacked bars. Pie is per-asset only. KEY CHOICE - donut vs pie: Donut (inner_size=50+) is preferred for modern dashboards — the hollow center can display a summary metric via a cards transform placed nearby. Plain pie (inner_size=0) is fine for simple 2-3 category splits. COLORS: Optional 'colors' list maps 1:1 to slices in order. Use named colors like Red, Blue, Success, Warning. If omitted, default palette is used. EXAMPLES: (1) Sector allocation: label=sector_name, value=sector_weight. Donut (inner_size=50) shows portfolio composition at a glance. Place alongside cards showing total AUM and number of positions. This is the standard allocation chart in Bloomberg PORT, Morningstar, and QuantConnect dashboards. (2) Asset class breakdown: label=asset_class ('Equity','Fixed Income','Cash'), value=allocation_percentage. colors=[Blue, Orange, Success]. 3 slices is ideal for pie — clear visual separation without clutter. (3) Win/loss composition: label=outcome ('Win','Loss','Break Even'), value=trade_count. colors=[Success, Error, Warning]. Shows proportion of winning vs losing trades at a glance. (4) Revenue source: label=source_type, value=revenue_amount. Donut (inner_size=60) with total revenue shown via a card widget placed nearby.
limitations: Not suitable for many categories (>8 slices become unreadable — use xy_bars instead). Cannot show trends over time (use lines or timeseries_lines). Cannot compare absolute magnitudes precisely (use xy_bars). Per-asset only — for cross-asset composition, use cs_pie or cs_bars with stack_type=Percent. Values are always normalized as percentages of total, so raw magnitude information is lost in the chart. Null labels are dropped.

name: String Contains

options.name: Operation
options.desc: Type of containment check

options.name: Pattern
options.desc: Pattern to search for

desc: Check if strings contain, start with, or end with a pattern. Returns boolean.
usageContext: Filter strings by pattern, check prefixes/suffixes. Common: ticker symbol patterns, file extensions, category prefixes.
limitations: Case-sensitive matching. Use string_case first for case-insensitive checks.

name: Qstick
desc: Qstick. Measures the ratio of black to white candlesticks, indicating buying and selling pressure.
usageContext: Moving average of (close - open) over a period. Positive = average bar is bullish (close > open), negative = bearish. Zero crossings signal shifts in candlestick dominance. PIPELINE PATTERN: compute qstick(period=8), use zero-line crossovers for candlestick trend direction. EXAMPLE: qstick crossing above zero = bullish candles beginning to dominate.
limitations: Only considers open-close relationship, ignoring wicks. Sensitive to period choice. Gap-heavy markets can distort readings. Less informative than volume-based indicators. Best as supplementary price-action confirmation tool.

name: Reference Futures

options.name: Reference Futures Ticker
options.desc: Futures ticker symbol (e.g., ES, CL, GC, ZN, NQ, ZC)

desc: Reference OHLCV data for any futures contract via Epoch Archive. Accepts any supported futures ticker symbol. WARNING: For futures, returns raw multi-contract data (not a continuation). Downstream transforms resolve via keep_last (arbitrary contract per date).
usageContext:
Raw OHLCV data for any futures ticker, independent of strategy universe.
Same as common_reference_futures but accepts any ticker string.
WARNING: For futures, this returns ALL contracts per date (List columns).
Downstream transforms resolve List columns via keep_last (not a proper continuation).
For proper front-month continuation, use futures_continuation() on market_data_source().
limitations:
Data sourced from Epoch Archive (not Polygon). NullPolicy=AllowAll.
FUTURES WARNING: Does NOT produce a continuation. Returns raw multi-contract data.
Downstream keep_last resolution picks an arbitrary contract per date.
For proper front-month continuation, use futures_continuation() on market_data_source().
Weekends/holidays have no bars.

name: Group By

options.name: Aggregation
options.desc: Aggregation function to apply

options.name: Quantile
options.desc: Quantile (0-1), for agg=Quantile

options.name: DDOF
options.desc: Degrees of freedom for Std/Var

desc: Groups data by key and aggregates using the specified function. Works on all data types (numeric, boolean, string).
usageContext: Aggregate values within groups defined by a key column. Essential for cross-sectional analysis: sector-level statistics, peer-relative metrics, and portfolio-level aggregations. Numeric supports Sum, Mean, Min, Max, Stddev, Variance, etc. Boolean supports AnyOf, AllOf. String supports First, Last.
limitations: Null values in the value column are dropped before aggregation. The group key must not be entirely null.

name: ArgMax (Timestamp)

options.name: Expanding Mode
options.desc: If true, returns expanding argmax (timestamp of max seen so far at each point). If false, returns global argmax timestamp for all rows.
options.tuningGuidance: true (default) = expanding mode: at each row, returns the timestamp of the maximum value seen from the start up to that row. Tracks when the current peak was established. false = global mode: returns the same timestamp for every row — the date of the overall series maximum. Useful for labeling the best day across an entire backtest.

desc: Returns the timestamp where the maximum value occurred. In expanding mode, tracks the running maximum's timestamp at each point. In global mode, broadcasts the single global argmax timestamp to all rows.
usageContext: Find when the maximum value occurred in a time series. Expanding mode (default): at each row, returns the timestamp of the highest value seen so far — useful for tracking when the equity curve peak was established, when the best return occurred, or when the high watermark was set for drawdown calculations. Global mode: returns the single overall maximum's timestamp for all rows — useful for labeling the best day in a backtest, identifying the all-time high date, or annotating peak performance on a chart. Trigger phrases: 'when did the maximum happen', 'best day', 'peak date', 'high watermark timestamp', 'highest point date', 'date of maximum'.
limitations: Returns the timestamp (date) of the maximum, not the maximum value itself. To get the actual maximum value, use cumulative(agg=Max). In expanding mode, ties are broken by first occurrence (earliest timestamp wins). NaN/null values in input are skipped — they do not update the running maximum. Output is a Timestamp column, not Decimal — cannot be used directly in arithmetic.

- Pairs trading: Load a correlated asset for spread construction.
- Beta hedging: Load SPY/benchmark to compute and hedge market beta.

Outputs: .o (open), .h (high), .l (low), .c (close), .v (volume).
Use for altcoins or custom pairs not in the curated dropdown.
Example: crypto_pairs(ticker="SOLUSD")().c for Solana close.

name: Keyword Match

options.name: Keywords
options.desc: List of keyword patterns to detect in text. 'patterns': array of strings (plain substrings or regex). 'case_sensitive': false by default (case-insensitive matching). 'use_regex': false by default (plain substring search). Example: {patterns: ["upgrade", "downgrade"], case_sensitive: false, use_regex: false}. With use_regex=true: {patterns: ["fraud|embezzle", "sec.+investigation"]}

desc: Check if ANY keyword pattern matches in text. Returns boolean (true/false). Use for signal generation from news, filtering by keywords, detecting specific events in text data. Academic: Tetlock (2007) shows media pessimism predicts downward price pressure; Loughran & McDonald (2011) demonstrate domain-specific lexicons outperform generic dictionaries by 73.8% in financial text classification. Empirical IC: ~0.08 when used with bullish/bearish keyword lists on news headlines.
usageContext:
ROLE: Boolean event detector from text — does text contain any keyword?

KEY CHOICE -- keyword_match vs keyword_count: keyword_match returns presence (boolean: any match found?) while keyword_count returns intensity (integer: how many matches?). Use keyword_match when you need binary signal/no-signal detection; use keyword_count when signal strength matters.

ACADEMIC: Tetlock (2007) "Giving Content to Investor Sentiment" shows media pessimism predicts downward price pressure on the Dow. Loughran & McDonald (2011) domain-specific lexicons show 73.8% improvement over Harvard General Inquirer for financial text. Dictionary-based signals have IC ~0.08 standalone, ~0.13 when combined with value factors.

USE CASES: 8-K material event detection (bankruptcy, acquisition, management change), earnings surprise identification (beat/miss keywords in headlines), FDA approval/rejection tracking, litigation and regulatory mention screening, adverse media screening for compliance.

EXAMPLES: (1) detect "upgrade" or "downgrade" in analyst notes for momentum signals. (2) filter bankruptcy-related filings using ["chapter 11", "bankruptcy", "insolvency"]. (3) screen for regulatory keywords ["sec investigation", "subpoena", "consent decree"] in news feeds.
limitations: Context-blind — no semantic understanding ("not guilty" matches "guilty"). No negation handling; combine with ML sentiment for higher accuracy. Case-insensitive by default; set case_sensitive=true for exact matching. Regex errors silently return false (non-matching). Requires domain-specific dictionaries for meaningful results. Typically detects ~10% of news items (vs ~45% for ML sentiment).

name: Treasury Auctions

options.name: Auction Type
options.desc: Select Treasury auction type (Notes, Bonds, Bills, TIPS)

desc: Load Treasury auction results from TreasuryDirect. Provides high yield, bid-to-cover ratio, and allocation percentage for Notes, Bonds, Bills, and TIPS auctions.
usageContext: The DataFrame index is the auction date. Use for yield analysis, demand assessment, and rate expectations. Example: common_treasury_auctions(auction_type="Note10Y")().high_yield for 10-Year Note auction yields.
limitations: Auction frequency varies: Notes/Bonds monthly, Bills weekly. TIPS auctions are quarterly. Data starts from ~2012. Some fields may be NaN for older auctions.

name: Streak Length

options.name: Direction
options.desc: Which direction to count streaks
options.tuningGuidance: up = consecutive true, down = consecutive false, bidirectional = positive for true/negative for false

desc: Counts consecutive occurrences of true/false values in a boolean series. Returns running count that resets when condition changes.
usageContext: Count consecutive true/false occurrences for winning/losing streak analysis, consecutive up/down day tracking, and regime duration measurement. Use direction=up for consecutive true count (bars in position, winning streak), direction=down for consecutive false count (bars out of position, losing streak), direction=bidirectional for signed streaks (positive for true, negative for false). Common queries: 'how many consecutive up days', 'longest winning streak', 'days since regime change'.
limitations: Input must be boolean. Null values reset the streak and output null. Only counts from current streak start — does not provide historical streak data.

name: Average True Range
desc: Average True Range. Measures market volatility by calculating the average range between price points.
usageContext: Essential for position sizing and stop placement. Use ATR multiples for stops (e.g., 2x ATR stop gives breathing room). Higher ATR = more volatile = smaller position or wider stops. Trend filters: rising ATR suggests expansion/breakout, falling ATR suggests consolidation. Not directional - only measures volatility magnitude.
limitations: Lagging - based on past volatility. Doesn't predict future volatility. Absolute value in price units - not normalized (use NATR for cross-asset comparison). Can be slow to adapt to regime changes with standard 14 period. Gaps affect calculation. Consider shorter periods (7-10) for faster adaptation.

name: Pivot Wider

options.name: Lookback Duration
options.desc: Forward-fill expiry duration (0 = no forward fill)

desc: Pivots event-based data from long to wide format. Creates a StructArray with fields for each unique key value. Works on all data types.
usageContext: Reshapes event-based long-format data (key, value) into wide-format StructArray with one field per unique key. Used for cross-sectional analysis of event data (e.g., analyst ratings by firm, news sentiment by source). 'lookback' Duration enables forward-fill for sparse event data.
limitations: Key column must be string type. Number of unique keys determines output tuple arity — large key spaces can cause memory issues.

name: Marubozu
desc: Candle with no upper or lower shadows. Indicates strong conviction in the direction of the trend.
usageContext: Generic marubozu detection (either bullish or bearish). No shadows means one side completely dominated. White/bullish marubozu: opened at low, closed at high. Black/bearish: opened at high, closed at low. Strongest single-candle momentum signal. PIPELINE PATTERN: detect marubozu, use as strong momentum confirmation. Use specific black_marubozu or white_marubozu for directional.
limitations: Generic pattern - use black_marubozu or white_marubozu for directional signals. Strict no-shadow requirement makes this rare. Can appear at exhaustion points. Wick thresholds configurable but affect detection frequency.

name: Hierarchical Risk Parity

options.name: Linkage Method
options.desc: Clustering linkage method: single, complete, average, ward

options.name: Lookback Period
options.desc: Number of periods for covariance estimation

options.name: Rebalance Frequency

options.name: Maximum Weight
options.desc: Maximum weight per asset (caps individual weights)

desc: Hierarchical Risk Parity uses hierarchical clustering to group correlated assets, then allocates weights through recursive bisection inversely proportional to cluster variance. Uses rolling estimation with configurable rebalance frequency. Reference: Lopez de Prado (2016). Does not require matrix inversion.
usageContext: hrp(returns=pct_change(close), linkage='single', lookback=252). Groups correlated assets and diversifies across clusters. Connect weight output to dynamic_size(type='percent') for sizing.
limitations: Cross-sectional only. Sensitive to linkage method choice. May produce unstable weights with short lookback.

name: Abandoned Baby Bear
desc: Bearish reversal pattern with a large up candle, followed by a gapped doji, and a gapped down candle. Signals potential downward trend.
usageContext: Rare, high-reliability bearish reversal. Three candles: (1) bullish continuation, (2) doji that gaps above day 1 (both shadows don't overlap), (3) bearish candle that gaps below the doji. The 'abandoned' doji island signals complete exhaustion. Strongest when appearing at resistance after extended uptrend. PIPELINE PATTERN: detect abandoned_baby_bear, confirm with volume and resistance level.
limitations: Extremely rare pattern due to strict gap requirements. Gaps less common in 24/7 markets (crypto, forex). Requires perfect doji which is also rare. When it occurs it's very reliable, but few trading opportunities. Consider evening_doji_star as a more common alternative.

name: Common Crypto Pairs

options.name: Crypto Pair
options.desc: Select the cryptocurrency pair

desc: Cryptocurrency data (BTC, ETH, SOL) for cross-asset correlation, crypto momentum, and hedging. Independent of strategy universe.
usageContext:
Outputs: .o (open), .h (high), .l (low), .c (close), .v (volume).
- Crypto momentum: Track BTC/ETH trends as reference for altcoin strategies.
- Cross-asset correlation: Study crypto-equity or crypto-macro relationships.
- Hedging: Use BTC as a hedge or risk proxy in portfolio context.
- Regime detection: Monitor BTC dominance shifts via pair comparisons.
limitations:
Inherits the strategy's timeframe (daily or intraday). NullPolicy=AllowAll.
Crypto trades 24/7 — daily bars cover full calendar days including weekends.

name: VWAP
desc: Volume Weighted Average Price per bar (provider 'vw').
usageContext: Institutional execution benchmark — price above VWAP indicates buying pressure, below indicates selling pressure. Use as a mean-reversion anchor: price tends to revert toward VWAP during range-bound sessions. Combine with standard deviation bands around VWAP for overbought/oversold zones. Filter trend direction: only take longs when price > VWAP.
limitations: Requires data provider to supply per-bar VWAP (vw column). Session-dependent — resets each trading day. Not meaningful on daily+ timeframes where VWAP equals the bar's own average price. Not available for futures — futures data providers do not supply per-bar VWAP.

name: Ease of Movement
desc: Ease of Movement. Relates price change to volume, identifying whether price changes are easy or difficult.
usageContext: Measures how easily price moves on volume. High positive EMV = price rising easily on low volume (bullish). Negative EMV = price falling easily. Near zero = high volume needed to move price (congestion). PIPELINE PATTERN: compute emv(), smooth with ma(), use zero-line crossovers for trend signals. EXAMPLE: EMV rising above zero confirms path of least resistance is upward.
limitations: Requires reliable volume data. Raw EMV very noisy - needs smoothing with moving average. Scale varies significantly across instruments. Less widely used than OBV or A/D. Interpretation can be ambiguous during low-volume periods.

name: Market Data Source
desc: Primary OHLCV time-series data source for the strategy's universe. Provides Open, High, Low, Close, and Volume data at the specified timeframe.
usageContext: Use as the primary data source for any strategy. Access price and volume data via outputs: src.o (open), src.h (high), src.l (low), src.c (close), src.v (volume).

name: Maximum Diversification

options.name: Lookback Period
options.desc: Number of periods for covariance estimation

options.name: Rebalance Frequency
options.desc: Number of periods between rebalancing (21 = monthly for daily data)

options.name: Window Type
options.desc: Rolling (fixed-size sliding) or Expanding (cumulative)

options.name: Maximum Weight
options.desc: Maximum weight per asset

desc: Maximum Diversification portfolio maximizes the diversification ratio DR = (w'σ)/σ_p where σ is individual volatilities and σ_p is portfolio volatility. Exploits correlation benefits without requiring return estimates.
usageContext: max_diversification(returns=pct_change(close), lookback=252). Maximizes benefit from diversification. Connect weight output to dynamic_size(type='percent') for sizing.
limitations: Cross-sectional only. May underweight low-correlation assets. Sensitive to correlation estimation.

name: Abandoned Baby Bull
desc: Bullish reversal pattern with a large down candle, followed by a gapped doji, and a gapped up candle. Signals potential upward trend.
usageContext: Rare, high-reliability bullish reversal. Three candles: (1) bearish continuation, (2) doji that gaps below day 1 (both shadows don't overlap), (3) bullish candle that gaps above the doji. The 'abandoned' doji island signals seller exhaustion. Strongest when appearing at support after extended downtrend. PIPELINE PATTERN: detect abandoned_baby_bull, confirm with volume and support level.
limitations: Extremely rare pattern due to strict gap requirements. Gaps less common in 24/7 markets (crypto, forex). Requires perfect doji which is also rare. When it occurs it's very reliable, but few trading opportunities. Consider morning_doji_star as a more common alternative.

name: Keyword Score

options.name: Keywords
options.desc: List of weighted keyword patterns. Each entry has 'pattern' (string) and 'weight' (double). Score = sum(count_i * weight_i) for each pattern. 'case_sensitive': false by default. 'use_regex': false by default. Example: {keywords: [{pattern: "fraud", weight: 5.0}, {pattern: "lawsuit", weight: 2.0}]}. Use positive weights for bullish terms, negative for bearish, or severity-based scaling.

desc: Compute weighted score from keyword pattern matches. Returns decimal (double). Each pattern has a weight; score = sum of (count * weight) across all patterns. Use for custom sentiment scoring with severity weights. Academic: Loughran-McDonald (2011) 6 sentiment categories; Jegadeesh & Wu (2013) 'Word Power' term-weighting; Garcia (2013) shows sentiment during recessions has stronger predictive power. Empirical: Risk keyword scores show IC ~-0.11 (high risk predicts poor returns); dictionary IC ~0.08-0.13 (declining with crowding); FinBERT 88.2% vs LM dictionary 62.1% accuracy.
usageContext:
ROLE: Weighted dictionary sentiment scoring — each pattern has a severity weight for importance-aware text scoring.

KEY CHOICE -- keyword_score vs keyword_count: keyword_score applies weights (importance matters: fraud=5 vs warning=1.5) while keyword_count treats all patterns equally (unweighted). Use keyword_score when different keywords carry different severity or sentiment intensity.

ACADEMIC: Loughran-McDonald (2011) 6 sentiment categories (negative, positive, uncertainty, litigious, strong modal, weak modal). Jegadeesh & Wu (2013) "Word Power" term-weighting predicts 10-K filing returns. Garcia (2013) shows sentiment has stronger predictive power during recessions. Dictionary IC ~0.08-0.13 standalone (declining with crowding); FinBERT achieves 88.2% vs LM dictionary 62.1% accuracy.

METHODOLOGY: score = sum(count_i * weight_i) for each pattern. Example: text with 2x "fraud" and 1x "warning" with weights fraud=5, warning=1.5 → score = 2*5 + 1*1.5 = 11.5.

PERFORMANCE: Dictionary-based sentiment IC ~0.08-0.13 as a standalone factor. Combine with value factors for synergy (combined IC ~0.13). Alpha decays with crowding — validate via backtesting.

EXAMPLES: (1) Risk scoring: {fraud: 5.0, sec_investigation: 4.0, lawsuit: 2.0, warning: 1.5} — higher score = higher risk. (2) Custom bull/bear sentiment: {upgrade: 1.0, beat: 0.8, downgrade: -1.0, miss: -0.8}. (3) Severity-adjusted news signals with threshold filtering (score > 3.0 → high risk).
limitations: Linear weighting only — no interaction effects between keywords. No context or negation handling ('not fraud' still matches 'fraud'). Combine with ML models (FinBERT) for higher accuracy. Validate weights via backtesting — arbitrary weights may not predict returns. Alpha decays with crowding as more participants use similar dictionaries.

name: Cross-Sectional Aggregation

options.name: Aggregation Type
options.desc: Type of cross-sectional aggregation
options.tuningGuidance: Mean: central tendency. Sum: totals. Count: coverage. Min/Max: extremes. Median: robust central tendency. Skew/Kurtosis: distribution shape. First/Last: boundary values. Any/All: boolean aggregation.

options.name: Group By
options.desc: Group assets before applying cross-sectional operation. When set, the transform operates within each group independently.
options.tuningGuidance: Use 'sector' for industry-neutral stock strategies. Use 'category' for futures. Use 'auto_detect' to let the system choose.

desc: Computes statistics ACROSS assets at each timestamp. Collapses a multi-asset DataFrame into a single time series using the specified aggregation. Supports Mean, Sum, Count, Product, Min, Max, Median, Std, Var, Skew, Kurtosis, and more.
usageContext: Compute universe-level statistics at each timestamp. The unified cs_agg replaces the legacy per-function transforms (cs_mean, cs_sum, cs_stddev, etc.) with a single transform controlled by the 'type' option. MARKET BREADTH: cs_agg(type=Mean) on binary advance/decline signals measures the percentage of stocks advancing - a classic market breadth indicator used by technicians since the 1930s (NYSE Advance/Decline Line). CROSS-SECTIONAL DISPERSION: cs_agg(type=Std) on returns measures return dispersion across the universe. High dispersion = stock-pickers market (individual stocks deviating from the mean). Low dispersion = beta-driven, macro-dominated market. Bridgewater, AQR, and Two Sigma use dispersion as a regime indicator. DISTRIBUTION MONITORING: cs_agg(type=Skew) and cs_agg(type=Kurtosis) on returns track the shape of the cross-sectional return distribution. Negative skew indicates more losers than winners; high kurtosis signals fat tails (extreme outlier stocks). EXAMPLES: (1) Market breadth: cs_agg(type=Mean) on a boolean signal where each asset is 1 if return > 0, else 0. Produces % of universe with positive returns each day. (2) Return dispersion regime filter: cs_agg(type=Std) on daily returns. When dispersion is high (above 12-month median), use stock-selection alpha strategies. When low, use broad market exposure. (3) Universe coverage: cs_agg(type=Count) tracks how many assets have valid data at each timestamp. Useful for monitoring data quality and survivorship. (4) Sector-level aggregation: Use group_by=sector with cs_agg(type=Mean) to compute average returns per sector, enabling sector rotation analysis.
limitations: Requires multiple assets (3+ for statistical measures like Std/Var, 5+ for Skew/Kurtosis to be meaningful). Skew and Kurtosis use sample estimators (ddof=1). For quantile computations with configurable q, use cs_quantile instead. Product aggregation can overflow with many assets or large values.

name: Chande Momentum Oscillator
desc: Chande Momentum Oscillator. Momentum oscillator calculating relative momentum of positive and negative price movements.
usageContext: Unbounded momentum oscillator (-100 to +100). Similar to RSI but uses raw sum of gains minus losses, not smoothed ratio. More responsive to short-term momentum changes. >50 = overbought, <-50 = oversold. PIPELINE PATTERN: compute cmo(), use +50/-50 as overbought/oversold thresholds with trend filter. EXAMPLE: CMO < -50 in uptrend = oversold pullback entry opportunity.
limitations: More volatile than RSI due to lack of smoothing. Can stay in extreme zones during trends. Less widely used than RSI. Thresholds need calibration per asset. Consider RSI for more stable signals.

name: Long Legged Doji
desc: Doji with long upper and lower shadows. Indicates significant volatility and indecision in the market.
usageContext: Doji with exceptionally long upper and lower shadows, showing extreme volatility with equal buyer/seller strength. Market explored both directions aggressively but settled at the open. Stronger reversal signal than standard doji due to volatile exploration. PIPELINE PATTERN: detect long_legged_doji after trend, expect potential reversal. EXAMPLE: long_legged_doji at resistance after uptrend = high-volatility indecision, potential top.
limitations: Neutral pattern - direction depends entirely on context and confirmation. Long shadow thresholds subjective. In ranging markets, long-legged dojis are common and less meaningful. Needs next-candle confirmation for direction.

name: Cross-Sectional Rank

options.name: Ascending
options.desc: If true, lowest value gets rank 1

desc: Assigns ordinal ranks (1, 2, 3, ...) to assets at each timestamp based on their values across the universe. NaN values are placed at the end of the ranking.
usageContext: Assign ordinal ranks to assets based on a signal at each timestamp. Rank 1 is the lowest value (ascending=true) or highest value (ascending=false). The foundation for quantile portfolio sorting in academic factor research. PORTFOLIO CONSTRUCTION: Convert ranks to portfolio weights. Linear weighting: weight = rank / sum(ranks). This gives higher-ranked assets more weight, producing a rank-weighted long-only portfolio. For long/short: assets in the top decile go long, bottom decile go short. KEY CHOICE - cs_rank vs cs_rank_quantile: Use cs_rank when you need integer ranks for exact position sizing or when the universe size is fixed. Use cs_rank_quantile when you need normalized [0,1] scores that are comparable across different universe sizes (e.g., comparing ranks from a 50-stock vs 500-stock universe). FACTOR RESEARCH: Standard Fama-French/Barra methodology sorts stocks into deciles by factor value. cs_rank provides the raw ranking; divide by cs_agg(type=Count) to compute percentile ranks manually, or use cs_rank_quantile directly. EXAMPLES: (1) Momentum decile sort: cs_rank(ascending=false) on 12-month returns. Rank 1 = highest momentum. Divide into deciles for the classic Jegadeesh-Titman portfolio. (2) Value ranking: cs_rank(ascending=true) on P/E ratio. Rank 1 = cheapest stock. (3) Composite rank: Average the ranks from momentum, value, and quality factors to create a multi-factor composite rank.
limitations: Requires multiple assets. NaN values receive the highest rank (placed at end). Tie-breaking is arbitrary for equal values. Integer output - for normalized [0,1] scores use cs_rank_quantile instead.

name: Cross-Sectional Winsorize

options.name: Lower Percentile
options.desc: Values below this percentile (across assets) are capped
options.tuningGuidance: Use 0.01-0.05 for light winsorization

options.name: Upper Percentile
options.desc: Values above this percentile (across assets) are capped
options.tuningGuidance: Use 0.95-0.99 for light winsorization

desc: Caps extreme values at specified percentile cutoffs ACROSS assets at each timestamp. Values below the lower percentile are set to the lower bound; values above the upper percentile are set to the upper bound. Preserves the number of data points while reducing outlier impact.
usageContext: Standard data cleaning step in cross-sectional factor pipelines. Applied BEFORE cs_zscore to prevent extreme values from distorting the mean and standard deviation used in z-score normalization. This is the same preprocessing used by Alphalens (Quantopian), Qlib (Microsoft), and institutional multi-factor platforms. KEY DIFFERENCE from time-series winsorize: Regular winsorize caps values based on each asset's own historical distribution. cs_winsorize caps based on the CROSS-SECTIONAL distribution at each timestamp (comparing across peers, not over time). STANDARD PIPELINE: The robust factor preprocessing pipeline is: (1) cs_winsorize(lower=0.05, upper=0.95) to cap outliers. (2) cs_zscore to standardize across the universe. Without winsorization, a single extreme value (e.g., a biotech stock with 500% return) can dominate the z-score distribution, pushing all other assets to near-zero z-scores and destroying the signal's discriminating power. TUNING GUIDANCE:   Conservative (0.01/0.99): Minimal impact, only caps extreme outliers.   Standard (0.05/0.95): Most common in academic factor research.   Aggressive (0.10/0.90): Heavy outlier suppression for noisy signals. EXAMPLES: (1) Factor preprocessing: cs_winsorize(lower=0.05, upper=0.95) on raw P/E ratios before cs_zscore. Removes the effect of stocks with negative or extreme P/E. (2) Return cleaning: cs_winsorize(lower=0.01, upper=0.99) on daily returns before computing cross-sectional statistics. Prevents IPOs, halted stocks, or corporate actions from distorting aggregate metrics.
limitations: Requires at least 2 assets. lower_limit must be less than upper_limit. With very few assets (< 20), the percentile cutoffs may not be meaningful. Does not remove outliers - it caps them at the boundary values, preserving the number of observations.

desc: Cross-sectional color-coded grid across assets. TWO MODES: 'correlation' computes an NxN pairwise correlation matrix between all assets (the standard portfolio diversification diagnostic). 'values' shows a 1xN aggregated metric grid where each asset gets one color-coded cell (visual ranking by color intensity).
usageContext: Cross-sectional color-coded grid in the DASHBOARD view that operates across all assets in the universe. TWO MODES with distinct use cases: MODE 1 — CORRELATION (mode=correlation): Computes an NxN pairwise Pearson correlation matrix. Both axes are asset names, and each cell shows the correlation coefficient between two assets (-1.0 to 1.0). Diagonal is always 1.0. The matrix is computed in parallel via TBB for performance. This is the STANDARD visualization for portfolio diversification analysis — quickly spot which assets move together (high positive correlation → red/hot) and which provide diversification (low/negative → blue/cool). MODE 2 — VALUES (mode=values): Shows a 1xN single-row grid where each asset gets one color-coded cell. The input column is time-aggregated per asset using 'agg' (Last, Mean, Sum, etc.) to produce one value per asset. Color intensity encodes magnitude for instant visual ranking. Think of it as a color-coded summary strip. KEY CHOICE — cs_heatmap (correlation) vs cs_scatter: Both show pairwise asset relationships. Correlation heatmap shows ALL pairs simultaneously in a matrix (ideal for 5-30 assets). cs_scatter shows the detailed point cloud for ONE pair. Use cs_heatmap for the overview, then cs_scatter to drill into specific pairs. KEY CHOICE — cs_heatmap (values) vs cs_bars: Both show one aggregated value per asset. cs_bars uses bar LENGTH for comparison (better for ranking, reading magnitudes). cs_heatmap values mode uses COLOR INTENSITY (better when displayed as part of a multi-metric dashboard where space is tight, or when pairing with the correlation matrix). Generally prefer cs_bars for single-metric ranking. KEY CHOICE — cs_heatmap (values) vs cs_summary_table: cs_summary_table shows exact numbers in a grid. cs_heatmap values mode shows color-coded cells for instant visual scanning. Use cs_summary_table when the user needs precise values; use cs_heatmap when the visual pattern matters more than exact numbers. KEY CHOICE — cs_heatmap vs heatmap: cs_heatmap operates ACROSS assets (assets become axes). heatmap operates WITHIN one asset with user-defined x, y, value columns. Use cs_heatmap for cross-asset correlation or comparison. Use heatmap for per-asset seasonality or 2D pattern analysis. EXAMPLES: (1) Portfolio correlation matrix: mode=correlation, input=daily_returns. The classic NxN heatmap showing which stocks/ETFs are correlated. Essential for diversification analysis, risk budgeting, and portfolio construction (Markowitz, HRP, risk parity). Set color_axis_min=-1, color_axis_max=1 for symmetric scale. (2) Sector correlation structure: mode=correlation, input=sector_returns. Shows how sectors co-move — helps identify regime changes (correlations spike in crises). max_assets=15 to keep the matrix readable. (3) Volatility comparison strip: mode=values, input=realized_vol, agg=Last. A single-row color strip where high-volatility assets glow hot and low-volatility assets stay cool. Compact way to scan risk across the portfolio. (4) Return attribution grid: mode=values, input=ytd_return, agg=Last. Quick visual scan of which assets contributed most (intense color) and least. Pair with cs_bars for the detailed ranking.
limitations: Dashboard widget, not the TV chart. Correlation mode requires at least 2 assets and becomes hard to read beyond ~30 assets (use max_assets to limit). Correlation is Pearson only — does not support Spearman or Kendall rank correlations. Values mode reduces each asset to ONE number — cannot show how values evolved over time (use cs_lines for curves). The matrix does not cluster or reorder assets by similarity — assets appear in their natural order. For per-asset 2D pattern analysis (month × year) use heatmap. For exact cross-asset numbers use cs_summary_table. For magnitude ranking use cs_bars.

name: Earnings
desc: Earnings announcements including EPS, revenue, and surprises. Access actual vs estimated figures, fiscal periods, and earnings importance ratings.
usageContext:
Quarterly and annual earnings announcements with actual vs estimated EPS and revenue.
- PEAD: Trade post-earnings announcement drift following surprises.
- Earnings momentum: Track consecutive beat/miss streaks for fundamental trajectory.
- Event overlays: Use as event markers on price charts around announcements.
- Screening: Filter by eps_surprise_percent or revenue_surprise_percent for signal generation.
Combine with price data for pre/post-announcement returns. Pairs with volatility transforms for earnings vol crush.
limitations:
Sparse: ~4-5 rows/year/asset (quarterly + annual). Most trading days empty. NullPolicy=AllowAll.
Use ffill to forward-fill last known values when joining with daily price data.
Coverage: From 2011-12-08. Large-cap US most complete; thins out for small-cap/international.
Nulls: estimated_eps/revenue null for thinly covered securities with no analyst consensus.

name: Cross-Sectional Rank Quantile

options.name: Ascending
options.desc: If true, lowest value gets 0.0, highest gets 1.0

desc: Assigns percentile ranks (0.0 to 1.0) to assets at each timestamp. Normalizes ordinal ranks to a uniform [0,1] scale for combining factors with different universe sizes.
usageContext: Assign normalized percentile ranks (0.0 to 1.0) to assets at each timestamp. The lowest value gets 0.0 (ascending=true) and the highest gets 1.0. KEY ADVANTAGE over cs_rank: Percentile ranks are comparable across different universe sizes. A rank_quantile of 0.9 means 'top 10%' whether the universe has 50 or 500 stocks. Integer ranks (cs_rank) depend on universe size, making cross-universe comparison difficult. MULTI-FACTOR COMBINATION: The standard approach for combining multiple factors is: (1) cs_rank_quantile each factor independently. (2) Average the percentile ranks. This produces a composite score in [0,1] regardless of the original factor units or distributions. Unlike cs_zscore, percentile ranks are bounded and robust to outliers - no winsorization needed. Used by MSCI Barra, Axioma, and Bloomberg PORT multi-factor models. QUINTILE/DECILE PORTFOLIOS: Multiply percentile rank by 5 and floor for quintile assignment, or by 10 for decile assignment. This is the standard academic methodology for constructing factor-sorted portfolios (Fama-French, Asness et al.). EXAMPLES: (1) Multi-factor composite: average of cs_rank_quantile(momentum), cs_rank_quantile(value), cs_rank_quantile(quality). Feed result into cs_select. (2) Quintile portfolio: quintile = floor(cs_rank_quantile(signal) * 5). Assets in quintile 4 (top 20%) go long, quintile 0 (bottom 20%) go short.
limitations: Requires multiple assets. Output is always in [0.0, 1.0]. Tie handling follows the underlying ordinal rank behavior. For unnormalized integer ranks use cs_rank.

name: Topic Classify

options.name: Topics
options.desc: Topic dictionary with topic names and associated keyword patterns. 'topics': array of {name: string, patterns: string[]}. 'default_topic': fallback topic when no patterns match (empty string → null). 'case_sensitive': false by default. 'use_regex': false by default. Tie-breaking: when topics have equal match counts, first topic in list wins. Example: {topics: [{name: "earnings", patterns: ["eps", "revenue"]}, {name: "legal", patterns: ["lawsuit", "litigation"]}], default_topic: "other"}

desc: Classify text into topics using dictionary-based matching. Returns topic name (string). Topic with highest keyword match count wins. Use for news categorization, event type detection, content routing. Academic: Garcia (2013) shows topic-specific sentiment drives returns with 10-day response horizon; theme-based sentiment alphas outperform aggregate sentiment. Advantages vs ML: interpretable, deterministic, no training data, fast, audit-friendly.
usageContext:
ROLE: Dictionary-based topic assignment — classifies text into the topic with the highest keyword match count.

KEY CHOICE -- topic_classify vs keyword_match: topic_classify categorizes (which topic?) while keyword_match detects (any match?). Use topic_classify when you need to route text into categories; use keyword_match for simple presence detection.

ACADEMIC: Garcia (2013) shows topic-specific sentiment drives returns with a 10-day response horizon. Theme-based sentiment alphas (earnings vs legal vs M&A) outperform aggregate sentiment scoring.

USE CASES: News stream categorization (earnings/legal/M&A/macro/product), 8-K event type routing by filing content, ESG topic tagging for compliance and reporting.

ADVANTAGES vs ML: Fully interpretable (every classification is explainable), deterministic (same input → same output), no training data required, fast execution, audit-friendly for compliance workflows.

EXAMPLES: (1) classify headlines into earnings/legal/product/financial using topic-specific dictionaries. (2) route SEC filings by content: earnings=[eps, revenue, guidance], legal=[lawsuit, settlement, sec]. (3) ESG topic tagging: environment=[emissions, carbon, waste], social=[diversity, safety, labor], governance=[board, audit, compensation].
limitations: No semantic understanding — relies on exact keyword matching. Polysemy struggles ('bank' could be financial or river bank). Requires manual dictionary curation per topic. Tie-breaking by topic order (first topic in list wins when equal counts). Empty default_topic returns null when no patterns match.

Assign per-asset risk budgets using conditional_select with is_asset_ref. Connect weight output to dynamic_size(type='percent') for sizing.

name: SVR L2

options.name: Regularization (C)
options.desc: Inverse of regularization strength

options.name: Epsilon
options.desc: Tolerance for stopping criterion

options.name: Window Size
options.desc: Size of training window (for rolling) or minimum window (for expanding)
options.tuningGuidance: 252 (default): ~1 year of daily data. Use 126 (~6 months) for faster adaptation to regime changes but less training data. Use 504 (~2 years) for more stable models at the cost of slower adaptation. Rule of thumb: window should contain at least 10x the number of features. For intraday bars, scale proportionally.

options.name: Retrain Frequency
options.desc: How often to retrain: 21 = 21 bars, 1M = monthly, 1Y = yearly, 1W = weekly
options.tuningGuidance: 21 (default): Retrain monthly on daily data. Use 1 for every-bar retraining (expensive but most adaptive). Use 63 (quarterly) for slow-changing models. Duration syntax: '1M' = calendar month, '1W' = week, '21' = 21 bars. More frequent retraining = higher computational cost but faster adaptation.

options.name: Window Type
options.desc: Rolling uses fixed-size window; Expanding grows from start
options.tuningGuidance: rolling (default): Fixed-size training window that slides forward. Model sees only recent data, adapts to regime changes, but forgets old patterns. expanding: Training window grows from start (GKX 2020 methodology). Model sees all historical data, more stable but slower to adapt. Use expanding for long-term factor models; rolling for tactical/short-horizon strategies.

options.name: Min Training Samples
options.desc: Minimum samples required before first prediction
options.tuningGuidance: 100 (default): Reasonable minimum for most models. For LightGBM, use 200+ for stable tree construction. For logistic regression, 50 may suffice. Rule of thumb: min_training_samples >= 10 * num_features. Lower values start predictions sooner but risk unreliable early predictions.

desc: L2-regularized support vector regression with rolling/expanding window training. Provides stable return prediction that adapts to changing market conditions.
usageContext: Use for adaptive return prediction with stable coefficient estimates (L2 regularization). L2 SVR provides robust return predictions that handle noisy financial data well. Good default choice when you don't need feature selection. Trigger phrases: 'stable regression', 'robust prediction', 'L2 SVR', 'Ridge-style return prediction'.
limitations: All features retained — no feature selection. Use svr_l1 if you need to identify which features are driving predictions.

name: Session Gap

options.name: Fill Percentage
options.desc: Minimum fill percentage for gap_filled signal
options.tuningGuidance: 100% (default) for complete fill. 50-80% for partial fill strategies.

desc: Detects opening gaps between trading sessions (overnight gaps, weekend gaps) and tracks gap-fill behavior. A gap occurs when the current session opens above (gap up) or below (gap down) the prior session's close.
usageContext: Track overnight gaps for gap fill strategies. Equities fill ~70% of gaps within the same session. Classify gaps by context: common gaps (filled quickly, low volume), breakaway gaps (high volume, start of trend — don't fade), exhaustion gaps (end of trend, volume spike), runaway gaps (mid-trend continuation). Combine gap_size with volume for confirmation — large gap + high volume = breakaway, large gap + declining volume = exhaustion. gap_retrace OUTPUT SCALE: Decimal fraction 0-1 (NOT percentage). 0.50 = 50% filled, 0.618 = 61.8% Fibonacci fill level, 1.0 = fully filled.
limitations: Only tracks session-to-session gaps. Works best on equity markets with clear sessions. Forex markets have minimal gaps (only weekend gaps). Crypto markets have no session gaps. Gap fill statistics vary significantly by asset and market regime.

name: Is Period Boundary

options.name: Period Type
options.desc: Calendar period for boundary detection. week: 7-day cycles (ISO Mon-Sun). month: calendar month transitions. quarter: 3-month blocks (Q1=Jan-Mar, etc.). year: calendar year transitions.

options.name: Boundary Type
options.desc: start: first bar of the new period (safe, no look-ahead). end: last bar of the current period (requires look-ahead to next bar to confirm the period changed).

options.name: Occurrence
options.desc: Which occurrence of the day anchor within the period. first/second/third/fourth/last. Combine with day_anchor for patterns like third Friday (OPEX). none = match any occurrence.

options.name: Day Anchor
options.desc: Weekday to anchor the boundary to. Combine with ordinal for nth-weekday patterns (e.g., ordinal=third, day_anchor=friday for OPEX). none = no weekday filter.

options.name: Day of Month
options.desc: Specific calendar day (1-31) for boundary. 0 = disabled. Values beyond month length snap to last day (e.g., 31 in February → 28/29). Snaps to nearest trading bar.

options.name: Month in Period
options.desc: Which month within the period. For quarter: 1-3 (1=first, 3=last month). For year: 1-12 (1=January, 12=December). 0 = disabled. Use with ordinal+day_anchor for patterns like OPEX (quarter, month_anchor=3, ordinal=third, day_anchor=friday) or Election Day (year, month_anchor=11, ordinal=second, day_anchor=tuesday).

options.name: Bar Offset
options.desc: Shift the boundary signal by N bars. -1 = T-1 pre-positioning (execute one bar before boundary). +1 = T+1 post-settlement (execute one bar after). Commonly used: -1 for pre-rebalance, +1 for post-settlement.

options.name: Timezone
options.desc: IANA timezone for boundary calculation. Determines when a 'day' starts and ends. Critical for intraday bars: 'America/New_York' ensures month boundaries align with US trading sessions, not UTC midnight.

desc: Detect period boundaries (start or end of week, month, quarter, year). Returns a boolean signal: true on bars that mark period transitions. Supports day anchoring (first Monday, last Friday), specific day-of-month, and bar offsets for T-1/T+1 pre/post-positioning patterns.
usageContext:
ROLE: Boolean rebalancing signals at period transitions. Returns true/false
per bar — use directly as a trade gate or filter condition.

KEY CHOICE -- is_period_boundary vs datetime_extract:
- is_period_boundary → BOOLEAN SIGNAL (true on boundary bar)
- datetime_extract → raw VALUE (e.g., month=1, day=15)
Use is_period_boundary when you need a trigger; use datetime_extract
when you need the actual date component for grouping or arithmetic.

BOUNDARY TYPES:
- start: first bar of new period (no look-ahead, safe for live trading)
- end: last bar before period change (requires look-ahead to next bar)

COMPOSABLE ANCHORS: ordinal × day_anchor × month_anchor
- ordinal: first/second/third/fourth/last (which occurrence)
- day_anchor: monday..friday (which weekday)
- month_anchor: 1-3 (quarter) or 1-12 (year) (which month)

OFFSET: T-1 pre-positioning (offset=-1), T+1 post-settlement (offset=+1).
Offset is in bars, not calendar days.

ACADEMIC & PRACTICAL PATTERNS:
- Turn-of-month (Ariel 1987): last + first few days of month outperform
- OPEX week effect: 3rd Friday of month, elevated volume and pinning
- Window dressing (quarter-end): institutional portfolio rebalancing
- Tax-loss harvesting (year-end): selling losers in Dec, buying back Jan
- January effect: year-start anomaly, stronger in small caps

EXAMPLES:
1. Monthly rebalance: rebal = is_period_boundary(period='month')(index())
2. Month-end signal: eom = is_period_boundary(period='month', boundary='end')(index())
3. First Monday: fm = is_period_boundary(period='month', ordinal='first', day_anchor='monday')(index())
4. T-1 before month end: t1 = is_period_boundary(period='month', boundary='end', offset=-1)(index())
5. OPEX (3rd Friday of quarter-end month):
   opex = is_period_boundary(period='quarter', ordinal='third', day_anchor='friday', month_anchor=3)(index())
6. Election Day (2nd Tuesday of November):
   elec = is_period_boundary(period='year', ordinal='second', day_anchor='tuesday', month_anchor=11)(index())
limitations:
No external holiday calendar — uses bar presence as proxy for trading days.
End detection requires look-ahead to the next bar (not suitable for
strict live-only backtests). First and last bars of the dataset are always
marked as start/end respectively. Day anchors snap to nearest available
bar if the target weekday is missing. No intraday period boundaries
(smallest period is week). Offset is in bars, not calendar days.

name: ML Z-Score

options.name: Window Size
options.desc: Size of training window (for rolling) or minimum window (for expanding)
options.tuningGuidance: 252 (default): ~1 year of daily data. Use 126 (~6 months) for faster adaptation to regime changes but less training data. Use 504 (~2 years) for more stable models at the cost of slower adaptation. Rule of thumb: window should contain at least 10x the number of features. For intraday bars, scale proportionally.

options.name: Retrain Frequency
options.desc: How often to retrain: 21 = 21 bars, 1M = monthly, 1Y = yearly, 1W = weekly
options.tuningGuidance: 21 (default): Retrain monthly on daily data. Use 1 for every-bar retraining (expensive but most adaptive). Use 63 (quarterly) for slow-changing models. Duration syntax: '1M' = calendar month, '1W' = week, '21' = 21 bars. More frequent retraining = higher computational cost but faster adaptation.

options.name: Window Type
options.desc: Rolling uses fixed-size window; Expanding grows from start
options.tuningGuidance: rolling (default): Fixed-size training window that slides forward. Model sees only recent data, adapts to regime changes, but forgets old patterns. expanding: Training window grows from start (GKX 2020 methodology). Model sees all historical data, more stable but slower to adapt. Use expanding for long-term factor models; rolling for tactical/short-horizon strategies.

options.name: Min Training Samples
options.desc: Minimum samples required before first prediction
options.tuningGuidance: 100 (default): Reasonable minimum for most models. For LightGBM, use 200+ for stable tree construction. For logistic regression, 50 may suffice. Rule of thumb: min_training_samples >= 10 * num_features. Lower values start predictions sooner but risk unreliable early predictions.

desc: Z-score normalization with rolling/expanding window training. Computes mean and standard deviation over the training window and normalizes test data accordingly.
usageContext: Use for adaptive feature normalization that updates statistics as data arrives. Computes mean and standard deviation from the training window, then normalizes test data using those statistics. Prevents look-ahead bias vs static normalization. PIPELINE PATTERN: (1) Create raw features via tuple_pack, (2) apply ml_zscore to normalize, (3) feed normalized features into classifier/regressor. KEY DIFFERENCE from zscore: ml_zscore is a rolling/expanding ML preprocessor that normalizes a TUPLE of features simultaneously. zscore operates on a single series. Trigger phrases: 'normalize features', 'standardize for ML', 'z-score preprocessing'.
limitations: Sensitive to outliers in training window. Use ml_robust instead for data with heavy tails or frequent outliers.

name: Switch
desc: Selects from a variable number of slot inputs based on an integer index. Works on all data types. Use for regime-switching, multi-strategy routing, or conditional selection based on a classifier output.
usageContext: Select between N strategies or values based on an integer index (zero-based). Common patterns: regime-switching (hmm.state selects between trend/mean-revert output), multi-strategy blending (index from classifier routes to strategy-specific signals), conditional labeling (index maps to category names). Example: selected = switch(regime_index, trend_signal, mean_revert_signal, neutral_signal). Index 0 selects first input, 1 selects second, etc. Out-of-range indices produce null.
limitations: Index must be valid integer 0 to N-1. Out-of-range indices produce null.

name: Ultimate Oscillator
desc: Ultimate Oscillator. Multi-timeframe momentum oscillator that uses weighted average of three oscillators.
usageContext: Larry Williams' multi-timeframe oscillator. Weighted average of buying pressure over 3 timeframes (typically 7, 14, 28 periods). Range 0-100. Overbought > 70, oversold < 30. Multi-timeframe design reduces false signals. Use with divergence for best results. PIPELINE PATTERN: compute ultosc(), combine with divergence detection for high-conviction reversals. EXAMPLE: ultosc < 30 + bullish divergence = strong mean-reversion long.
limitations: Complex three-period setup makes optimization harder. Fixed period ratios may not suit all instruments. Less responsive than single-timeframe oscillators. Divergence signals develop slowly. Less popular than RSI or Stochastic.

name: Maximum Sharpe Ratio

options.name: Lookback Period
options.desc: Number of periods for estimation

options.name: Rebalance Frequency
options.desc: Number of periods between rebalancing (21 = monthly for daily data)

options.name: Window Type
options.desc: Rolling (fixed-size sliding) or Expanding (cumulative)

options.name: Risk-Free Rate
options.desc: Annual risk-free rate

options.name: Annualization Factor
options.desc: Factor to annualize returns (252 for daily)

options.name: Maximum Weight
options.desc: Maximum weight per asset

desc: Maximum Sharpe Ratio portfolio (tangency portfolio) maximizes risk-adjusted returns. Optimizes (μ-rf)/σ where μ is expected return and σ is portfolio volatility.
usageContext: max_sharpe(returns=pct_change(close), risk_free_rate=0.02). Optimal portfolio for capital allocation line. Connect weight output to dynamic_size(type='percent') for sizing.
limitations: Cross-sectional only. Sensitive to expected return estimates. May produce extreme weights without constraints.

name: Four Price Doji
desc: Special doji where open, high, low, and close are all at the same price. Extreme indecision in the market.
usageContext: Extreme case where O=H=L=C - literally no price movement during the session. Signals either complete indecision or extremely low liquidity. Very rare in liquid markets. When appearing in liquid markets, signals a pause before a potentially large move. PIPELINE PATTERN: detect four_price_doji as extreme indecision warning. EXAMPLE: four_price_doji after extended trend = potential exhaustion and reversal setup.
limitations: Extremely rare in liquid markets. Often indicates low liquidity or holiday trading rather than meaningful indecision. No directional bias at all. Needs strong contextual analysis. Consider standard doji for more frequent signals.

name: Exponential Decay
desc: Exponential Decay. Applies exponential decay to each element in the input over the specified period.
usageContext: Applies exponentially decreasing weight to signal values over time. Signal decays smoothly toward zero without reaching it abruptly. More natural decay curve than linear decay. PIPELINE PATTERN: generate event signal, apply edecay for smoothly fading importance. EXAMPLE: edecay on earnings surprise flag creates gradually diminishing weight for post-event trading signals.
limitations: Never reaches exactly zero - asymptotic approach. Period parameter controls decay rate but interpretation is less intuitive than linear decay. Sensitive to period choice. Consider decay for signals that should hard-expire.

name: Income Statement

options.name: Reporting Period
options.desc: Select financial statement reporting period

desc: Load income statement fundamental data . Provides revenue, expenses, earnings, and profitability metrics over time.
usageContext:
Income statement data from SEC filings.
- Growth investing: Track revenue growth, margin expansion, earnings trajectory.
- Profitability screening: Compare operating margins across periods.
- Earnings quality: Analyze revenue mix and expense composition.
Combine with balance_sheet and cash_flow for full fundamental picture.
Use finance_ratio transform to compute derived ratios from raw data.
limitations:
Sparse: Quarterly (~4 rows/year) or annual (~1 row/year) per asset. NullPolicy=AllowAll.
Use ffill to forward-fill last known values when joining with daily price data.
SEC-filed US equities only. Reporting lag: typically 30-60 days after period end.
Keyed to filing_date (when filed with SEC), not period_end.

name: Balance of Power
desc: Balance of Power. Measures buying and selling pressure by comparing closing price to trading range.
usageContext: Measures dominance of buyers vs sellers: (close - open) / (high - low). Range -1 to +1. Positive = buyers dominating, negative = sellers. Smooth with MA for clearer signals. PIPELINE PATTERN: compute bop(), apply ma() for smoothing, use zero crossovers. EXAMPLE: smoothed BOP crossing above zero = buyers gaining control.
limitations: Very noisy on individual bars - requires smoothing. Doji bars (open = close) produce zero BOP regardless of range. Can be misleading with gap openings. Less widely used than RSI or MACD.

name: Falling

options.name: Length
options.desc: Number of consecutive falling bars required
options.tuningGuidance: 2-3 for short-term, 5+ for strong trend confirmation

desc: Returns true if the source has been strictly falling (each bar lower than previous — lower-lows) for the specified number of consecutive bars. False if any bar is flat or up.
usageContext: Pine Script ta.falling() equivalent. Confirm downtrend strength by requiring N consecutive lower values. Use as breakdown filter: falling(close, 3) after support break confirms bearish momentum. Mirror of rising() for short setups.
limitations: Requires strict consecutive falls — any flat or up bar breaks the streak. Use length=1 for basic lower-low detection, 3+ for strong confirmation.

options.desc: Filter which assets to display based on ranking criteria. Each filter specifies: rank ('top'/'bottom'), count (number of assets), column (metric to rank by). Chain multiple filters with op ('AND'/'OR').

options.name: Maximum Assets
options.desc: Maximum number of assets to display (0 = no limit). Applied after filters.

options.name: Display Order
options.desc: Display order within dashboard category (lower values appear first, 0 = default position)

desc: Cross-sectional bubble chart where each asset becomes an individually named bubble with three dimensions. Each asset is aggregated to a single labeled point at (agg(x), agg(y)) with size=agg(z). Use for risk-return-size maps, factor comparisons with magnitude encoding, and portfolio allocation visualizations.
usageContext: TRIGGER PHRASES: Use when the user asks for 'labeled asset bubbles', 'risk-return-size map', 'three-dimensional asset comparison', 'bubble chart with asset names', 'portfolio bubble map'. Plot a LABELED BUBBLE CHART where EACH ASSET becomes a NAMED BUBBLE with three dimensions. Unlike cs_bubble which shows multiple points per asset over time, cs_labeled_bubble aggregates each asset to a SINGLE labeled bubble — ideal for risk-return-size maps, factor comparisons with magnitude encoding, and cross-sectional snapshots with three variables. INPUTS: x (Number), y (Number), z (Number). Each asset's series are aggregated using the 'agg' function (default: Last). Z controls bubble size. DATA LABELS: Enabled by default (data_labels=True). Set data_labels=False to hide. COLORS: Per-asset colors via 'colors' option, or uses default color cycling. SIZING: min_size, max_size, size_by control bubble scaling. REFERENCE LINES: Both x_reference_lines (vertical) and y_reference_lines (horizontal). CS_LABELED_BUBBLE vs CS_LABELED_SCATTER: cs_labeled_bubble adds a Z dimension (bubble size). Use cs_labeled_scatter when two dimensions suffice. Use cs_labeled_bubble when you need three-dimensional encoding (position + size). CS_LABELED_BUBBLE vs CS_BUBBLE: cs_labeled_bubble shows ONE aggregated point per asset. cs_bubble shows all data points per asset over time. EXAMPLES: (1) Risk-return-size: x=volatility, y=return, z=market_cap, agg=Mean. (2) Factor map with magnitude: x=value_score, y=momentum_score, z=trading_volume. (3) Portfolio allocation: x=weight, y=return, z=risk_contribution.
limitations: Multi-asset only (isCrossSectional=true). Each asset is reduced to a SINGLE bubble via aggregation. max_assets defaults to 20. With many assets, labels may overlap. No trend line support in v1 (BubbleDef does not support overlay lines).

name: Williams Accumulation/Distribution
desc: Williams Accumulation/Distribution. Measures buying/selling pressure by comparing closing price to midpoint of range.
usageContext: Williams' version of accumulation/distribution. Uses true range concept: if close > previous close, AD = close - true low; if close < previous close, AD = close - true high. Cumulative total shows buying vs selling pressure. PIPELINE PATTERN: compute wad(), look for divergences with price trend. EXAMPLE: rising WAD with falling price = accumulation (hidden bullish divergence).
limitations: Cumulative indicator - absolute values not meaningful, focus on direction. Less popular than standard A/D or OBV. True range calculation differs from standard A/D making comparison difficult. Requires quality volume data.

name: Economic Revisions

options.name: FRED Series ID
options.desc: FRED series ID to analyze revisions for. Best for series with significant revisions: PAYEMS (NFP), GDPC1 (Real GDP), CPIAUCSL (CPI), INDPRO (Industrial Production).

desc: FRED revision analysis showing how economic data was revised over time. Compares initial release values to latest revised values for each observation. Useful for understanding data quality and revision patterns.
usageContext: Use to analyze revision patterns. economic_revisions(series_id="PAYEMS")().revision_delta shows NFP revision magnitude. economic_revisions(series_id="GDPC1")().revision_count shows GDP revision frequency.
limitations: Requires FRED API key. Revision data availability varies by series. Very long date ranges may be slow due to vintage date fetching.

name: Relative Strength Index
desc: Relative Strength Index. Momentum oscillator measuring speed and change of price movements, indicating overbought/oversold conditions.
usageContext: Core momentum indicator for overbought (>70) and oversold (<30) conditions. Use for mean-reversion entries, divergence signals, or momentum confirmation. Common patterns: RSI >70 = overbought (potential reversal), RSI <30 = oversold (potential bounce). Combine with price action for best results. Divergence (price makes new high but RSI doesn't) signals weakening momentum.
limitations: Lagging indicator - signals occur after price moves. Can stay overbought/oversold during strong trends. Standard 70/30 thresholds may need adjustment for different assets. Whipsaws in ranging markets. Consider using dynamic overbought/oversold levels or combine with trend filters.

name: Cash Flow

options.name: Reporting Period
options.desc: Select financial statement reporting period

desc: Load cash flow statement fundamental data . Provides operating, investing, and financing cash flows to analyze liquidity and capital allocation.
usageContext:
Cash flow statement data from SEC filings.
- Quality investing: Free cash flow (Operating CF - CapEx) is the key quality metric.
- Capital allocation: Track investing vs financing activities.
- Liquidity analysis: Monitor operating cash flow trends for sustainability.
Combine with balance_sheet and income_statement for full fundamental picture.
Use finance_ratio transform to compute derived ratios from raw data.
limitations:
Sparse: Quarterly (~4 rows/year) or annual (~1 row/year) per asset. NullPolicy=AllowAll.
Use ffill to forward-fill last known values when joining with daily price data.
SEC-filed US equities only. Reporting lag: typically 30-60 days after period end.
Keyed to filing_date (when filed with SEC), not period_end.

name: Rate of Change
desc: Rate of Change. Measures percentage change between current price and price n periods ago.
usageContext: Decimal ratio of price change over n periods: (price - price_n) / price_n. OUTPUT SCALE: Decimal fraction, NOT multiplied by 100. A 5% gain outputs 0.05, a 10% loss outputs -0.10. Use roc > 0.05 for 5% threshold (not roc > 5). Normalized version of mom() - comparable across instruments. PIPELINE PATTERN: compute roc(period=12), use for momentum ranking across assets or overbought/oversold detection. EXAMPLE: roc(period=12) > 0.20 = strong 20% 12-bar momentum, potential trend continuation.
limitations: Comparison to single historical bar makes it sensitive to that bar's value. Can spike on gap days. Unbounded - no fixed overbought/oversold levels. Better for relative comparison than absolute thresholds.

name: Exponentially Weighted Moving Covariance

options.name: Span
options.desc: Span for exponential weighting (decay = 2/(1+span)). Higher values give more weight to history.
options.tuningGuidance: Use span=10-20 for fast-adapting risk models. Use span=30-60 for balanced adaptation. Use span=100+ for strategic risk analysis with smooth estimates. Roughly corresponds to rolling window of span/2 bars but with smoother transitions.

desc: Calculates covariance between two series using exponential weighting, emphasizing recent observations while smoothly incorporating history. Adapts faster than rolling covariance to changing relationships.
usageContext: Use for adaptive risk models where recent comovement is more relevant than distant history. Ideal for real-time portfolio risk monitoring, dynamic hedging ratio calculation, or fast-adapting risk parity strategies. Exponential weighting provides continuous adaptation without the edge effects of rolling windows. KEY DIFFERENCE from rolling_cov: Faster adaptation to regime changes with smooth transitions (no window edge effects). Use rolling_cov when you need a clear lookback period; use ewm_cov when you need smooth, fast-adapting covariance for dynamic risk models. Trigger phrases: 'adaptive covariance', 'dynamic risk', 'real-time portfolio risk', 'fast-adapting covariance', 'exponential weighted covariance'.
limitations: Not normalized - depends on input scales. Use ewm_corr for standardized measure. Span parameter requires tuning. Early values unstable. No intuitive lookback period like rolling windows.

name: Ichimoku Kinko Hyo

options.name: Tenkan-sen Period
options.desc: Conversion line period: midpoint of highest high and lowest low
options.tuningGuidance: Standard 9 (represents 1.5 weeks in Japanese trading). Shorter periods for intraday, longer for weekly charts.

options.name: Kijun-sen Period
options.desc: Base line period and forward displacement for Senkou spans
options.tuningGuidance: Standard 26 (one month in Japanese trading). Also determines the forward shift for Senkou Span A/B and backward shift for Chikou.

options.name: Senkou Span B Period
options.desc: Period for Senkou Span B (slowest cloud boundary)
options.tuningGuidance: Standard 52 (two months). Longer periods create wider, more significant cloud zones. Shorter periods for faster markets.

desc: Ichimoku Kinko Hyo ('one glance equilibrium chart') - Japanese trend-following system providing five lines: Tenkan-sen (conversion), Kijun-sen (base), Senkou Span A/B (cloud), and Chikou Span (lagging). The cloud (Kumo) between Senkou A and B defines support/resistance zones and trend direction.
usageContext: Comprehensive trend-following system that provides trend direction, support/resistance, and momentum confirmation in a single indicator. Developed by Goichi Hosoda (1968). KEY SIGNALS: (1) TK Cross: Tenkan crosses above Kijun = bullish (below = bearish). (2) Price vs Cloud: Price above cloud = bullish, below = bearish, inside = neutral. (3) Cloud color: Senkou A above B = bullish cloud, below = bearish. Cloud flips signal potential trend reversals 26 bars ahead. (4) Chikou confirmation: Chikou above price from 26 bars ago confirms bullish momentum. SIGNAL STRENGTH: Strongest signals occur when all five conditions align (price above cloud, bullish TK cross, bullish cloud color, Chikou above past price). PIPELINE PATTERN: (1) Compute Ichimoku on daily OHLC, (2) enter long when price breaks above cloud AND TK cross is bullish, (3) use cloud boundaries as trailing stop zones, (4) exit when price enters cloud from above or TK cross reverses. EXAMPLES: (1) Cloud breakout: Price breaks above thick bullish cloud = strong support established. Enter long, stop below cloud bottom (Senkou B). (2) Flat Kijun as support: When Kijun-sen flattens, it acts as strong support/resistance. Use as entry level for pullback trades. (3) Cloud twist: When Senkou A and B cross (cloud changes color), signals trend change 26 bars ahead - prepare for reversal.
limitations: Senkou spans are forward-shifted by kijun periods, which uses future-looking values in the cloud calculation. Chikou is backward-shifted. Both shifts mean current cloud values were calculated using data from 26 bars ago - not truly predictive. Complex multi-signal system requires experience to interpret correctly. Parameters optimized for Japanese markets (1.5 weeks, 1 month, 2 months) may need adjustment for 24/7 markets like crypto. Less effective in ranging markets.

name: Average Directional Movement Index
desc: Average Directional Movement Index. Measures the strength of a trend, regardless of its direction.
usageContext: Measures trend strength (not direction). ADX >25 = trending, <20 = ranging/choppy. Use as filter: trade trend strategies when ADX >25, mean-reversion when ADX <20. Rising ADX = strengthening trend, falling ADX = weakening trend. Combine with +DI/-DI for direction. High ADX doesn't indicate bullish/bearish, just strong trend.
limitations: Significant lag - based on smoothed moving averages. Slow to signal trend changes. Can stay high during corrections within trends. No direction info (use DI indicators). Works best with 14-25 period on daily charts. Not suitable for very short timeframes. Requires patience - signals develop slowly.

name: String Case

desc: Convert string case. Upper/lower for full conversion, capitalize for first character only, title for titlecase (first char of each word), swapcase to invert case.
usageContext: Normalize text case for comparison or display. Common: uppercase ticker symbols, lowercase for case-insensitive matching, titlecase for labels.
