desc: Expand numeric data using linear interpolation between valid values.
usageContext: Linear interpolation for smooth transitions between coarse data points. Produces intermediate values between known points rather than repeating the last value. 'limit' and 'limit_direction' control interpolation bounds.
limitations: Only works with numeric (Decimal) data. Target must be finer than input. Execution handled by orchestrator — TransformData() is never called directly.

name: ArgMin (Timestamp)

options.name: Expanding Mode
options.desc: If true, returns expanding argmin (timestamp of min seen so far at each point). If false, returns global argmin timestamp for all rows.
options.tuningGuidance: true (default) = expanding mode: at each row, returns the timestamp of the minimum value seen from the start up to that row. Useful for tracking when the current trough occurred. false = global mode: returns the same timestamp for every row — the date of the overall series minimum. Useful for labeling the worst day across an entire backtest.

desc: Returns the timestamp where the minimum value occurred. In expanding mode, tracks the running minimum's timestamp at each point. In global mode, broadcasts the single global argmin timestamp to all rows.
usageContext: Find when the minimum value occurred in a time series. Expanding mode (default): at each row, returns the timestamp of the lowest value seen so far — useful for tracking when the current drawdown trough happened, when the worst loss occurred, or when the portfolio hit its lowest point up to that date. Global mode: returns the single overall minimum's timestamp for all rows — useful for labeling the worst day in a backtest, identifying the deepest trough date, or annotating the all-time low on a chart. Trigger phrases: 'when did the minimum happen', 'worst day', 'trough date', 'drawdown trough timestamp', 'lowest point date', 'date of minimum'.
limitations: Returns the timestamp (date) of the minimum, not the minimum value itself. To get the actual minimum value, use cumulative(agg=Min). In expanding mode, ties are broken by first occurrence (earliest timestamp wins). NaN/null values in input are skipped — they do not update the running minimum. Output is a Timestamp column, not Decimal — cannot be used directly in arithmetic.

name: Klinger Volume Oscillator
desc: Klinger Volume Oscillator. Compares volume to price trends to identify reversals and divergence.
usageContext: Compares volume flow (accumulation vs distribution) using the high-low-close trend. Positive KVO = volume flowing into the security. Uses 34/55 EMA periods by default with a 13-period signal line. Signal line crossovers indicate momentum shifts. PIPELINE PATTERN: compute kvo(), add signal line via ma(), trade crossovers. EXAMPLE: KVO crossing above signal line at oversold levels = bullish.
limitations: Complex calculation makes it harder to interpret intuitively. Many parameters to tune. Less widely known and tested than OBV or A/D. Can produce many false crossovers in ranging markets. Requires high-quality volume data.

name: Cross-Sectional Weighted Mean

options.name: Group By
options.desc: Group assets before applying cross-sectional operation. When set, the transform operates within each group independently.
options.tuningGuidance: Use 'sector' for industry-neutral stock strategies. Use 'category' for futures. Use 'auto_detect' to let the system choose.

desc: Computes weighted average across assets at each timestamp. Formula: sum(weights * values) / sum(weights). Inputs are provided as struct columns with '#values' and '#weights' fields per asset.
usageContext: Compute value-weighted returns or statistics across a universe of assets. This is the standard method for constructing portfolio-level returns when assets have different weights (market cap, risk budget, signal strength). FAMA-FRENCH FACTOR CONSTRUCTION: The canonical Fama-French (1993) methodology constructs factors as the return difference between value-weighted portfolios. For example, the HML (High-Minus-Low) factor:   (1) Sort stocks into value/growth using book-to-market.   (2) cs_weighted_mean on value portfolio returns, weighted by market cap.   (3) cs_weighted_mean on growth portfolio returns, weighted by market cap.   (4) HML = value_return - growth_return. This produces the same value-weighted long/short factor returns used in academic finance (Ken French's data library, AQR factor data). BENCHMARK REPLICATION: Compute cap-weighted index returns by feeding stock returns as values and market cap as weights. Reproduces S&P 500, Russell 2000, or any cap-weighted benchmark without needing actual index data. WEIGHTED ALPHA: Weight asset alpha scores by conviction level or position size to compute portfolio-level expected alpha. EXAMPLES: (1) Cap-weighted portfolio return: values=daily_returns, weights=market_cap. Produces a single time series of the portfolio's daily value-weighted return. (2) Risk-parity weighted signal: values=momentum_score, weights=1/volatility. Produces a risk-parity-weighted composite momentum signal for the universe. (3) Revenue-weighted fundamental: values=ROE, weights=revenue. Larger companies have more influence on the aggregate metric.
limitations: Requires struct columns with '#values' and '#weights' fields per asset. Plain numeric columns will throw an error. Both values and weights must be numeric. NaN values or NaN weights are excluded from the calculation. Zero weights effectively exclude the asset. All-zero weights produce NaN output.

name: Returns

options.name: Period
options.desc: Number of periods for return calculation
options.tuningGuidance: Period 1 for single-bar returns (most common). Larger periods for multi-bar returns.

options.name: Type
options.desc: Return calculation method
options.tuningGuidance: Simple: percentage returns (Xt-Xn)/Xn. Log: log(Xt/Xn), symmetric and additive. Monetary: absolute difference Xt-Xn. Directional: sign of change (-1, 0, 1).

desc: Calculates returns between current and lagged values with multiple calculation methods.
usageContext: Calculate historical returns for volatility estimation, risk analysis, and feature engineering. OUTPUT SCALE: Simple and log returns output decimal fractions, NOT multiplied by 100. A 5% gain outputs 0.05, a 10% loss outputs -0.10. Use > 0.05 for 5% threshold (not > 5). Simple returns for intuitive P&L interpretation and cumulative product across assets. Log returns for statistical analysis — additive across time periods, symmetric around zero, required for variance/covariance estimation and portfolio aggregation. Monetary returns for absolute P&L tracking and position sizing in dollar terms. Directional returns (-1, 0, +1) for classification labels in ML models and trend regime identification.
limitations: First 'period' values will be null. Simple returns are asymmetric (50% loss needs 100% gain to recover). Log returns require strictly positive prices (undefined for zero or negative values). Monetary returns are not comparable across assets with different price levels.

name: White Marubozu
desc: Bullish candle with no upper or lower shadows (wicks). Strong buying pressure with opening at low and closing at high.
usageContext: Complete buyer dominance - opened at low and closed at high with zero wicks. Strongest single-candle bullish signal. Buyers controlled the entire session without any seller pushback. In uptrend = strong continuation. At resistance = decisive breakout. PIPELINE PATTERN: detect white_marubozu, use as high-conviction bullish signal. EXAMPLE: white_marubozu breaking above resistance = strong breakout confirmation.
limitations: Very rare with strict no-shadow requirement. Wick threshold is configurable but affects frequency. Can appear as climactic buying (potential top). Single candle - always confirm with next candle and context.

name: ArgMinMax (Timestamps)

options.name: Expanding Mode
options.desc: If true, returns expanding argmin/argmax timestamps. If false, returns global argmin/argmax timestamps for all rows.
options.tuningGuidance: true (default) = expanding: at each row, tracks both min and max timestamps seen so far. false = global: broadcasts the overall min and max timestamps to all rows.

desc: Returns timestamps where both minimum and maximum values occurred. Outputs two columns: min_loc (timestamp of minimum) and max_loc (timestamp of maximum). More efficient than calling arg_min and arg_max separately when both are needed.
usageContext: Find when both the minimum and maximum values occurred in a single transform call. Prefer this over separate arg_min + arg_max when you need both timestamps — it avoids redundant iteration over the data. Use cases: peak-to-trough analysis for drawdown timing, identifying the range (best day vs worst day) in a backtest, and labeling both extremes on equity curve charts. Outputs two Timestamp columns: min_loc and max_loc, accessible via the standard output id with #min_loc and #max_loc suffixes. Trigger phrases: 'peak and trough dates', 'min and max timestamps', 'range timing'.
limitations: Returns timestamps, not values — use cumulative(agg=Min) and cumulative(agg=Max) for values. In expanding mode, ties are broken by first occurrence for both min and max independently. NaN/null values in input are skipped for both min and max tracking. Outputs are Timestamp columns — cannot be used directly in arithmetic operations.

name: Analyst Ratings
desc: Analyst ratings and price target changes. Includes rating actions (upgrade/downgrade), price targets, and firm recommendations.
usageContext:
Analyst rating changes and price target revisions from brokerage firms.
- Analyst momentum: Trade direction of upgrades/downgrades, weight by importance.
- Contrarian: Fade uniform consensus (all bullish/bearish).
- Price target convergence: Compare current price to consensus target for mean-reversion.
- Event overlays: Mark institutional-driven price moves on charts.
Combine with price data for post-rating drift analysis.
limitations:
Sparse: 0-30+ rows/year/asset depending on coverage. Most trading days empty. NullPolicy=AllowAll.
Use ffill to forward-fill last known values when joining with daily price data.
Coverage: From 2011-12-08. Skewed toward large/mid-cap US. Small-cap/international may have zero coverage.
Nulls: price_target null when firm issues rating without target. previous_rating null on initiates_coverage_on.
Multiple firms may cluster on same date (e.g., post-earnings).

name: Datetime Extract

options.name: Datetime Component
options.desc: Component to extract. Integer outputs: year (e.g. 2024), month (1-12), day (1-31), hour (0-23), minute (0-59), second (0-59), quarter (1-4), day_of_week (0=Mon..6=Sun ISO), day_of_year (1-366), week (1-53 ISO). Boolean output: is_leap_year. Timestamp output: date (truncated to midnight). Integer output: time_of_day (minutes since midnight).

options.name: Timezone
options.desc: IANA timezone for extraction (e.g., 'America/New_York', 'Europe/London'). Timestamps are converted to this timezone before extraction. Critical for intraday: US DST shifts (Mar/Nov) create a 3-week gap with EU DST (last Sun Mar/Oct). Always convert before extracting hour/day components.

desc: Extract a datetime component (year, month, day, hour, etc.) from a timestamp. For bar timestamps, use datetime_extract(index()). For data source timestamps, pass them directly.
usageContext:
COMPONENTS (14 total):
Integer: year, month (1-12), day (1-31), hour (0-23), minute (0-59),
  second (0-59), quarter (1-4), day_of_week (0=Mon ISO), day_of_year (1-366),
  week (1-53 ISO), time_of_day (minutes since midnight)
Boolean: is_leap_year
Timestamp: date (truncated to midnight in target timezone)

KEY CHOICE -- datetime_extract vs is_period_boundary:
- datetime_extract → raw VALUE for grouping, filtering, plotting
  (e.g., month=1 for January bars)
- is_period_boundary → BOOLEAN SIGNAL for rebalancing triggers
  (e.g., true on first bar of each month)

ACADEMIC REFERENCES:
- January effect (Wachtel 1942): month==1 tends to outperform
- Sell in May (Bouman & Jacobsen 2002): month 5-10 underperformance
- Monday effect (Cross 1973, French 1980): day_of_week==0 lower returns
- Turn-of-month (Ariel 1987): last/first days of month outperform
- Pre-FOMC drift (Lucca & Moench 2015): hour-level pre-announcement drift
- Quad witching: 3rd Friday of Mar/Jun/Sep/Dec, elevated volume

TIMEZONE GOTCHAS: US DST (2nd Sun Mar / 1st Sun Nov) vs EU DST
(last Sun Mar / last Sun Oct) creates a 3-week offset gap each spring/fall.
Always apply timezone conversion BEFORE extracting hour/day components.

EXAMPLES:
1. Monthly seasonality: m = datetime_extract(component='month')(index())
2. Intraday session: h = datetime_extract(component='hour', timezone='America/New_York')(index())
3. Day-of-week effect: dow = datetime_extract(component='day_of_week')(index())
4. Quarter grouping: q = datetime_extract(component='quarter')(econ.observation_date)
limitations:
ISO conventions: day_of_week 0=Monday..6=Sunday (not 0=Sunday). time_of_day
returns total minutes since midnight (0-1439), not HH:MM. date component
truncates to midnight in the target timezone. is_leap_year returns boolean
(not integer). week uses ISO 8601 numbering (week 1 contains first Thursday).
Requires timestamp input — use index() to pass bar timestamps.

name: Positive Volume Index
desc: Positive Volume Index. Shows price movements on days when volume increases, highlighting public participation.
usageContext: Tracks price changes only on days when volume increases from the prior day. Theory: public/crowd trades on high-volume days. Rising PVI = public is bullish. Use alongside NVI: NVI for smart money direction, PVI for crowd direction. PIPELINE PATTERN: compute pvi() and nvi() together, compare trends for smart-money vs crowd divergence. EXAMPLE: PVI falling while NVI rising = public selling but smart money accumulating (contrarian bullish).
limitations: Crowd behavior theory is difficult to validate. Cumulative and path-dependent. Less useful in modern markets with algorithmic trading blurring smart/dumb money distinction. Best used alongside NVI for context. Rarely useful as standalone.

Select from curated indicators covering inflation, rates, employment, GDP, housing, credit spreads, energy prices, and more.

desc: Aggregate data from higher frequency to lower frequency timeframe. Works on all data types. Compiler auto-inserts when referencing a different timeframe.
usageContext: Multi-timeframe strategy alignment. Aggregates high-frequency data (e.g., 1Min) to lower frequency (e.g., 1D). Compiler auto-inserts when a node references a different timeframe. 'how' option controls aggregation: last (default), mean, sum, min, max, ohlc (numeric only).
limitations: Target timeframe must be coarser than input. Execution handled by orchestrator — TransformData() is never called directly.

name: Retracements
desc: Calculates percentage retracements from swing highs and lows, measuring how much price has pulled back from a prior swing point.
usageContext: Measure pullback depth from swing points for retracement entries. Deeper retracements (50-70%) offer better risk/reward but fewer triggers. Shallow retracements (20-30%) indicate strong momentum.
limitations: Requires swing_highs_lows input. Retracement % doesn't guarantee reversal - can retrace 100% (full reversal). Doesn't predict how far retracement will go. Works best in trending markets.

name: Volume Weighted Moving Average
desc: Volume Weighted Moving Average. Moving average that weights price by volume, giving more importance to high-volume price moves.
usageContext: Moving average weighted by volume - gives more weight to high-volume price levels. Better represents institutional/smart money positioning than simple MAs. Use like SMA but with volume confirmation built-in. Breaks more significant than SMA breaks. Good for identifying support/resistance with volume context. Compare to SMA to see volume impact.
limitations: Requires quality volume data - unreliable on low-volume or manipulated volume. Calculation heavier than simple MAs. Less widely used than SMA/EMA. Volume weighting can distort in illiquid periods. Best on liquid instruments with genuine volume. Consider VWAP for intraday instead.

name: Commodity Channel Index
desc: Commodity Channel Index. Identifies cyclical turns in price and measures variations from the statistical mean.
usageContext: Unbounded oscillator measuring deviation from statistical mean. Typical range: -100 to +100, but can go beyond. CCI >+100 = overbought, <-100 = oversold. Unlike RSI/Stoch, extreme readings can persist in trends. Use for: mean-reversion in ranges (fade extremes), trend-following in trends (ride extremes), divergence detection. Zero-line crosses indicate momentum shifts.
limitations: Unbounded nature makes fixed thresholds less reliable than RSI. Extreme readings normal in strong trends - not always reversal signals. Requires context (trending vs ranging) to interpret correctly. Default 20-period may need adjustment. More volatile than RSI. Consider using with ADX to distinguish trending/ranging regimes.

desc: Categorical bar chart in the dashboard. Labeled mode: group values by label (months, sectors). Series mode: each column becomes a bar with BarSeriesSchema. Supports grouped, stacked, and 100%% stacked layouts.
usageContext: Categorical bar chart in the DASHBOARD view for comparing discrete categories. Bar length encodes magnitude, making relative differences instantly readable. This is the standard chart for any 'compare X across categories' question. THREE MODES: (A) Labeled mode: provide label + values inputs. Rows are grouped by label (e.g., month names, sector names, strategy names). Each unique label becomes one bar (or group). The label column provides X-axis categories, the values column provides bar heights. Values with the same label are aggregated using 'agg'. (B) Series mode: provide only values input (no label), no stack on BarSeriesSpec. Each value column becomes one bar. Use BarSeriesSchema for per-series names and colors. Categories are series names. (C) Grouped mode: provide only values input with stack set on BarSeriesSpec. The stack field defines X-axis categories (e.g., 'Emerging Markets', 'U.S. Large Cap'). The name field defines legend entries (e.g., 'Held', 'Sold'). CRITICAL: names MUST be reused across stack groups — inputs with the same name become one Highcharts series with one value per stack category. The stack label already identifies the group on the x-axis, so names should describe WHAT the bar measures within the group, not WHICH group it belongs to. Example: 4 regimes × 3 horizons = 12 inputs. Use name='1M' for all 4 regime inputs at the 1M horizon, name='3M' for the next 4, name='6M' for the last 4. Use color on each spec to differentiate groups visually (e.g., Blue for regime A, Indigo for regime B). WRONG: name='RegimeA 1M', name='RegimeB 1M' — creates separate sparse series with bad spacing. RIGHT: name='1M' + stack='Regime A', name='1M' + stack='Regime B' — creates one '1M' series with values at both x-axis positions. This creates true grouped bar charts (e.g., 3 bars per category across 4 categories = 12 inputs, 3 series). STACK TYPES: NoStack (default — ungrouped), Normal (stacked — bar segments sum to total), Percent (100% stacked — shows proportional composition). For grouped side-by-side bars, set stack on each BarSeriesSpec instead. SPECIAL FEATURES: x_category_type converts numeric labels to readable names: Month (1-12 → Jan-Dec), DayOfWeek (0-6 → Mon-Sun). color_by_value=true colors bars green (positive) and red (negative). reference_lines add horizontal threshold lines. Vertical/horizontal orientation. Data labels show values on bars. KEY CHOICE - xy_bars vs HISTOGRAM: xy_bars shows aggregated values for NAMED categories (months, sectors, strategies). Histogram shows FREQUENCY DISTRIBUTION of continuous data (how many returns fell in each bin?). Use xy_bars when each bar represents a meaningful entity. Use histogram when you want the shape of a distribution. KEY CHOICE - xy_bars vs PIE: Both show categorical breakdowns. Use xy_bars when comparing absolute magnitudes or when there are many categories (>5). Use pie when the insight is 'part of whole' composition with few categories (2-8). Bars are always better for precise comparison; pie charts are better for showing proportional splits. KEY CHOICE - xy_bars vs SUMMARY_TABLE: xy_bars gives a VISUAL comparison where the user sees relative magnitude at a glance. summary_table gives EXACT numbers in a grid with headers. Best practice: use both in the same dashboard category for complementary views. KEY CHOICE - xy_bars vs cs_bars: xy_bars is PER-ASSET (one chart per stock), categories are arbitrary labels (months, sectors). cs_bars is CROSS-SECTIONAL (one chart for ALL stocks), categories are asset names. Use xy_bars when categorizing one asset's data. Use cs_bars when comparing across assets. EXAMPLES: (1) Monthly returns: label=month_number, values=monthly_return, x_category_type=Month, color_by_value=true. Green bars for positive months, red for negative. Pair with summary_table RowSpec mode for the matching statistics grid. This is the standard monthly return bar chart seen in pyfolio and QuantStats. (2) Strategy attribution: label=component_name, series=[{name:'Allocation', color:Blue}, {name:'Selection', color:Orange}], stack_type=Normal. Stacked bars show total and decomposition per component. The standard Brinson attribution visualization. (3) Day-of-week seasonality: label=day_number, values=avg_return, x_category_type=DayOfWeek, vertical=true. Shows if returns cluster on specific days. (4) Sector weight comparison: values=(sector_weight_portfolio, sector_weight_benchmark), series=[{name:'Portfolio', color:Blue}, {name:'Benchmark', color:Orange}]. Grouped bars compare portfolio vs benchmark sector allocations side-by-side. (5) Grouped bar chart (Held vs Sold): values=(eem_ytd, eem_sold, efa_ytd, efa_sold, ...), series=[{name:'Held', color:Blue, stack:'Emerging Markets'}, {name:'Sold', color:Gray, stack:'Emerging Markets'}, {name:'Held', color:Blue, stack:'Developed Markets'}, ...]. Stack names become x-axis categories, series names become legend entries. Produces 2 bars per category across 5 categories.
limitations: Dashboard widget, not the TV chart. Not suitable for large continuous data — use histogram for distribution analysis. For cross-asset comparisons use cs_bars. For time-synchronized bar panels in the TV chart use timeseries_bars. Each bar represents one category — cannot show trends over a continuous X-axis (use xy_lines for that). Label + values mode requires one label column and one values column; for multi-series with labels, compute separate DataFrames.

options.name: Days Before Holiday
options.desc: Number of trading days before holiday

options.name: Days After Holiday

desc: Detects trading days before and after market holidays based on the pre-holiday effect documented by Lakonishok & Smidt (1988) and Ariel (1990). Research shows pre-holiday returns averaged 9-14 times the normal daily return during 1963-1982, with one-third of total annual stock market returns earned on just 8 pre-holiday trading days per year. The strongest effects occur before Independence Day, Thanksgiving, and Christmas. The mechanism is attributed to reduced volume, lower selling pressure, short-covering before multi-day closures, and positive investor sentiment.
usageContext:
Use to exploit the pre-holiday rally effect for timing entries and position management.
- Go long 1 day before holidays (days_before=1) for the strongest pre-holiday premium.
- Target Independence Day, Thanksgiving, and Christmas -- these holidays show the most consistent effects.
- Use days_after=1 to capture post-holiday continuation (less documented but observable around Thanksgiving).
- Reduce short exposure before holidays -- reduced volume creates unfavorable conditions for short sellers.
- Combine with turn_of_month when holidays fall near month boundaries for compounding seasonal effects.
- Use as a risk management filter: avoid initiating new positions on low-volume pre-holiday sessions.
limitations:
The pre-holiday premium has diminished significantly since the 1980s as documented by Ko (2021) and
international studies (Meneu & Pardo 2004). Only 8 pre-holiday days per year means very small sample size
for statistical significance in recent data. Requires accurate holiday calendar data -- currently only US
Federal holidays are supported (USFederalHolidayCalendar). Reduced volume before holidays increases bid-ask
spreads and slippage. The effect is measured in single-digit basis points per event, which may not survive
transaction costs. International holidays are not supported and may conflict with US-focused strategies on
global assets.

name: Reference Stocks

options.name: Reference Ticker
options.desc: Stock ticker symbol (e.g., SPY, QQQ, DIA, IWM, AAPL, TSLA)

desc: Any stock as reference data for pairs, spreads, or cross-asset analysis outside the strategy universe. Accepts any valid stock ticker.
usageContext:
Outputs: .o (open), .h (high), .l (low), .c (close), .v (volume).
Use for any stock ticker not in the curated dropdown.
Example: reference_stocks(ticker="TSLA")().c for Tesla close.
limitations:
Inherits the strategy's timeframe (daily or intraday). NullPolicy=AllowAll.
Weekends/holidays have no bars.

name: Linear Fit (Rolling OLS)

options.name: Window Size
options.desc: Rolling window size for OLS regression
options.tuningGuidance: Use 20-60 for tactical pairs trading. Use 60-120 for more stable hedge ratios. Match to expected holding period - shorter windows for intraday, longer for swing trading.

desc: Rolling ordinary least squares (OLS) regression. Fits y = slope*x + intercept over a rolling window. Returns slope, intercept, and residual (y - predicted) at each bar.
usageContext: Essential for pairs trading hedge ratio estimation and spread construction. Use to find dynamic relationship between two assets. The slope represents the hedge ratio, residual is the spread to trade. Also useful for detrending and factor exposure estimation. KEY DIFFERENCE from multi_linear_fit: linear_fit handles exactly 2 series (one X, one Y). For 2+ independent variables (e.g., Fama-French factors), use multi_linear_fit instead. Trigger phrases: 'hedge ratio', 'spread construction', 'regression', 'OLS', 'detrend', 'linear relationship', 'slope', 'residual', 'pairs trading spread'.
limitations: Linear relationship only - doesn't capture non-linear dependencies. Window size critical: too small creates noisy estimates, too large misses regime changes. Sensitive to outliers. Assumes homoscedastic errors.

name: Break of Structure & Change of Character

options.name: Use Close Price
options.desc: Use close price for break detection instead of high/low wicks
options.tuningGuidance: False (default) = wick-based breaks, more signals but some false. True = close-based breaks, more conservative but misses some valid breaks.

desc: Detects Break of Structure (BOS) and Change of Character (CHOCH) patterns, which signal potential trend changes and market structure shifts.
usageContext: Core SMC concept for trend analysis. BOS (Break of Structure) = price breaks previous swing confirming trend continuation. CHOCH (Change of Character) = break of counter-trend structure suggesting reversal. Use with swing_highs_lows input.
limitations: Requires swing_highs_lows as input - can't use standalone. Lagging since waits for structure break confirmation. False signals in choppy markets. Best on trending instruments.

name: Typical Price
desc: Typical Price. Average of high, low, and close prices for each period, representing a balanced price.
usageContext: Average of H, L, C: (H+L+C)/3. Most commonly used alternative price representation in technical analysis. Used in CCI, MFI, and many other indicators internally. Represents a balanced view of the bar. PIPELINE PATTERN: use typprice() as input to custom indicators. EXAMPLE: cci() uses typical price internally for its calculation.
limitations: Ignores open price. Equal weighting of H, L, C may not reflect where most trading occurred. Close-weighted alternatives (wcprice) may be more appropriate when closing price matters most.

name: Common Reference Futures

options.name: Reference Futures Contract
options.desc: Select the reference futures contract

desc: Reference OHLCV data for curated futures contracts via Epoch Archive. Returns RAW multi-contract data (all available contracts per date). When consumed by downstream transforms, List columns are resolved to keep_last (last contract in list per date — NOT a proper front-month continuation). For proper continuous series, use futures_continuation() on market_data_source().
usageContext:
Raw OHLCV data for a curated futures contract, independent of strategy universe.
WARNING: For futures, this returns ALL contracts per date (List columns).
Downstream transforms resolve List columns via keep_last, which picks the last
contract in the list — NOT a proper front-month continuation.
- Use for: non-futures asset classes (stocks, indices, FX, crypto) where there are no duplicate rows.
- For futures cross-asset ratios/spreads: use futures_continuation() on market_data_source() instead.
- Acceptable for rough correlation/regime signals where exact contract selection doesn't matter.
limitations:
Data sourced from Epoch Archive (not Polygon). NullPolicy=AllowAll.
FUTURES WARNING: Does NOT produce a continuation. Returns raw multi-contract data.
Downstream keep_last resolution picks an arbitrary contract per date.
For proper front-month continuation, use futures_continuation() on market_data_source().
Weekends/holidays have no bars.

name: Cumulative

options.name: Aggregation
options.desc: Cumulative aggregation operation applied over the expanding window from series start
options.tuningGuidance: sum: running totals for P&L, cumulative volume, and equity curves. product: compounding returns — always pass (1+r) format, e.g. 1.02 for +2%. max/min: running high/low watermarks for drawdown calculations and trailing stops. mean: running average that smooths noise as sample size grows. stddev/variance: expanding volatility — use ddof=1 for sample (default), ddof=0 for population. median: robust expanding center — less sensitive to outliers than mean. quantile: expanding percentile controlled by q parameter. skew: expanding distribution asymmetry — near 0 for symmetric returns. kurtosis: expanding tail thickness — excess kurtosis, 0 for normal. count: expanding observation counter — useful for coverage tracking. first: constant first value — baseline reference for drift calculations. last: identity (returns each row's value) — useful in schema contexts.

options.name: Quantile
options.desc: Quantile value (0.0-1.0), used when agg=Quantile
options.tuningGuidance: 0.5 = median (default). 0.25 = Q1 lower quartile. 0.75 = Q3 upper quartile. 0.05/0.95 = 5th/95th percentile for tail analysis. 0.0 = expanding minimum (equivalent to agg=Min). 1.0 = expanding maximum (equivalent to agg=Max).

options.name: Degrees of Freedom
options.desc: Delta degrees of freedom for stddev/variance calculations. Divides by (n - ddof) instead of n.
options.tuningGuidance: 1 = sample estimator (Bessel's correction, default) — standard for financial data. 0 = population estimator — use when the series is the complete population. Higher values are rarely needed outside specialized statistical contexts.

options.name: Biased Estimator
options.desc: Use biased estimator (true) or unbiased/sample estimator (false) for skew and kurtosis
options.tuningGuidance: true (default) = biased estimator, matches scipy.stats default. false = applies correction factors for small samples — use when n < 50.

desc: Calculates running cumulative values from series start using an expanding window. Supports 14 aggregation operations: Sum, Product, Max, Min, Mean, Std, Var, Median, Quantile, Skew, Kurtosis, Count, First, and Last. Native cumulative operations (sum, product, max, min, mean) are optimized; statistical operations (std, var, median, quantile, skew, kurtosis) use expanding windows.
usageContext: Use cumulative transforms to build expanding-window aggregations from the start of a time series. Common patterns: (1) Equity curves — cumulative(agg=Sum) on daily P&L to track account growth. (2) Compounding returns — cumulative(agg=Product) on (1+daily_return) to compute total return. (3) High/low watermarks — cumulative(agg=Max) on equity for peak tracking, then compare with current value to compute drawdown. cumulative(agg=Min) for trough tracking. (4) Running statistics — cumulative(agg=Mean) for expanding average that stabilizes over time; cumulative(agg=Std) for expanding volatility estimate that improves with more data. (5) Distribution monitoring — cumulative(agg=Skew) and cumulative(agg=Kurtosis) to track how return distributions evolve as sample size grows. (6) Coverage tracking — cumulative(agg=Count) counts non-null observations seen so far. (7) Expanding percentiles — cumulative(agg=Quantile, q=0.05) tracks the expanding 5th percentile for VaR-style analysis. (8) Resettable accumulation — cumulative(agg=Min)(price, bear_entry) tracks the trough price that resets each time a new bear market begins, enabling per-cycle return computation. Trigger phrases: 'running total', 'cumulative sum', 'compound return', 'equity curve', 'high watermark', 'expanding average', 'expanding volatility', 'running count', 'resettable cumulative', 'per-cycle accumulation'.
limitations: Without a reset input, always calculates from the first observation in the series. An optional boolean reset input is supported for Min, Max, Sum, and Product: when the reset condition fires, the accumulator resets to the current bar's value after outputting the current result. Reset is not supported for statistical operations (Std, Var, Median, Quantile, Skew, Kurtosis). For windowed aggregations, use rolling_agg instead. Product aggregation requires (1+return) format; raw returns will produce incorrect results. Std and Var produce NaN for the first row (insufficient data for ddof=1). Skew requires at least 3 observations; Kurtosis requires at least 4. Any, All, and CountDistinct aggregations are not supported and will throw runtime errors. NaN values in input are dropped for all aggregation types (nullPolicy=DropNulls).

name: Dividends

options.name: Dividend Type
options.desc: Filter by dividend type

desc: Retrieve historical cash dividend distributions with key dates and payout information. Includes split-adjusted amounts and historical adjustment factors for accurate total return calculations.
usageContext:
Historical dividend distributions including declaration, ex-dividend, record, and pay dates.
- Dividend capture: Time entries around ex-dividend dates for yield harvesting.
- Income analysis: Track payout consistency, frequency changes, and yield trends.
- Fundamental screening: Filter by distribution_type for special vs recurring dividends.
- Price adjustment: Use split_adjusted_cash_amount and historical_adjustment_factor for adjusted returns.
Combine with price data to calculate dividend yield and total return.
limitations:
Sparse: Typically 1-12 rows/year/asset depending on frequency (quarterly=4, monthly=12). NullPolicy=AllowAll.
Use ffill to forward-fill last known values when joining with daily price data.
Keyed to ex_dividend_date. declaration_date, record_date, pay_date are separate output columns.

name: Stock Splits
desc: Retrieve historical stock split events, including execution dates and ratio factors, to understand changes in a company's share structure over time.
usageContext:
Historical stock split events with ratio and adjustment factors.
- Event-driven: Detect split announcements for pre/post-split drift analysis.
- Data integrity: Use historical_adjustment_factor to normalize pre-split prices.
- Corporate action awareness: Distinguish forward_split, reverse_split, stock_dividend.
Combine with price data to verify split-adjusted price continuity.
limitations:
Sparse: Most stocks split rarely (0-2 events per decade). NullPolicy=AllowAll.
Use ffill to forward-fill last known values when joining with daily price data.
Price bars are typically already split-adjusted.

name: Ticker Events
desc: Retrieve a timeline of key events associated with a given ticker, CUSIP, or Composite FIGI. This experimental endpoint highlights ticker changes such as symbol renaming or rebranding, helping users maintain continuity in their records and analyses.
usageContext:
Ticker lifecycle events: symbol changes, delistings, new listings, spinoffs.
- Data continuity: Track ticker renames (e.g., FB -> META) for historical data stitching.
- Delisting risk: Monitor delisting events for risk management.
- Corporate action awareness: Identify spinoffs and structural changes.
limitations:
Sparse: Rare events (0-3 per ticker lifetime). NullPolicy=AllowAll.
Currently ticker_change is the primary supported event type.

name: Short Interest
desc: Retrieve bi-monthly aggregated short interest data reported to FINRA by broker-dealers for specified stock tickers. Short interest represents the total number of shares sold short but not yet covered or closed out, serving as a market sentiment indicator. Use cases include market sentiment analysis, short-squeeze prediction, risk management, and trading strategy refinement. Data is available across all plan tiers, updated bi-weekly with historical depth varying by subscription level (Basic: 2 years; Starter+: all history).
usageContext:
Bi-monthly aggregated short interest reported to FINRA by broker-dealers.
- Short squeeze detection: Monitor days_to_cover spikes for squeeze setups.
- Sentiment gauge: Rising short interest signals bearish conviction.
- Contrarian: Heavily shorted names can rally sharply on covering.
Combine with short_volume for daily vs positional short activity comparison.
limitations:
Sparse: Bi-monthly FINRA reporting (~2 rows/month). Most trading days empty. NullPolicy=AllowAll.
Use ffill to forward-fill last known values when joining with daily price data.
short_interest != short_volume. This is outstanding positions, not daily flow.

name: Value When

options.name: Occurrence
options.desc: Which occurrence to return (0 = most recent, 1 = second most recent, etc.)
options.tuningGuidance: Use 0 for most recent signal, 1+ for historical signals

desc: Returns the value of source when condition was true on its nth occurrence. Occurrence 0 is most recent, 1 is second most recent, etc.
usageContext: Pine Script ta.valuewhen() equivalent. Capture values at signal time — entry price for P&L tracking (valuewhen(entry_signal, close, 0)), pivot levels for support/resistance (valuewhen(pivot_high, high, 0)), or replay signal values for analysis. Use occurrence > 0 for historical signals: valuewhen(cond, close, 1) returns price at second-most-recent signal.
limitations: Returns NA if condition has not occurred enough times. Searches all history — may be slow on very long series with many occurrences.

name: Time Series Forecast
desc: Time Series Forecast. Linear regression projection that extends the regression line to predict future values.
usageContext: Forward-projected linear regression value - the next predicted point on the regression line. Leads price slightly compared to linreg. Price above TSF = bullish momentum, below = bearish. PIPELINE PATTERN: compute tsf(period=20), use as adaptive trend line. Compare price to TSF for trend position. EXAMPLE: price crossing above TSF = regression-confirmed uptrend start.
limitations: Linear projection is simplistic - markets are not linear. Can overshoot in volatile markets. More sensitive to recent data than linreg. Forward projection is one step only - not a multi-step forecast. Consider using with stderr bands.

name: Previous High Low

options.name: Interval
options.desc: Number of periods back to reference (1 = previous period)
options.tuningGuidance: 1 (default) = immediately previous period. 2+ for older reference levels. Usually 1 is most relevant for trading.

options.name: Time Frame Type
options.desc: Type of period to reference
options.tuningGuidance: Day = most common for intraday strategies. Week for swing trading breakouts. Hour for scalping. Month for position trading.

desc: Identifies the previous high or low levels within a given interval and tracks when current price breaks these levels.
usageContext: Track key reference levels from previous periods for breakout trading. Previous day high/low crucial for intraday strategies. Break above prev high = bullish, below prev low = bearish.
limitations: Only tracks one previous period - can't access multiple historical levels. Breaks can be false (whipsaw). Works best on liquid instruments with clear daily ranges.

name: Annualized Historical Volatility
desc: Annualized Historical Volatility. Measures price dispersion around the mean, expressed as an annualized percentage.
usageContext: Annualized standard deviation of log returns. OUTPUT SCALE: Decimal fraction, NOT multiplied by 100. A typical equity outputs ~0.20 (meaning 20% annualized vol), highly volatile assets ~0.80+. Use volatility > 0.30 for 30% threshold (not > 30). Use for position sizing (inverse vol), volatility targeting, and regime detection. PIPELINE PATTERN: compute volatility(period=20), use for risk-parity allocation. EXAMPLE: target 10% portfolio vol: size each position as 0.10 / asset_vol.
limitations: Assumes log-normal returns and no serial correlation. Backward-looking - cannot predict vol regime changes. Annualization assumes 252 trading days. Sensitive to period choice. Consider GARCH for forward-looking vol estimates.

name: News

options.name: Channels
options.desc: Filter by news channels (e.g., 'Top Stories', 'Markets', 'Earnings')

options.name: Channels Match Mode
options.desc: How to match channels: AnyOf (match any), AllOf (match all), Exact (match exactly)

options.name: Tags
options.desc: Filter by news tags (e.g., 'Technology', 'Healthcare')

options.name: Tags Match Mode
options.desc: How to match tags: AnyOf (match any), AllOf (match all), Exact (match exactly)

options.name: Authors
options.desc: Filter by author names (matches if any author matches)

options.name: Additional Tickers
options.desc: Additional tickers for cross-asset news. Primary asset ticker is added automatically. Only specify for sector peers or related symbols.

desc: Retrieve real-time structured, timestamped news articles from Benzinga, including headlines, full-text content, tickers, categories, and more. Each article entry contains metadata such as publication time and topic channels. Articles can be filtered by ticker and time, and are returned in a consistent format for easy parsing and integration. Use Cases: Market news feeds, alerting systems, portfolio monitoring, dashboards.
usageContext:
News articles for the strategy's primary asset.
- Sentiment trading: Pipe through sentiment transforms to get numeric scores for signals.
- Event detection: Monitor headlines for earnings, M&A, regulatory, or market-moving events.
- Targeted filtering: Set channels (e.g., 'Earnings', 'Markets') and tags (e.g., 'Technology')
  options to narrow news to relevant categories. Use tags_match_mode='AllOf' for strict filtering.
- Cross-asset context: Add related tickers via the tickers option for sector/peer news.
Combine with price data to measure news-driven price impact.
limitations:
Sparse: Variable frequency — 0 to dozens of articles per day depending on ticker. NullPolicy=AllowAll.
Output is text (titles, descriptions, tags). Do NOT ffill raw articles.
Pipe through sentiment analysis transforms to get numeric scores, then ffill the score.

options.name: Chart Title

options.desc: Number of bins for the histogram

options.desc: Opacity for histogram bar fill (0.0 - 1.0)

options.desc: Horizontal/vertical threshold lines with optional labels, colors, and dash styles

options.desc: Horizontal shaded bands on Y axis (e.g., frequency zones)

options.desc: Number of decimal places for Y axis values

options.desc: Format type for X axis values (Auto, Decimal, Percent, Monetary, Integer)

options.name: X Axis Decimal Places
options.desc: Number of decimal places for X axis values

options.name: Display Order
options.desc: Display order within dashboard category (lower values appear first, 0 = default position)

desc: Histogram showing distribution of values across bins. Pre-aggregates data server-side into bins with counts for machine-readable output.
usageContext: Show the FREQUENCY DISTRIBUTION of a single numeric series in the DASHBOARD view. Takes one numeric column, divides the value range into equal-width bins, and plots a bar for each bin whose height is the count of observations falling in that bin. Pre-aggregates data server-side so tearsheet protos contain machine-readable bin counts, analytics (mean, std, mode, skewness, kurtosis), enabling AI analysis jobs to validate distribution shape directly from the proto. TRIGGER PHRASES: Use when the user asks for 'distribution', 'histogram', 'frequency', 'how are returns distributed', 'shape of returns', 'return spread', 'P&L distribution', 'show the spread', 'binned counts', 'how often does X occur', 'fat tails', 'skewness visual', 'is it normally distributed'. HISTOGRAM vs cs_histogram: Use histogram for per-asset distribution. Use cs_histogram to overlay multiple asset distributions on one chart for comparison. HISTOGRAM vs BOXPLOT: Histogram shows the FULL SHAPE (skewness, bimodality, kurtosis). Boxplot summarizes as quartiles and outlier dots. Use histogram when the shape itself is the insight. Use boxplot when comparing distributions side-by-side.
limitations: Single input column only - for cross-asset distribution overlay use cs_histogram. Shows raw frequency counts, not probability density. Single-asset only (isCrossSectional=false) - each asset gets its own histogram.

name: Short Volume
desc: Retrieve daily aggregated short sale volume data reported to FINRA from off-exchange trading venues and alternative trading systems (ATS). Unlike short interest metrics that measure outstanding positions at specific intervals, this endpoint captures daily trading activity of short sales, helping analysts detect market sentiment shifts and identify short-selling trends. Use cases include intraday sentiment analysis, short-sale trend identification, liquidity analysis, and trading strategy optimization. Available across all Stocks plans with data updated daily and historical availability ranging from 2 years (Basic) to all history (Starter and above).
usageContext:
Daily aggregated short sale volume from FINRA off-exchange venues and ATS.
- Sentiment: short_volume_ratio above 40-50% may signal bearish pressure or market-making.
- Flow analysis: Compare daily short flow vs outstanding short_interest for positioning context.
- Mean-reversion: Spikes in short volume ratio can precede reversals.
Combine with short_interest for full short picture (daily flow + outstanding positions).
limitations:
short_volume != short_interest. This is daily short SALE volume, not outstanding short positions.
Includes off-exchange and ATS venues only (FINRA-reported). Does not capture all exchange volume.
NullPolicy=AllowAll. Daily frequency on trading days.
