Rule of thumb: min_training_samples >= 10 * num_features. Lower values start predictions sooner but risk unreliable early predictions.

desc: DBSCAN clustering with rolling/expanding window training for adaptive anomaly detection. Number of clusters adapts to data density. Points not in any cluster are marked as anomalies.

outputs.name: True if point classified as noise (cluster_label == -1)
Number of distinct clusters found (excluding noise)

usageContext: Use for anomaly detection without fixed cluster count.
limitations: Sensitive to epsilon and min_points. Density thresholds may need adjustment over time.

name: Bill Williams Alligator

options.name: Jaw Period
options.desc: SMMA period for the Jaw line (slowest, blue in traditional coloring)
options.tuningGuidance: Standard 13 for daily charts. The Jaw represents long-term trend direction. Increase for weekly charts, decrease for intraday.

options.name: Teeth Period
options.desc: SMMA period for the Teeth line (medium, red in traditional coloring)
options.tuningGuidance: Standard 8. Medium-term trend line. Should be between Jaw and Lips periods.

options.name: Lips Period
options.desc: SMMA period for the Lips line (fastest, green in traditional coloring)
options.tuningGuidance: Standard 5. Fastest line, reacts first to price changes. Crossovers of Lips over Teeth generate early signals.

options.name: Apply Forward Offset
options.desc: Apply traditional Williams forward offsets (Jaw=8, Teeth=5, Lips=3 bars). WARNING: Enables data leak in backtesting - only use for visualization.

desc: Bill Williams Alligator indicator using Smoothed Moving Averages (SMMA/Wilder's smoothing). Three lines represent different timeframe trends: Jaw (slow), Teeth (medium), Lips (fast). When lines intertwine, the 'alligator sleeps' (ranging market). When they separate and align, the 'alligator feeds' (trending market).
usageContext: Identify trending vs ranging market conditions using Bill Williams' Alligator metaphor. The three SMMA lines (Jaw=13, Teeth=8, Lips=5) represent slow, medium, and fast trends. KEY STATES: (1) 'Alligator Sleeping': Lines intertwine and cross frequently - market is ranging, avoid trend-following entries. (2) 'Alligator Awakening': Lines begin to separate - potential trend start. (3) 'Alligator Feeding': Lines are well-separated and aligned (Lips > Teeth > Jaw for uptrend) - strong trend, hold positions. (4) 'Alligator Sated': Lines begin converging - trend weakening, prepare to exit. PIPELINE PATTERN: (1) Compute Alligator on daily OHLC, (2) detect alignment state (all three ascending = bullish, descending = bearish), (3) enter on Lips crossing above Teeth (bullish) or below (bearish), (4) exit when lines begin intertwining. EXAMPLES: (1) Trend entry: Wait for Alligator to 'awaken' after a sleep phase. Enter long when Lips crosses above Teeth AND Teeth above Jaw. Exit when Lips crosses back below Teeth. (2) Ranging filter: When Jaw-Lips spread < threshold, classify as ranging and suppress all trend-following signals, avoiding whipsaw losses. (3) Multi-timeframe: Compute on daily for direction, hourly for entry timing.
limitations: Lagging indicator due to SMMA smoothing - late entries in fast-moving markets. Performs poorly in choppy, sideways markets where lines frequently intertwine. apply_offset=true introduces data leak in backtesting (forward-shifted values). No built-in signal generation - requires interpretation rules. Less effective on low-liquidity assets with gappy price action.

name: Hurst Exponent (Expanding)

options.name: Minimum Period
options.desc: Minimum number of observations before computing Hurst exponent. First (min_period - 1) values will be null.
options.tuningGuidance: Use 20-50 for most applications. Higher values (100+) give more reliable estimates but delay the first output. Expanding window grows from min_period to full series length.

desc: Expanding-window Hurst exponent using rescaled range (R/S) analysis. Estimates the long-memory parameter H from the beginning of the series to each bar. H < 0.5 indicates mean-reverting behavior, H = 0.5 random walk, H > 0.5 trending/persistent. Uses lag grid {1, 2, 4, 8} for R/S calculation.
usageContext: Estimate the long-memory characteristic of a time series using expanding-window rescaled range (R/S) analysis, following Mandelbrot's (1971) methodology. The Hurst exponent H classifies market regimes into three categories: H < 0.5 (anti-persistent/mean-reverting), H = 0.5 (random walk/efficient), H > 0.5 (persistent/trending). KEY DIFFERENCE from rolling_hurst_exponent: This version uses an expanding window from the start of the series. It gives a progressively more stable estimate as data accumulates, but cannot detect regime changes. Use rolling_hurst_exponent for time-varying regime detection. Use this expanding version for establishing the long-term character of a series (e.g., 'is this asset fundamentally mean-reverting?'). PIPELINE PATTERN: (1) Compute expanding Hurst on price series to determine overall character, (2) if H < 0.45, deploy mean-reversion strategies (Bollinger Bands, zscore), (3) if H > 0.55, deploy trend-following strategies (moving average crossovers). EXAMPLES: (1) Strategy selection: Compute Hurst on 2 years of daily closes. H = 0.38 suggests the asset mean-reverts - prefer pairs trading or z-score strategies over momentum. (2) Asset screening: Compute expanding Hurst across a universe. Assets with H < 0.4 are strong mean-reversion candidates; H > 0.6 are trending candidates. (3) Pair validation: After identifying a cointegrated pair with engle_granger, compute Hurst on the spread. H << 0.5 confirms the spread mean-reverts.
limitations: Expanding window means the estimate becomes increasingly stable but cannot detect regime changes. Fixed lag grid {1, 2, 4, 8} may not be optimal for all time scales. Requires sufficient data (50+ bars) for meaningful estimates. Results depend on whether input is price levels vs returns - log prices recommended. Small sample bias tends to overestimate H. Not suitable for intraday data with market microstructure noise.

name: Accumulation/Distribution Oscillator
desc: Accumulation/Distribution Oscillator. Indicates momentum in the Accumulation/Distribution Line using two moving averages.
usageContext: MACD-style oscillator applied to the A/D line. Difference between short and long EMA of A/D. Positive values = accumulation momentum, negative = distribution momentum. Zero-line crossovers signal volume momentum shifts. PIPELINE PATTERN: compute adosc(), look for zero-line crossovers or divergences with price. EXAMPLE: adosc turning positive while price is at support = accumulation starting, potential long entry.
limitations: Double-lagging - smoothed version of already cumulative A/D line. Inherits all A/D limitations. Short/long period parameters need tuning. Less intuitive than raw OBV for quick volume analysis. Best as confirmation, not primary signal.

name: Economic Calendar

options.name: Data Source
options.desc: Data source: CalendarSource.FRED for economic release dates, CalendarSource.Treasury for Treasury auction calendar

options.name: FRED Release ID
options.desc: FRED release ID for specific release schedule. Common IDs: 50=NFP, 10=CPI, 53=GDP, 46=Retail Sales, 101=FOMC. Set to 0 for all releases.

options.name: Treasury Security Type
options.desc: Treasury security type: TreasurySecurityType.Note, .Bond, or .Bill. Only used when source=CalendarSource.Treasury.

options.name: Treasury Term
options.desc: Treasury term filter (e.g., TreasuryTerm.Y10, TreasuryTerm.W4). Only used when source=CalendarSource.Treasury. Omit or leave empty for all terms.

desc: Economic event calendar for macro event detection. FRED mode: release dates for major economic data (NFP, CPI, GDP). Treasury mode: auction dates and schedules.
usageContext: Use for event-driven strategies. FRED: economic_calendar(source=CalendarSource.FRED, release_id=50)().is_released for NFP dates. Treasury: economic_calendar(source=CalendarSource.Treasury, security_type=TreasurySecurityType.Note, term=TreasuryTerm.Y10)().is_released.
limitations: FRED releases: depends on FRED API availability. Treasury: TreasuryDirect API may have delays in publishing schedules.

name: Average Price
desc: Average Price. Calculates the average of open, high, low, and close prices.
usageContext: Simple average of OHLC: (O+H+L+C)/4. Provides a smoothed single price series incorporating all bar information. Use as input to other indicators instead of raw close for less noisy signals. PIPELINE PATTERN: compute avgprice(), feed into ma() or rsi() for smoother indicator output. EXAMPLE: rsi(avgprice()) is smoother than rsi(close).
limitations: Equal weighting of all four prices may not reflect actual trading activity (close is usually most important). Slightly lags close price. Consider typprice or wcprice for close-weighted alternatives.

name: Average Directional Movement Rating
desc: Average Directional Movement Rating. Smoothed version of ADX, provides trend direction information.
usageContext: Smoothed ADX - average of current ADX and ADX n periods ago. Reduces ADX whipsaws by providing a more stable trend strength reading. Same interpretation as ADX: >25 = trending, <20 = ranging. PIPELINE PATTERN: use adxr as smoother alternative to adx for regime filtering. EXAMPLE: only take trend-following signals when adxr > 25 for more stable filtering.
limitations: Even more lagging than ADX due to additional smoothing. Slower to react to trend changes. Same directional blindness as ADX - use DI for direction. Less commonly used than raw ADX. Consider ADX if faster response needed.

name: Awesome Oscillator
desc: Awesome Oscillator. Measures market momentum by comparing a 5-period and 34-period simple moving average.
usageContext: Bill Williams' momentum indicator. Difference between 5-period and 34-period SMA of median price ((H+L)/2). Positive = bullish momentum, negative = bearish. KEY SIGNALS: zero-line crossover, saucer (AO stays same side but dips and recovers), twin peaks divergence. PIPELINE PATTERN: compute ao(), look for saucer setups or zero crossovers. EXAMPLE: AO above zero + saucer (dip and recovery) = continuation buy.
limitations: Fixed 5/34 periods - not adjustable in standard implementation. Uses median price rather than close. Saucer pattern identification is subjective. Similar to MACD but less flexible. Best in trending markets, produces many false signals in ranges.

name: Absolute Price Oscillator
desc: Absolute Price Oscillator. Shows the difference between two exponential moving averages as an absolute value.
usageContext: Difference between fast and slow EMA in absolute price units. Positive = fast EMA above slow (bullish momentum). Same concept as MACD line but without signal line. PIPELINE PATTERN: compute apo(), use zero-line crossovers for trend direction. EXAMPLE: APO crossing above zero = bullish momentum starting.
limitations: Absolute values make cross-asset comparison impossible (use PPO instead). No signal line like MACD - fewer signal types. Simpler but less informative than MACD. Best used as a quick momentum check, not primary indicator.

name: Hidden Markov Model

options.name: Number of States
options.desc: Number of hidden states (regimes)

options.name: Max Iterations
options.desc: Maximum Baum-Welch iterations. 300 is usually sufficient for convergence.

options.name: Convergence Tolerance
options.desc: Stops training when log-likelihood improvement < tolerance. Default 1e-10 ensures thorough convergence.

options.name: Window Size
options.desc: Size of training window (for rolling) or minimum window (for expanding)
options.tuningGuidance: 252 (default): ~1 year of daily data. Use 126 (~6 months) for faster adaptation to regime changes but less training data. Use 504 (~2 years) for more stable models at the cost of slower adaptation. Rule of thumb: window should contain at least 10x the number of features. For intraday bars, scale proportionally.

options.name: Retrain Frequency
options.desc: How often to retrain: 21 = 21 bars, 1M = monthly, 1Y = yearly, 1W = weekly
options.tuningGuidance: 21 (default): Retrain monthly on daily data. Use 1 for every-bar retraining (expensive but most adaptive). Use 63 (quarterly) for slow-changing models. Duration syntax: '1M' = calendar month, '1W' = week, '21' = 21 bars. More frequent retraining = higher computational cost but faster adaptation.

options.name: Window Type
options.desc: Rolling uses fixed-size window; Expanding grows from start
options.tuningGuidance: rolling (default): Fixed-size training window that slides forward. Model sees only recent data, adapts to regime changes, but forgets old patterns. expanding: Training window grows from start (GKX 2020 methodology). Model sees all historical data, more stable but slower to adapt. Use expanding for long-term factor models; rolling for tactical/short-horizon strategies.

options.name: Min Training Samples
options.desc: Minimum samples required before first prediction
options.tuningGuidance: 100 (default): Reasonable minimum for most models. For LightGBM, use 200+ for stable tree construction. For logistic regression, 50 may suffice. Rule of thumb: min_training_samples >= 10 * num_features. Lower values start predictions sooner but risk unreliable early predictions.

desc: Hidden Markov Model with rolling/expanding window training. Adapts state transitions and emissions to evolving market dynamics.
usageContext: Use for adaptive sequential regime detection with temporal dependencies. Rolling variant of hmm — retrains on a sliding window.
limitations: State labels may swap between windows. Higher computational cost.

name: Bollinger Bands
desc: Bollinger Bands. Volatility bands placed above and below a moving average, adapting to market conditions.
usageContext: Three bands: middle (SMA), upper (+2 stddev), lower (-2 stddev). Mean-reversion: price at bands suggests overbought/oversold. Breakout: squeeze (narrow bands) precedes big moves. Price riding upper band = strong uptrend. Width measures volatility. Combine with %B indicator for normalized position. Use band walks for trend continuation.
limitations: Not directional on its own - just identifies extremes. Bands can expand indefinitely in trending markets (no fixed overbought/oversold). Squeeze detection requires bband_width. Default 20-period/2-stddev may need adjustment per asset. Can give false signals in strong trends when price 'walks the bands'.

name: Keltner Channels

options.name: Rolling Period
options.desc: Period for the EMA center line and ATR band width calculation
options.tuningGuidance: Standard 20 for daily charts. Use 10-15 for more responsive channels. Use 50 for long-term trend channels. Must match your trading timeframe.

options.name: Band Multiplier
options.desc: ATR multiplier for upper and lower band distance from center
options.tuningGuidance: Standard 2.0 ATR. Use 1.5 for tighter channels (more signals). Use 2.5-3.0 for wider channels (fewer but stronger breakout signals). In TTM Squeeze strategy, use 1.5 to compare with Bollinger Bands.

desc: ATR-based price channel developed by Chester Keltner (1960), modernized by Linda Raschke. Upper band = EMA + multiplier * ATR, Lower band = EMA - multiplier * ATR. Channel width adapts to volatility via ATR. Smoother than Bollinger Bands because ATR is less affected by individual outlier closes.
usageContext: ATR-based adaptive price channels for breakout detection, trend following, and volatility analysis. Developed by Chester Keltner (1960), modernized by Linda Bradford Raschke with ATR-based bands. KEY SIGNALS: (1) Price closing above upper band = strong bullish breakout. (2) Price closing below lower band = strong bearish breakout. (3) Price returning inside channels from outside = potential reversal. TTM SQUEEZE STRATEGY: When Bollinger Bands (2 std dev) move INSIDE Keltner Channels (1.5 ATR), volatility is compressed (squeeze). When Bollinger Bands expand back outside Keltner Channels, the squeeze fires and a large directional move is expected. KEY DIFFERENCE from Bollinger Bands: Keltner uses ATR (true range) rather than standard deviation. ATR is more stable because it incorporates gaps and intra-bar range. Result: smoother channels, fewer false breakout signals, but slightly slower to react to sudden volatility changes. PIPELINE PATTERN: (1) Compute Keltner Channels(20, 2.0), (2) classify price position: above upper = breakout, between bands = ranging, below lower = breakdown, (3) for TTM Squeeze, also compute Bollinger Bands and compare widths. EXAMPLES: (1) Trend entry: Price breaks above upper Keltner after squeeze = enter long. (2) Mean reversion: In ranging market, buy near lower channel, sell near upper. (3) TTM Squeeze: Bollinger inside Keltner for 6+ bars then expands = fire, enter in direction of momentum oscillator.
limitations: Only outputs upper and lower bands (no middle EMA line in output). ATR smoothing means the channel adapts slower than raw-range-based envelopes. Gap-heavy instruments may have persistently wide channels. The TTM Squeeze comparison requires computing Bollinger Bands separately. No built-in signal generation - interpretation rules needed.

name: Keyword Count

options.name: Keywords
options.desc: List of keyword patterns to count in text. 'patterns': array of strings (plain substrings or regex). 'case_sensitive': false by default. 'use_regex': false by default. Each pattern's occurrences are counted independently and summed. Example: {patterns: ["risk", "uncertainty"], case_sensitive: false}

desc: Count total occurrences of all keyword patterns in text. Returns integer. More granular than keyword_match — returns intensity (how many?) not just presence (any?). Academic: Jegadeesh & Wu (2013) demonstrate term-weighting in 10-K filings predicts returns; keyness analysis via log-likelihood ratio identifies statistically significant term frequencies. Use for risk intensity scoring, keyword frequency analysis, measuring signal strength from text.
usageContext:
ROLE: Quantifies text signal intensity via keyword frequency — counts how many times patterns appear.

KEY CHOICE -- keyword_count vs keyword_match: keyword_count returns intensity (integer: how many matches?) while keyword_match returns presence (boolean: any match at all?). Use keyword_count when signal strength/density matters; use keyword_match for simple event detection.

ACADEMIC: Jegadeesh & Wu (2013) "Word Power: A New Approach for Content Analysis" show term-weighting in 10-K filings predicts cross-sectional returns. Keyness analysis via log-likelihood ratio identifies statistically significant term frequencies vs background corpus.

USE CASES: Risk disclosure intensity in 10-K MD&A sections (count "risk", "uncertainty", "litigation"), FOMC minutes "uncertainty" mention frequency as macro signal, earnings call keyword attention metrics, media saturation measurement.

BEST PRACTICE: Normalize by text length for cross-document comparison (count / word_count). Forward-fill sparse news signals with ffill() for daily frequency.

EXAMPLES: (1) count "risk" occurrences in MD&A for disclosure intensity scoring. (2) sum bullish word frequency ["upgrade", "outperform", "beat"] in headlines. (3) measure litigation mention density ["lawsuit", "settlement", "damages"] across filings.
limitations: Counts all non-overlapping substring matches; does not weight by importance (use keyword_score for weighted counting). No text-length normalization built in — divide by word count externally for density. Forward-fill needed for sparse news data (news arrives irregularly). No TF-IDF weighting; all pattern occurrences weighted equally.

name: TIPP

options.name: Multiplier
options.desc: Cushion multiplier
options.tuningGuidance: 4.0 (default, higher than CPPI because ratcheting floor is more conservative). Same leverage mechanics as CPPI — higher = more aggressive above floor, faster deleveraging near floor.

options.name: Floor Percent
options.desc: Floor as percentage of max equity (ratcheting)
options.tuningGuidance: 0.85 (default) = locks in 85% of peak equity. 0.90-0.95 very conservative (locks 90-95% of peak). Lower values allow more room after drawdown from peak but protect less profit.

desc: Time-Invariant Portfolio Protection. Like CPPI but floor ratchets up with max equity. Floor = max_equity * floor_pct. More conservative than CPPI.
usageContext:
Time-Invariant Portfolio Protection (TIPP), introduced by Estep & Kritzman (1988).
Like CPPI but with a ratcheting floor that increases with the portfolio's high-water mark.

FORMULA: risky_allocation = multiplier * max(0, portfolio_value - floor)
where floor = max(floor_pct * initial_equity, floor_pct * max_equity_seen).

The key difference from CPPI is the RATCHETING FLOOR: as the portfolio reaches new highs,
the floor increases to lock in profits. The floor NEVER decreases, even if equity drops.

TIPP vs CPPI DECISION TREE:
- Want to protect initial capital only? -> Use CPPI (fixed floor).
- Want to protect accumulated profits? -> Use TIPP (ratcheting floor).
- TIPP is always more conservative than CPPI after a drawdown from highs, because its floor
  is higher (based on peak equity rather than initial equity).

EXAMPLES:
(1) Conservative: tipp(multiplier=3.0, floor_pct=0.90) -- 90% of peak equity as floor
(2) Standard: tipp(multiplier=4.0, floor_pct=0.85) -- 85% of peak, 4x cushion
(3) Aggressive: tipp(multiplier=5.0, floor_pct=0.75) -- 75% of peak, 5x cushion
limitations:
Floor only increases (ratchets up with high-water mark) and never decreases. This makes TIPP
progressively more conservative over time as the floor approaches current equity after a run-up
followed by drawdown. With high multipliers, allocation can exceed 100% (implicit leverage).
No inputs - reads equity from execution context automatically. Cannot reset the floor mid-strategy.

name: Cross-Sectional Selection

options.name: Direction
options.desc: Select top or bottom assets
options.tuningGuidance: top: long positions, momentum winners. bottom: short positions, value stocks.

options.name: Mode
options.desc: Selection mode: fixed count or percentage
options.tuningGuidance: count: fixed portfolio size. percent: adapts to universe size changes.

options.name: K Value
options.desc: Number of assets (count mode) or percentage (percent mode, 1-100)
options.tuningGuidance: Count: 3-5 concentrated, 10-30 diversified. Percent: 10-20% typical.

options.name: Group By
options.desc: Group assets before applying cross-sectional operation. When set, the transform operates within each group independently.
options.tuningGuidance: Use 'sector' for industry-neutral stock strategies. Use 'category' for futures. Use 'auto_detect' to let the system choose.

desc: Selects top or bottom K assets (by fixed count or percentage) at each timestamp. Returns a boolean mask where true indicates the selected assets. Foundation for long/short portfolio construction and quantile portfolio sorting.
usageContext: Core building block for cross-sectional portfolio construction. Replaces the legacy top_k, bottom_k, top_k_percent, and bottom_k_percent transforms with a unified interface. At each rebalance timestamp, cs_select evaluates all assets and returns a boolean mask indicating which are selected. LONG/SHORT CONSTRUCTION: Use two cs_select instances - direction=top for the long leg and direction=bottom for the short leg. Feed any scoring signal: momentum scores, z-scored fundamentals, composite alpha signals, or ML model predictions. MODE CHOICE - count vs percent:   count: Fixed portfolio size (e.g., always hold top 10). Simplest to implement.     Portfolio concentration stays constant regardless of universe changes. Standard     in academic factor studies (Fama-French use count-based decile sorts).   percent: Adaptive portfolio size (e.g., top 20% of universe). Automatically adjusts     when stocks enter/leave the universe. Better for live strategies with index     reconstitution. Used by MSCI factor indices and S&P sector rotation. K VALUE GUIDANCE: For count mode, k=3-5 gives concentrated exposure (higher tracking error, higher potential alpha). k=10-30 gives diversified factor exposure (lower idiosyncratic risk). For percent mode, k=10-20 is typical for quintile/decile sorts. EXAMPLES: (1) Momentum long/short: cs_select(direction=top, mode=count, k=10) on 12-month returns for the long leg. cs_select(direction=bottom, mode=count, k=10) for shorts. (2) Value quintile sort: cs_select(direction=top, mode=percent, k=20) on book-to-market z-scores to select the cheapest 20% of the universe each month. (3) ML-driven selection: Feed LightGBM predicted return scores into cs_select to pick the top k assets with highest predicted alpha at each rebalance. (4) Sector-neutral selection: Use group_by=sector to select top k within each sector, ensuring diversified sector exposure.
limitations: Requires the universe to contain more assets than k (count mode) or enough assets for the percentage to produce at least 1 selection. NaN/null values are excluded from ranking - an asset with NaN is never selected. In case of ties, selection among tied assets is arbitrary (implementation-dependent). For deterministic tie breaking, pre-sort with a secondary signal before feeding into cs_select.

name: Bollinger Bands Width
desc: Measures the width of Bollinger Bands to identify volatility expansion and contraction. Narrows during low volatility and widens during high volatility.
usageContext: Detect volatility squeezes (narrow width) that often precede large price moves. Calculate historical width percentile (percentrank of bband_width) to identify extreme compression — width below 20th percentile of its 252-bar range signals consolidation. Width expansion marks trend initiation — filter headfakes by requiring sustained expansion (2-3 bars of increasing width). Combine with %B for direction: expansion + %B > 0.8 = bullish breakout, expansion + %B < 0.2 = bearish.
limitations: Width alone doesn't indicate breakout direction. Requires additional confirmation. Width normalization differs across asset classes — equities typically have lower baseline width than commodities or crypto. Squeeze duration is unpredictable.

name: Linear Regression Intercept
desc: Linear Regression Intercept. Calculates the y-intercept values for linear regression analysis.
usageContext: Y-intercept of the rolling linear regression. Combined with linregslope, fully defines the regression line: value = intercept + slope * position. Useful for building custom regression-based indicators or channels. PIPELINE PATTERN: compute linregintercept + linregslope for custom regression line calculations.
limitations: Primarily a building block - rarely used directly for trading signals. Interpretation requires understanding of regression mathematics. Sensitive to period choice. Use linreg or tsf for more intuitive trend analysis.

name: Boxplot - ONE PER ASSET

options.name: Mode
options.desc: Mode: 'grouped' groups rows by label column, 'variadic' creates one box per input series

options.name: Chart Title
options.desc: Title for the generated boxplot

options.name: X Axis Label
options.desc: Label for the x-axis

options.name: Y Axis Label
options.desc: Label for the y-axis

options.name: Category
options.desc: Category for grouping in dashboard

options.name: Show Outliers
options.desc: Display outlier points beyond whiskers

options.name: Whisker IQR Multiplier
options.desc: IQR multiplier for whisker length (default: 1.5)

options.name: Box Colors
options.desc: Colors for each boxplot (e.g., Red, Blue, Success)

options.name: Fill Color
options.desc: Fill color for all boxes (overridden by per-box colors if specified)

options.name: Median Color
options.desc: Color of the median line

options.name: Median Width
options.desc: Width of the median line in pixels

options.name: Stem Color
options.desc: Color of the stem (vertical line from box to whisker)

options.name: Stem Width
options.desc: Width of the stem line in pixels

options.name: Whisker Color
options.desc: Color of the whisker lines

options.name: Whisker Width
options.desc: Width of the whisker lines in pixels

options.name: Whisker Length
options.desc: Length of whiskers as percentage (e.g., '50%', '75%')

options.name: Outlier Color
options.desc: Fill color of outlier markers

options.name: Outlier Line Color
options.desc: Border color of outlier markers

options.name: Outlier Line Width
options.desc: Border width of outlier markers in pixels

options.name: Outlier Radius
options.desc: Radius of outlier markers in pixels

options.name: Box Line Width
options.desc: Width of the box border in pixels

options.name: Show Data Labels
options.desc: Display median values on boxes

options.name: Data Label Format
options.desc: Format string for data labels (e.g., '{point.median}')

options.name: Y Axis Format
options.desc: Format type for Y axis values (Auto, Decimal, Percent, Monetary, Integer)

options.name: Y Axis Decimal Places
options.desc: Number of decimal places for Y axis values

options.name: X Category Type
options.desc: How to interpret X labels: Exact (as-is), Month (1-12→Jan-Dec), DayOfWeek (1-7→Mon-Sun), Quarter (1-4→Q1-Q4)

options.name: Display Order
options.desc: Display order within dashboard category (lower values appear first, 0 = default position)

options.name: Series Names
options.desc: Labels for each input series in variadic mode. ALWAYS provide this when using multiple inputs — without it, boxplot axes show raw internal IDs ($0, $1). One name per input (e.g., ['SMA 20', 'SMA 50']).

desc: Boxplot showing distribution statistics via quartiles, whiskers, and outliers. Two modes: (1) Grouped mode with (label, values) groups by label — one box per group, (2) Variadic mode with series_names option creates one boxplot per input series.
usageContext: Show DISTRIBUTION SUMMARY of numeric data as a box-and-whisker plot in the DASHBOARD view. Each box shows Q1, median, Q3 (the interquartile range), with whiskers extending to the data range within whisker_iqr * IQR (default 1.5×), and individual outlier dots beyond. This is the standard five-number-summary visualization used in every statistics and finance context. TRIGGER PHRASES: Use when the user asks for 'boxplot', 'box plot', 'box and whisker', 'whisker plot', 'quartile plot', 'distribution comparison', 'compare distributions', 'show the spread', 'median and IQR', 'outlier detection', 'five-number summary', 'compare grouped distributions', 'grouped boxplot', 'side-by-side distributions'. TWO MODES: (A) Grouped mode: provide label + values inputs. Rows are grouped by label, producing one box per unique label. Use when the user wants to compare distributions across categories (months, sectors, regimes, strategies). Group order is preserved from the data. This is the 'grouped boxplot' or 'side-by-side boxplot'. (B) Variadic mode: provide multiple value columns via NumericTuple + series_names option. Each column becomes a separate box. Use when comparing distributions of different metrics for the same asset (e.g., compare returns, volatility, Sharpe). BOXPLOT vs HISTOGRAM: Boxplot summarizes a distribution as five numbers + outliers, making it compact and ideal for SIDE-BY-SIDE COMPARISON of multiple distributions. Histogram shows the FULL SHAPE (skewness, bimodality, kurtosis) of ONE distribution. Use boxplot when comparing 3+ groups. Use histogram when the shape itself is the insight. Best practice: pair a histogram (for the detailed shape of the key metric) with a grouped boxplot (for the multi-group comparison) in the same dashboard category. BOXPLOT vs CARDS: Cards show single aggregate numbers (mean, std, max). Boxplot shows the full distributional shape in one compact glyph. Use cards for headline KPIs. Use boxplot when the user wants to see spread, skew, and outliers visually. BOXPLOT vs SUMMARY_TABLE: summary_table can show percentile rows (P25, P50, P75), but as numbers in a grid. Boxplot makes the same information VISUAL — differences in median, spread, and outliers are instantly readable. Use both together: boxplot for the visual, summary_table for exact numbers. BOXPLOT vs cs_boxplot: boxplot (this transform) is PER-ASSET — one chart per stock, groups are arbitrary labels. cs_boxplot is CROSS-SECTIONAL — one chart for ALL stocks, each asset is a box. Use boxplot when comparing categories within one asset. Use cs_boxplot when comparing distributions across assets. EXAMPLES: (1) Monthly return distributions: label=month_name, values=daily_returns. One box per month showing how daily returns are distributed in each month. Quickly reveals which months have higher volatility (wider boxes) or more outliers. (2) Regime comparison: label=regime_label (Bull/Bear/Sideways), values=daily_returns. Side-by-side boxes show how return distributions differ by market regime. The classic regime analysis visualization. (3) Strategy comparison: series_names=['Momentum','Value','Quality'], values=(momentum_returns, value_returns, quality_returns). Three boxes comparing factor return distributions. Shows which factor has higher median, tighter spread, or more extreme outliers. (4) Drawdown depth by year: label=year, values=drawdown_depth. Shows how severe drawdowns were in each year — widening boxes indicate increasing risk over time.
limitations: Dashboard widget, not the TV chart. Does not show the FULL distribution shape — for bimodality, kurtosis, or exact density use histogram. Does not support multiple overlaid distributions in one box (for that, use separate boxes via grouped mode). Single-asset only (isCrossSectional=false) — each asset gets its own boxplot chart. For cross-asset distribution comparison use cs_boxplot. No kernel density estimation (KDE) or fitted normal overlay — use bellcurve alongside for normality testing. Cannot show time evolution — for how a distribution changes over time, create separate grouped boxplots per period or use xy_lines of rolling statistics.

name: Chaikins Volatility
desc: Chaikins Volatility. Measures volatility by tracking the difference between high and low prices over a period.
usageContext: Measures rate of change of the high-low range EMA. OUTPUT SCALE: Pre-multiplied percentage (already x100). CVI = 10 means the range EMA increased 10%. CVI = -5 means 5% contraction. Zero-crossings signal volatility regime shifts. Positive = range expanding (volatility increasing), negative = range contracting. PIPELINE PATTERN: compute cvi(period=10), watch for transitions from negative to positive for breakout setups. EXAMPLE: cvi turning positive after extended negative = volatility expanding, potential breakout.
limitations: Based on high-low range only - doesn't account for gaps. Less smooth than ATR. Rate of change calculation adds noise. Less widely used than ATR or Bollinger Bands for volatility measurement.

name: Vertical Horizontal Filter
desc: Vertical Horizontal Filter. Identifies trending and ranging markets by measuring price direction versus volatility.
usageContext: Ratio of net price change to sum of absolute changes over a period. High VHF = trending (net change close to total change), low VHF = ranging (changes cancel out). Use to select strategy type: trend-following when VHF high, mean-reversion when low. PIPELINE PATTERN: compute vhf(period=28), switch between strategies based on VHF level. EXAMPLE: vhf > 0.5 = trending regime, use momentum strategies.
limitations: Threshold for trending vs ranging varies by asset and timeframe. Less popular than ADX for regime detection. No directional information. Can oscillate near threshold causing strategy-switching whipsaws. Consider ADX as more widely validated alternative.

name: Cross-Sectional Z-Score

options.name: Group By
options.desc: Group assets before applying cross-sectional operation. When set, the transform operates within each group independently.
options.tuningGuidance: Use 'sector' for industry-neutral stock strategies. Use 'category' for futures. Use 'auto_detect' to let the system choose.

desc: Normalizes each asset's value ACROSS assets at each timestamp, not over time. At each point in time, calculates: z_i = (value_i - mean_across_assets) / std_across_assets. Returns null when cross-sectional standard deviation is near zero.
usageContext: Fundamental preprocessing step in virtually every cross-sectional factor strategy. Transforms raw factor values into standardized scores with mean=0 and std=1 across the universe at each timestamp. This enables fair comparison and combination of factors measured in different units (e.g., P/E ratios vs momentum returns vs volatility estimates). KEY DIFFERENCE from time-series zscore: Regular zscore normalizes each asset independently over its own history (z = (x - rolling_mean) / rolling_std). cs_zscore normalizes ACROSS the universe at each point in time. Both are used in quant pipelines but answer different questions. Time-series zscore: 'is this asset's current value unusual relative to its own history?' Cross-sectional zscore: 'is this asset's current value unusual relative to its peers RIGHT NOW?' FACTOR PIPELINE: The standard Barra/MSCI multi-factor model pipeline is: (1) Compute raw factors (momentum, value, quality, etc.) per asset. (2) cs_winsorize to cap outliers (e.g., 5th/95th percentile). (3) cs_zscore to standardize. (4) Combine z-scored factors with equal or optimized weights into a composite. (5) cs_select or cs_rank on the composite for portfolio construction. This pipeline is used by Alphalens (Quantopian), Qlib (Microsoft), QuantConnect, and virtually all institutional quant platforms. EXAMPLES: (1) Multi-factor composite: z_score each factor independently, then average: composite = (cs_zscore(momentum) + cs_zscore(value) + cs_zscore(quality)) / 3. Feed composite into cs_select(direction=top, k=20) for long portfolio. (2) Statistical arbitrage: cs_zscore on price ratios. Assets with z > 2 are relatively expensive (short candidates), z < -2 are cheap (long candidates). (3) Sector-neutral z-scoring: Use group_by=sector to normalize within each sector, removing sector-level effects and isolating pure stock-specific signals.
limitations: Requires at least 3 assets (need >1 for meaningful standard deviation). Recommended 10+ assets for stable z-score estimates. Returns null/NaN when cross-sectional standard deviation is near zero (all assets have equal values). Sensitive to outliers - use cs_winsorize beforehand for robust normalization. Different from time-series zscore: normalizes ACROSS assets, not over time.

name: Directional Indicator
desc: Directional Indicator. Components of ADX that measure positive and negative price movement strength.
usageContext: Two outputs: +DI (positive directional indicator) and -DI (negative). OUTPUT SCALE: 0-100 (pre-multiplied percentage). +DI = 25 means 25% of price movement is upward. +DI > -DI = uptrend, -DI > +DI = downtrend. Crossovers signal trend direction changes. Combine with ADX for both direction and strength. PIPELINE PATTERN: compute di(), use +DI/-DI crossover filtered by adx > 25 for high-conviction trend entries. EXAMPLE: +DI crossing above -DI while ADX > 25 = strong bullish trend signal.
limitations: Crossovers can whipsaw in choppy markets without ADX filter. Lagging like all smoothed indicators. Based on Wilder's smoothing (similar to EMA). Default 14 period. Must be used with ADX to filter low-conviction signals.

name: Directional Movement
desc: Directional Movement. Identifies whether prices are trending by comparing consecutive highs and lows.
usageContext: Raw directional movement: +DM = current high - previous high (if positive and greater than -DM), -DM = previous low - current low (if positive and greater than +DM). Foundation for DI and ADX calculations. Rarely used directly - typically use DI or ADX instead. PIPELINE PATTERN: building block for custom directional indicators. EXAMPLE: use dm() for raw trend direction before smoothing into DI/ADX.
limitations: Raw values are noisy and not normalized. Primarily useful as a building block for DI and ADX rather than standalone. Zero values common (inside bars). Use DI or ADX for practical trading signals.

name: Detrended Price Oscillator
desc: Detrended Price Oscillator. Eliminates long-term trends to focus on short to medium-term cycles.
usageContext: Removes trend to isolate cyclical patterns. Computes price minus a displaced moving average. Positive = price above cycle midpoint, negative = below. Use to identify overbought/oversold within cycles. PIPELINE PATTERN: compute dpo(), identify cycles by zero crossings, buy at cycle troughs, sell at peaks. EXAMPLE: dpo crossing above zero after deep negative reading = cycle bottom.
limitations: Not a leading indicator despite removing trend. Displaced MA means last n/2 bars are estimates. Cycle identification is subjective. Doesn't work well when dominant cycle length changes. Best in markets with clear cyclical behavior.

name: Fisher Transform
desc: Fisher Transform. Converts prices to a Gaussian normal distribution to identify extreme price movements.
usageContext: Transforms price into a Gaussian normal distribution using inverse hyperbolic tangent. Output has clear turning points at extremes. Two lines: Fisher and Signal. Crossovers generate trade signals. Values above +1.5 or below -1.5 indicate extremes. PIPELINE PATTERN: compute fisher(), trade signal-line crossovers at extreme levels. EXAMPLE: Fisher crossing below signal above +2.0 = strong reversal short.
limitations: Can produce sharp, large-magnitude moves that trigger stops. Prone to false signals in strongly trending markets. Period sensitivity is high. Less intuitive than RSI. Extreme readings can persist in trends.

name: Forecast Oscillator
desc: Forecast Oscillator. Compares price to linear regression forecast value, indicating when price deviates from trend.
usageContext: Percentage difference between price and its linear regression forecast. Positive = price above regression (extended), negative = below (compressed). Use to identify when price overextends from its trend. PIPELINE PATTERN: compute fosc(), fade extreme readings back toward zero. EXAMPLE: fosc > +5% = price significantly above trend, potential mean-reversion short.
limitations: Based on linear regression which assumes linear trends. Period sensitivity affects which 'trend' is measured. Can stay extended in strong trends. Percentage output depends on regression accuracy.

name: Linear Regression Slope
desc: Linear Regression Slope. Measures the rate of change in linear regression values, indicating trend strength.
usageContext: Slope of the rolling linear regression - measures trend speed and direction. OUTPUT SCALE: Raw price units per bar — NOT normalized. A slope of 0.50 on a $100 stock means price increases $0.50/bar. Compare across instruments by dividing by price: normalized_slope = linregslope / price. Positive slope = uptrend, negative = downtrend. Magnitude indicates trend strength. Zero-crossings signal trend reversals. PIPELINE PATTERN: compute linregslope(period=20), use sign for trend direction and magnitude for strength. EXAMPLE: linregslope > 0 and increasing = accelerating uptrend.
limitations: Not normalized - slope magnitude depends on price level. Compare slopes across instruments by normalizing (divide by price). Sensitive to outliers at start and end of regression window. Consider R-squared for trend quality.

limitations: Computationally more expensive than static GARCH. Requires sufficient data in each window. step_size must be >= forecast_horizon.

name: Linear Regression
desc: Linear Regression. Plots a best-fit line through price data, showing overall direction of price movement.
usageContext: Rolling linear regression value - the predicted price at each point on the best-fit line. Acts as a dynamic support/resistance level. Price above linreg = bullish, below = bearish. PIPELINE PATTERN: compute linreg(period=20), use as trend filter or dynamic S/R. Add stderr bands for regression channels. EXAMPLE: buy when price pulls back to linreg from above, sell when breaks below.
limitations: Assumes linear relationship, which markets rarely maintain. Endpoint sensitivity - new data points can shift the line significantly. Less stable than moving averages. Consider using TSF for the forward-projected value instead.

name: CPPI

options.name: Multiplier
options.desc: Cushion multiplier (higher = more aggressive)
options.tuningGuidance: 3.0 (default) balanced risk/return. 1.5-2.0 conservative — slower leverage buildup, gentler deleveraging. 4.0-5.0 aggressive — faster leverage AND faster deleveraging near floor. Higher multiplier means more sensitivity to cushion changes in both directions.

options.name: Floor Percent
options.desc: Floor as percentage of initial equity (0.8 = 80%)
options.tuningGuidance: 0.80 (default) = 80% floor, tolerates 20% max drawdown. Set as 1 - max_acceptable_drawdown. 0.90 conservative (10% max DD), 0.70 aggressive (30% max DD). Floor is fixed at strategy start.

desc: Constant Proportion Portfolio Insurance. allocation = multiplier * max(0, equity - floor). Floor = initial_equity * floor_pct. Deleverages as equity approaches floor.
usageContext:
Constant Proportion Portfolio Insurance (CPPI), introduced by Black & Jones (1987) and
Perold (1986). Dynamically adjusts equity allocation based on a "cushion" above a fixed floor.

FORMULA: risky_allocation = multiplier * max(0, portfolio_value - floor)
where floor = initial_equity * floor_pct.

The multiplier controls aggressiveness: higher multiplier means more leverage when above floor
but faster deleveraging as equity drops toward floor. The floor is FIXED at strategy start
(based on initial equity) and never changes.

MULTIPLIER/FLOOR TRADEOFF:
- High multiplier (5) + high floor (0.90): Aggressive above floor but tight safety net.
- Low multiplier (2) + low floor (0.70): Conservative but more room before deleveraging.

WHEN TO USE vs TIPP: Use CPPI when you want a fixed floor based on initial capital (e.g.,
"never lose more than 20% of starting capital"). Use TIPP when you want the floor to ratchet
up with high-water marks (protecting profits).

EXAMPLES:
(1) Conservative: cppi(multiplier=2.0, floor_pct=0.90) -- 90% floor, 2x cushion
(2) Standard: cppi(multiplier=3.0, floor_pct=0.80) -- 80% floor, 3x cushion
(3) Aggressive: cppi(multiplier=5.0, floor_pct=0.70) -- 70% floor, 5x cushion
limitations:
Allocation goes to zero when equity reaches the floor (portfolio_value <= floor), and stays
at zero until equity recovers above floor. With high multipliers, allocation can exceed 100%
of equity (implicit leverage). No inputs - reads equity from execution context automatically.
Floor is static (set at strategy start from initial_equity * floor_pct) and never increases.

name: Chande Kroll Stop

options.name: ATR Period
options.desc: Period for ATR calculation used in initial stop distance
options.tuningGuidance: Standard 10. Shorter periods make stops tighter (more responsive). Longer periods create wider stops (more conservative, fewer whipsaws).

options.name: Stop Period
options.desc: Period for the highest/lowest of the initial stop levels
options.tuningGuidance: Standard 20. Controls how far back the stop tracks. Longer periods create trailing stops that are slower to tighten.

options.name: ATR Multiplier
options.desc: Multiplier for ATR to determine stop distance from extreme
options.tuningGuidance: Standard 3.0. Higher values give wider stops (hold through volatility). Lower values (1.5-2.0) for tighter stops with more frequent exits.

desc: Volatility-adaptive trailing stop system by Tushar Chande and Stanley Kroll. Uses ATR to set dynamic stop levels that trail price at a volatility-adjusted distance. Long stop trails below price during uptrends; short stop trails above during downtrends.
usageContext: Adaptive trailing stop system using ATR-based volatility bands, developed by Tushar Chande and Stanley Kroll. Automatically adjusts stop distance based on market volatility - wider stops in volatile markets, tighter in calm markets. KEY USAGE: (1) Exit management: Use long_stop as trailing stop for long positions - exit when price closes below long_stop. Use short_stop for short positions. (2) Entry signals: When price crosses above short_stop, bullish. When price crosses below long_stop, bearish. (3) Trend direction: When long_stop > short_stop, market is in uptrend. PIPELINE PATTERN: (1) Enter based on another indicator (Vortex, Alligator), (2) set initial stop at chande_kroll long_stop level, (3) trail the stop as long_stop rises during uptrend. Exit on stop hit. KEY DIFFERENCE from fixed ATR trailing stop: Chande-Kroll uses a two-step process (ATR stop, then highest/lowest of that stop) which creates a smoother, less reactive trailing stop that avoids premature exits. EXAMPLES: (1) Long position management: Enter long on breakout, set stop at long_stop. As price rises, long_stop trails up but never down. Exit when close < long_stop. (2) Direction filter: Only allow long entries when long_stop > short_stop, confirming uptrend environment.
limitations: Three parameters can be over-optimized. Wider stops (high multiplier) reduce whipsaws but increase drawdown per trade. Narrower stops increase trade frequency and costs. Not suitable for ranging markets where stops get hit repeatedly. ATR-based, so affected by overnight gaps and illiquid periods.

name: Mass Index
desc: Mass Index. Identifies potential reversals by examining high-low range expansion and contraction.
usageContext: Identifies potential trend reversals using range expansion/contraction cycles. KEY SIGNAL: 'reversal bulge' - Mass Index rises above 27 then falls below 26.5. This indicates range expansion followed by contraction, preceding a reversal. Direction determined by trend context, not the indicator. PIPELINE PATTERN: compute mass(period=25), watch for bulge pattern. EXAMPLE: mass rises above 27 then drops below 26.5 during uptrend = potential bearish reversal setup.
limitations: Only identifies potential reversal setups, not direction. Reversal bulge pattern is relatively rare. Fixed thresholds (27/26.5) may not work for all instruments. Requires trend analysis for directional context. Less versatile than ATR.

name: Maximum In Period
desc: Maximum In Period. Finds the maximum value in the specified period for each element position.
usageContext: Rolling maximum over a lookback window. Foundation for Donchian channels and highest-high breakout strategies. Use to identify resistance levels, compute rolling ranges (max - min), or detect new highs. PIPELINE PATTERN: compute max(period=20) as upper channel, enter long on breakout above. EXAMPLE: max(period=52) on weekly data gives 52-week high for trend context.
limitations: Lagging by definition - reports past maximum. Sensitive to outliers and spikes. Single extreme value dominates until it exits the window, causing step-function drops. Consider ATR-based levels for smoother boundaries.

name: Median Price
desc: Median Price. Simple average of the high and low prices for each period.
usageContext: Midpoint of bar range: (H+L)/2. Represents the center of trading activity for each bar. Used internally by Awesome Oscillator and some other indicators. Good proxy for 'fair value' within a bar. PIPELINE PATTERN: use medprice() as input to indicators for range-centered analysis. EXAMPLE: ma(medprice()) tracks the center of ranges rather than closing prices.
limitations: Ignores open and close entirely - misses directional information. Sensitive to wicks/shadows that may be noise. Less commonly used as standalone than typical price. Consider typprice for a version that includes close.

name: Money Flow Index
desc: Money Flow Index. Volume-weighted RSI that measures buying and selling pressure based on price and volume.
usageContext: Volume-weighted RSI - accounts for money flow not just price. MFI >80 = overbought with strong buying volume, <20 = oversold with strong selling volume. More reliable than RSI when volume confirms price moves. Use divergences (price new high but MFI doesn't = bearish). Failure swings (MFI fails to exceed previous high/low) signal reversals. Combine with RSI for confirmation.
limitations: Requires quality volume data - unreliable with sporadic/low volume. More parameters than RSI = more curve-fitting risk. Can give early signals in strong trends. 80/20 thresholds may need adjustment per asset. Lagging like RSI. Works best on liquid instruments with consistent volume. Consider volume profile analysis for illiquid assets.

name: Morning Doji Star
desc: Bullish reversal pattern with a down candle, followed by a doji gapped down, then an up candle gapped up. Stronger signal than Morning Star.
usageContext: Enhanced morning star where the middle candle is specifically a doji. Three candles: (1) bearish, (2) doji gapped down (total indecision at the bottom), (3) bullish closing into day 1. The doji middle candle makes this more reliable than standard morning star. PIPELINE PATTERN: detect morning_doji_star at support for high-probability long entries.
limitations: Rarer than standard morning star due to doji requirement. Gap requirement may not apply in all markets. Three-candle pattern develops slowly. Day 3 should close well into day 1 body for validity. Needs volume confirmation.

name: Minimum In Period
desc: Minimum In Period. Finds the minimum value in the specified period for each element position.
usageContext: Rolling minimum over a lookback window. Foundation for Donchian channels and lowest-low support strategies. Use to identify support levels, compute rolling ranges (max - min), or detect new lows. PIPELINE PATTERN: compute min(period=20) as lower channel, enter short on breakdown below. EXAMPLE: min(period=52) on weekly data gives 52-week low for trend context.
limitations: Lagging by definition - reports past minimum. Sensitive to flash crashes and outlier lows. Single extreme value dominates until it exits the window. Consider ATR-based levels for smoother support boundaries.

name: Mesa Sine Wave
desc: Mesa Sine Wave. Identifies market cycles using sine waves derived from price data.
usageContext: Ehlers' Mesa Sine Wave identifies market cycles using digital signal processing. Two outputs: sine and lead sine. Crossovers signal cycle turning points. When sine crosses above lead = cycle bottom (buy). When sine crosses below lead = cycle top (sell). PIPELINE PATTERN: compute msw(), trade sine/lead crossovers. EXAMPLE: sine crossing above lead sine = cycle trough, anticipate upswing.
limitations: Assumes markets have dominant cycles, which isn't always true. Works best in clearly cyclical markets. Can produce false signals in trending markets without clear cycles. Complex underlying math. Period parameter critical for cycle detection accuracy.

name: Black Marubozu
desc: Bearish candle with no upper or lower shadows (wicks). Strong selling pressure with opening at high and closing at low.
usageContext: Complete seller dominance - opened at high and closed at low with zero wicks. Strongest single-candle bearish signal. Sellers controlled the entire session without any buyer pushback. In downtrend = strong continuation. At support = decisive breakdown. PIPELINE PATTERN: detect black_marubozu, use as high-conviction bearish signal. EXAMPLE: black_marubozu at key support = strong breakdown confirmation.
limitations: Very rare with strict no-shadow requirement. Wick threshold is configurable but affects frequency. Can appear as capitulation selling (potential bottom). Single candle - always confirm with next candle and context.

name: Normalized Average True Range
desc: Normalized Average True Range. ATR expressed as a percentage of closing price, allowing comparison across securities.
usageContext: ATR as percentage of closing price: (ATR / close) * 100. Enables volatility comparison across different price levels and instruments. NATR of 2% means average true range is 2% of price. Use for position sizing: allocate inversely proportional to NATR. PIPELINE PATTERN: compute natr(period=14), rank assets by NATR for volatility-based portfolio allocation. EXAMPLE: NATR = 1.5% = low volatility, NATR = 5% = high volatility, size positions accordingly.
limitations: Same lag as ATR - based on past volatility. Percentage normalization can be misleading near zero or for very low-priced instruments. Not suitable for instruments with negative values. Consider realized volatility for more standard statistical measure.

name: Negative Volume Index
desc: Negative Volume Index. Shows price movements on days when volume decreases, highlighting smart money activity.
usageContext: Tracks price changes only on days when volume decreases from the prior day. Theory: smart money operates on low-volume days. Rising NVI = smart money bullish. NVI above its 255-day MA = historically 96% chance of bull market. PIPELINE PATTERN: compute nvi(), apply ma(period=255), use crossovers for long-term bull/bear signals. EXAMPLE: NVI crossing above its 255-day MA = long-term bullish regime.
limitations: Very long-term indicator - not suitable for short-term trading. The smart money theory is debatable. Cumulative nature makes values path-dependent. Requires very long history for MA signals. Binary volume classification (up/down) is simplistic. Rarely used as standalone indicator.

name: On Balance Volume
desc: On Balance Volume. Running total of volume that adds when price rises and subtracts when price falls.
usageContext: Cumulative volume indicator for confirming trends and spotting divergences. Rising OBV with rising price = healthy uptrend (volume confirms). OBV diverging from price = potential reversal (e.g., price makes new high but OBV doesn't = bearish divergence). Use to identify accumulation/distribution phases. Most powerful for divergence detection.
limitations: Cumulative nature means scale can be misleading - focus on direction and divergences not absolute values. Doesn't account for volume magnitude of individual bars. Can be distorted by large volume spikes. Best on liquid assets with consistent volume. Requires long history to establish baseline. Consider normalizing or using rate of change.

name: Percentage Price Oscillator
desc: Percentage Price Oscillator. Shows relationship between two moving averages as a percentage, similar to MACD.
usageContext: Percentage difference between fast and slow EMA: (fast - slow) / slow * 100. Same concept as MACD but normalized as percentage, enabling cross-asset comparison. Positive = bullish momentum, negative = bearish. PIPELINE PATTERN: compute ppo(), compare momentum across assets or use zero-line crossovers. EXAMPLE: PPO > 0 for stock A and < 0 for stock B = relative strength favors A.
limitations: No signal line in standard implementation (unlike MACD). Percentage normalization helps comparison but removes absolute magnitude information. Same lag issues as MACD. Less widely used than MACD despite better normalization.

name: Parabolic SAR
desc: Parabolic SAR. Identifies potential reversals in price movement, providing entry and exit signals.
usageContext: Trailing stop-and-reverse system by Welles Wilder. Dots below price = uptrend, above = downtrend. When price crosses SAR, trend reverses and SAR flips sides. Acceleration factor increases as trend progresses, tightening the trailing stop. PIPELINE PATTERN: compute psar(), use SAR flips as entry/exit signals. EXAMPLE: SAR flipping from above to below price = bullish reversal signal, enter long.
limitations: Whipsaws heavily in ranging markets - generates many false reversals. Fixed acceleration factor parameters may not suit all markets. Always in the market (long or short) - no neutral position. Works best in strongly trending markets. Combine with ADX to filter ranges.
